async def call_llm(prompt: str):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        r = await client.post("http://llm/generate", json={"prompt": prompt})
        return r.json()["answer"]

@app.post("/ask")
async def ask(question: str):
    emb = await embed(question)
    docs = await search_vector_db(emb)

    context = "\n".join(docs)
    prompt = f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}\nAnswer:"
    answer = await call_llm(prompt)

    return {"answer": answer}
  • Why asyncio is better here
    • Each step is network I/O-bound.
    • Async allows thousands of concurrent users with fewer OS threads.
    • Lower latency under load and better resource utilization.

In summary:

  • Threading: OS threads, good for blocking I/O, limited by GIL for CPU-bound work.
  • asyncio: Single-threaded event loop with coroutines, excellent for high-concurrency I/O-bound workloads, especially modern LLM/RAG backends.
Q14.WHAT ARE PYTHON METACLASSES? [Input Token: 705 | Output Token: 3270] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:

    • In Python, metaclasses are “classes of classes.”
    • A metaclass controls how classes are created, just like a class controls how its instances are created.
    • By default, all new-style classes use type as their metaclass.

  • Why important in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:

    • Used to build framework-like abstractions (e.g., model registries, configuration systems, ORM-like layers for models).
    • Useful for auto-registration of models, schema validation, or enforcing interfaces in ML pipelines.
    • Shows deep understanding of Python internals, which matters when building complex ML/GenAI libraries.

  • Why important in Python/Rust backend interviews:

    • Used in ORMs (Django, SQLAlchemy), framework internals, and declarative APIs.
    • Demonstrates ability to design declarative DSLs, plugin systems, and framework-level abstractions.
    • Rust doesn’t have metaclasses, but similar patterns appear via macros, derive, and traits; comparing them shows strong systems design understanding.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • Normal OOP:

    • You define a class → Python uses the class to create objects.
    • Example:
      class Model:
    pass

m = Model()  # instance of Model

  • With metaclasses:

    • You define a class → Python uses a metaclass to create that class object.
    • The class itself is an instance of a metaclass.
    • Example:
      class Model(metaclass=MyMeta):
    pass
    • Here:
      • Model is an instance of MyMeta
      • m = Model() is an instance of Model

  • Key idea:

    • Metaclass customizes:
      • How the class is constructed (via __new__ / __init__)
      • What attributes/methods the class has
      • Registration, validation, modification of class attributes
      • Enforcing patterns (e.g., all models must define predict)

  • Core mechanisms:

    • type is the built-in metaclass:
      • type(name, bases, namespace) → creates a new class.
    • Custom metaclass:
      • Subclass type
      • Override __new__ and/or __init__
      • Optionally override __call__ to customize instance creation.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Metaclass (subclass of type):

    • __new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace)
    • __init__(cls, name, bases, namespace)
    • __call__(cls, *args, **kwargs) (controls instance creation)

  • Class using metaclass:

    • Declared with metaclass=:
      class MyClass(Base, metaclass=MyMeta):
    ...

  • Instances:

    • Created as usual: obj = MyClass(...)
    • But behavior may be influenced by metaclass logic.

Technologies / Context in AI/ML/GenAI

  • Python frameworks:
    • Django ORM: ModelBase metaclass for models.Model
    • SQLAlchemy: DeclarativeMeta for declarative models
    • Pydantic v1: ModelMetaclass for model validation
  • ML/GenAI-specific uses:
    • Auto-registering model classes for:
      • LLM tools
      • Prompt templates
      • Vector store adapters
    • Enforcing that every pipeline step implements certain methods (fit, transform, predict).

Data Flow and Processing Stages (Conceptual)

  • Class definition time:

    • Python reads class body → builds a namespace dict.
    • Python calls metaclass.__new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace).
    • Optionally calls metaclass.__init__(cls, name, bases, namespace).

  • Instance creation time:

    • When you call the class: obj = MyClass(...)
    • Python invokes MyClass.__call__ (inherited from metaclass).
    • Usually type.__call__ → __new__ → __init__ on the instance.
    • Custom metaclass can change this flow.

API Endpoints / Contracts (Conceptual)

  • For a framework-style design, your metaclass contract might be:

    • Input:

      • name: class name string
      • bases: base classes tuple
      • namespace: class attributes dict

    • Output:

      • A fully constructed class object with:
        • Extra attributes
        • Registration in a global registry
        • Validated schema

    Example for a model registry in an ML system:

    MODEL_REGISTRY = {}

class ModelMeta(type):
    def __new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace):
        cls = super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace)
        if not name.startswith("_"):
            MODEL_REGISTRY[name] = cls
        return cls

Model Lifecycle Integration

  • Training:
    • Metaclasses can enforce that all model classes implement train, save, load.
  • Evaluation:
    • Automatically add evaluation hooks or metrics attributes.
  • Deployment:
    • Auto-register classes to a factory used by a REST API or inference service.
  • Monitoring:
    • Inject logging, tracing, or metrics decorators at class creation time.

Scalability Considerations

  • Metaclasses operate at class creation time, not per request:
    • Overhead is usually small and one-time.
  • Useful for:
    • Large codebases where many model types or pipeline steps must follow consistent rules.
    • Maintaining extensible plugin architectures in ML/GenAI systems.

Performance Considerations

  • Avoid heavy work in metaclass __new__/__init__:
    • Do not load big models or datasets there.
    • Keep it to validation, registration, light transformations.
  • Instance creation (__call__) can affect runtime performance if overridden heavily.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart TD
    A[Write class definition<br>class MyModel(Base, metaclass=MyMeta): ...] --> B[Python collects class body<br>into namespace dict]
    B --> C[Determine metaclass<br>MyMeta or inherited]
    C --> D[Call MyMeta.__new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace)]
    D --> E[Create class object<br>cls = MyModel]
    E --> F[Optional: MyMeta.__init__(cls, name, bases, namespace)]
    F --> G[Class ready to use<br>MyModel in code]
    G --> H[Instance creation<br>obj = MyModel(...)]
    H --> I[MyMeta.__call__(cls, *args, **kwargs)]
    I --> J[Instance obj of MyModel]

Step-by-Step Flow

Step 1: Class Definition

  • You write:
    class MyModel(BaseModel, metaclass=ModelMeta):
    lr = 0.01
    def train(self, data): ...
  • Python:
    • Creates namespace = {'lr': 0.01, 'train': <function ...>}
    • Determines metaclass = ModelMeta

Step 2: Class Creation via Metaclass

  • Python calls:
    cls = ModelMeta.__new__(ModelMeta, "MyModel", (BaseModel,), namespace)
ModelMeta.__init__(cls, "MyModel", (BaseModel,), namespace)
  • In __new__ / __init__, you can:
    • Validate presence of train
    • Register MyModel into a registry
    • Add helper methods, properties, or metadata

Step 3: Instance Creation

  • When you do:
    model = MyModel()
  • Python calls:
    ModelMeta.__call__(MyModel, *args, **kwargs)
  • Which usually:
    • Creates an instance (__new__)
    • Initializes it (__init__)

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

Python: Basic Custom Metaclass

class InterfaceCheckingMeta(type):
    def __new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace):
        # Skip base abstract class
        cls = super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace)
        if name != "BaseStep":
            required_methods = ["fit", "transform"]
            for method in required_methods:
                if method not in namespace:
                    raise TypeError(f"{name} must implement {method}()")
        return cls


class BaseStep(metaclass=InterfaceCheckingMeta):
    pass


class StandardScaler(BaseStep):
    def fit(self, X):
        ...

    def transform(self, X):
        ...
  • This ensures all pipeline steps implement fit and transform.

Python: Model Registry for GenAI Pipelines

MODEL_REGISTRY = {}

class ModelMeta(type):
    def __new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace):
        cls = super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace)
        # Avoid registering abstract/base classes
        if not namespace.get("__abstract__", False):
            MODEL_REGISTRY[name] = cls
        return cls


class BaseLLM(metaclass=ModelMeta):
    __abstract__ = True
    def generate(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError


class OpenAILLM(BaseLLM):
    def generate(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        # call OpenAI API
        ...


class LocalLLM(BaseLLM):
    def generate(self, prompt: str) -> str:
        # call local model via vLLM or Text-Generation-Inference
        ...


# Factory usage
def get_llm(name: str) -> BaseLLM:
    return MODEL_REGISTRY[name]()

Rust Analogy

  • Rust doesn’t have metaclasses, but similar compile-time abstraction patterns:
    • Traits: enforce interfaces.
    • Macros / derive macros: generate boilerplate, auto-registration.
    • Attribute macros to transform types at compile time.
  • Example analogy: a Rust #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] macro plays a similar meta-programming role as a Python metaclass that injects serialization methods.

Advantages

  • Enforce contracts:
    • Ensure certain methods/attributes exist on classes.
  • Declarative DSLs:
    • Create clean declarative APIs like Django models, Pydantic, SQLAlchemy.
  • Auto-registration:
    • Build plugin systems and registries for:
      • ML models
      • Vector store connectors
      • RAG pipeline components
  • Code reduction:
    • Inject boilerplate into classes at creation time.
  • Framework building:
    • Ideal for designing internal ML/GenAI frameworks and libraries.

Limitations

  • Complexity:
    • Harder to read and debug; many devs are unfamiliar with them.
  • Overuse risk:
    • Can make code “magic-heavy” and opaque.
  • Tooling:
    • Static analysis and IDEs may struggle with heavy metaclass magic.
  • Testing:
    • Errors occur at class definition time, not instance time, which can confuse newcomers.
  • Alternatives:
    • Often, class decorators, simple factory functions, or composition are simpler.

Interview Tips

  • Key points to remember:

    • A metaclass is a class factory.
    • Default metaclass is type.
    • You create a metaclass by subclassing type.
    • Main methods: __new__, __init__, __call__.
    • Major real-world use: Django models, SQLAlchemy, Pydantic.

  • Common interview questions:

    • What is a metaclass and why would you use one?
    • How is type related to metaclasses?
    • Show a simple example of a metaclass enforcing an interface.
    • Compare metaclasses vs class decorators.
    • Where do you see metaclasses in popular Python frameworks?

  • Tricky areas:

    • Understanding the three levels:
      • Instance → Class → Metaclass
    • Distinguishing class creation time vs instance creation time.
    • Overriding __new__ vs __init__ in metaclasses.

  • Good concise explanation for interviews:

    • “A metaclass is the class of a class. It defines how classes are constructed. In Python, type is the default metaclass. By subclassing type, I can enforce contracts, auto-register classes, or inject behavior at class creation time—similar to how frameworks like Django and Pydantic work.”

Real-World Example

Use Case: RAG Pipeline Component Registry

  • You want a pluggable RAG system:
    • Different components:
      • Embedder (e.g., OpenAI, sentence-transformers)
      • Vector store (e.g., Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant)
      • Retriever strategies
    • You want new components to be auto-registered.
RAG_COMPONENTS = {
    "embedder": {},
    "vector_store": {},
    "retriever": {},
}

class RAGComponentMeta(type):
    def __new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace):
        cls = super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace)
        kind = namespace.get("COMPONENT_KIND")
        if kind and not namespace.get("__abstract__", False):
            RAG_COMPONENTS[kind][name] = cls
        return cls


class BaseEmbedder(metaclass=RAGComponentMeta):
    __abstract__ = True
    COMPONENT_KIND = "embedder"
    def embed(self, text: str): raise NotImplementedError


class OpenAIEmbedder(BaseEmbedder):
    def embed(self, text: str):
        # call OpenAI embeddings API
        ...


class SentenceTransformersEmbedder(BaseEmbedder):
    def embed(self, text: str):
        # use local transformer model
        ...


# Usage in backend (FastAPI):
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/embed")
def embed(text: str, embedder_name: str = "OpenAIEmbedder"):
    EmbedderCls = RAG_COMPONENTS["embedder"][embedder_name]
    embedder = EmbedderCls()
    return {"embedding": embedder.embed(text)}
  • This pattern:
    • Enables easy plugin-based architecture for GenAI backends.
    • Keeps the API layer simple and decoupled from concrete implementations.
    • Uses metaclasses to centralize knowledge of available components.
Q15.EXPLAIN PYTHON'S MRO (METHOD RESOLUTION ORDER? [Input Token: 709 | Output Token: 2974] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:
    Python’s MRO (Method Resolution Order) is the algorithm Python uses to determine which class’s method/attribute gets called first when multiple inheritance is involved.
  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:
    • Many ML/GenAI frameworks (e.g., PyTorch, FastAPI-based services, LangChain components) use complex class hierarchies and mixins.
    • Understanding MRO helps debug behavior when overriding methods in models, trainers, callbacks, or pipeline components.
  • Importance in Python/Rust backend interviews:
    • Critical when designing framework-style code, mixins, plugins, or service base classes.
    • Helps avoid subtle bugs in large backend systems with multiple inheritance.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • Core idea:
    • When you call obj.method(), Python searches for method following a specific linear order of classes.
    • This order is computed by the C3 linearization algorithm for new-style classes (all modern Python classes).
  • Key points:
    • Uses depth-first, left-to-right, but with constraints to keep inheritance consistent.
    • Ensures:
      • Local precedence: Left base classes are preferred over right ones.
      • Monotonicity: Subclass MRO respects the order of parent MROs.
      • No ambiguity: Raises TypeError if no consistent order exists.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Classes:
    • Single inheritance: class B(A): ...
    • Multiple inheritance: class C(A, B): ...
  • MRO-related components:
    • __mro__ attribute (tuple of classes)
    • mro() method (returns the same order as a list)
    • C3 linearization algorithm (internal to CPython)

Technologies / Context in AI/ML

  • Python frameworks:
    • PyTorch: nn.Module subclasses + custom mixins for logging, checkpointing.
    • FastAPI: dependency classes mixing base handlers and utility mixins.
    • LangChain / LlamaIndex: composable classes with multiple inheritance for tools, chains, retrievers.
  • Backend services:
    • Custom BaseService, AuthMixin, LoggingMixin, etc.

Data Flow & Processing (Conceptual)

  • When calling obj.method():
    • Python:
      • Looks at obj.__class__.__mro__
      • Searches each class in that order
      • Uses the first class where method is found

Model Lifecycle / Code Lifecycle Context

  • Training / Pipeline classes:
    • You might have BaseTrainer, LoggingMixin, CheckpointMixin, etc.
    • MRO determines which train() or save() method is used.
  • Deployment / Serving:
    • Custom request handlers using multiple inheritance for auth, rate limiting, logging.
    • MRO decides which dispatch() or handle() is invoked.

Scalability & Performance Considerations

  • MRO computation:
    • Done once per class definition (class creation time).
    • Lookup using __mro__ is O(N) where N is number of classes in the hierarchy (usually small).
  • In practice:
    • Overhead is negligible compared to network/IO/ML inference.
    • Important for correctness, not performance.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

Example Multiple Inheritance

classDiagram
    class A {
      +method()
    }
    class B {
      +method()
    }
    class C {
      +method()
    }
    class D {
    }

    A <|-- C
    B <|-- C
    A <|-- D
    C <|-- D
  • Suppose:
class A: 
    def method(self): print("A")

class B(A):
    def method(self): print("B")

class C(A):
    def method(self): print("C")

class D(B, C):
    pass
  • MRO of D is:
D.__mro__ == (D, B, C, A, object)

Step-by-Step Flow

1. How Python Finds a Method

  • Step 1: Get the class of the instance:
    • cls = obj.__class__
  • Step 2: Get the MRO:
    • order = cls.__mro__ or cls.mro()
  • Step 3: Scan in order:
    • For each class in order:
      • If method in class’s __dict__, use that implementation.
      • Stop at the first match.

2. How MRO is Computed (C3 Linearization – Intuition)

Given:

class D(B, C)
  • Inputs:
    • D’s parents: [B, C]
    • B’s MRO: B.__mro__
    • C’s MRO: C.__mro__
  • C3 algorithm merges:
    • D + merge(MRO(B), MRO(C), [B, C])
  • Constraints:
    • Preserve parent order (B before C).
    • Preserve each parent’s own MRO.
    • No class appears twice.

3. Simple Examples

Single inheritance

class A: ...
class B(A): ...
class C(B): ...

C.__mro__  # (C, B, A, object)

Diamond inheritance

class A: ...
class B(A): ...
class C(A): ...
class D(B, C): ...

D.__mro__  # (D, B, C, A, object)

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

Python: Inspecting and Using MRO

class A:
    def who(self): print("A")

class B(A):
    def who(self): print("B")

class C(A):
    def who(self): print("C")

class D(B, C):
    pass

d = D()

print(D.__mro__)   # (<class '__main__.D'>, <class '__main__.B'>, <class '__main__.C'>, <class '__main__.A'>, <class 'object'>)
print(D.mro())     # same, as a list

d.who()            # Output: "B" (B wins over C due to MRO)

Example with Mixins in an ML/Backend Context

class LoggingMixin:
    def save(self):
        print("LoggingMixin.save")
        super().save()

class CheckpointMixin:
    def save(self):
        print("CheckpointMixin.save")
        super().save()

class BaseModel:
    def save(self):
        print("BaseModel.save")

class Model(LoggingMixin, CheckpointMixin, BaseModel):
    pass

print(Model.mro())
# [Model, LoggingMixin, CheckpointMixin, BaseModel, object]

m = Model()
m.save()
# LoggingMixin.save
# CheckpointMixin.save
# BaseModel.save
  • MRO controls the order of mixin behavior chaining via super().

Python: Using super() Correctly with MRO

  • Modern pattern: always call super() in cooperative multiple inheritance:
class A:
    def process(self):
        print("A")
        super().process()

class B(A):
    def process(self):
        print("B")
        super().process()

class C(A):
    def process(self):
        print("C")
        super().process()

class D(B, C):
    def process(self):
        print("D")
        super().process()

class Base:
    def process(self):
        print("Base")

D.__mro__  # (D, B, C, A, Base, object)

Rust Contrast (Why MRO is Python-Specific)

  • Rust:
    • No classical OOP inheritance; uses traits and composition.
    • No MRO because there is no multiple inheritance of implementation.
    • Trait method conflicts are resolved explicitly by fully-qualified syntax:
      trait A { fn foo(&self); }
trait B { fn foo(&self); }

struct S;

impl A for S { fn foo(&self) { println!("A"); } }
impl B for S { fn foo(&self) { println!("B"); } }

fn main() {
    let s = S;
    A::foo(&s); // explicitly choose
    B::foo(&s);
}
  • Interview angle:
    • Python uses MRO for dynamic multiple inheritance.
    • Rust avoids this class of problems via traits and explicit disambiguation.

Advantages

  • Predictable method lookup:
    • Deterministic, consistent order across the class hierarchy.
  • Supports multiple inheritance safely:
    • C3 linearization avoids ambiguous resolutions.
  • Enables mixin patterns:
    • Clean composition of behaviors (LoggingMixin, AuthMixin, etc.).
  • Works seamlessly with super():
    • Cooperative multiple inheritance allows chaining behaviors.

Limitations

  • Complexity in deep hierarchies:
    • MRO can be hard to reason about with many mixins.
  • Subtle bugs if super() is not used consistently:
    • One class not calling super() breaks the chain.
  • Can produce TypeError if inheritance graph is inconsistent:
    • E.g., conflicting orders that cannot be linearized.
  • Readability:
    • Overuse of multiple inheritance makes code harder to understand and maintain.

Interview Tips

  • Key points to remember:
    • MRO is the order Python uses to search for attributes/methods.
    • Modern Python classes use C3 linearization.
    • Inspect using Class.__mro__ or Class.mro().
    • MRO is especially important when:
      • Using multiple inheritance.
      • Using super() in mixins / base classes.
  • Common interview questions:
    • “Explain Python’s MRO and how it works with multiple inheritance.”
    • “What is C3 linearization?”
    • “Given this class hierarchy, what is the MRO?” (They may ask you to compute it.)
    • “Why does super() behave differently in multiple inheritance?”
    • “How does MRO influence mixin design?”
  • Tricky areas:
    • Diamond inheritance:
      class A: ...
class B(A): ...
class C(A): ...
class D(B, C): ...
      • Why MRO is (D, B, C, A, object) and not something else.
    • super() in multiple inheritance:
      • It follows MRO, not “parent” in the source code sense.
    • Inconsistent MRO:
      class X: ...
class Y: ...
class A(X, Y): ...
class B(Y, X): ...
class C(A, B): ...  # TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order

Real-World Example

Use Case: RAG/LLM Service with Mixins

  • Suppose you build a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) service with a class hierarchy:
class LoggingMixin:
    def handle_request(self, req):
        print("log request")
        return super().handle_request(req)

class AuthMixin:
    def handle_request(self, req):
        print("auth check")
        return super().handle_request(req)

class RateLimitMixin:
    def handle_request(self, req):
        print("rate limit")
        return super().handle_request(req)

class BaseRAGHandler:
    def handle_request(self, req):
        print("run RAG pipeline")
        # 1. embed query
        # 2. search vector DB
        # 3. call LLM
        return "answer"
  • Compose them:
class RAGHandler(LoggingMixin, AuthMixin, RateLimitMixin, BaseRAGHandler):
    pass

print(RAGHandler.mro())
# [RAGHandler, LoggingMixin, AuthMixin, RateLimitMixin, BaseRAGHandler, object]

handler = RAGHandler()
resp = handler.handle_request({"query": "What is MRO?"})

  • Execution order (due to MRO):

    • LoggingMixin.handle_request
    • AuthMixin.handle_request
    • RateLimitMixin.handle_request
    • BaseRAGHandler.handle_request

  • In a FastAPI backend:

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request

app = FastAPI()
rag_handler = RAGHandler()

@app.post("/rag")
async def rag_endpoint(request: Request):
    body = await request.json()
    return {"answer": rag_handler.handle_request(body)}
  • Why MRO matters here:
    • Controls the order of logging → auth → rate limiting → RAG pipeline.
    • Changing inheritance order changes behavior:
      class RAGHandler(AuthMixin, LoggingMixin, RateLimitMixin, BaseRAGHandler):
    ...
    • Now MRO changes and so does the call chain.

In interviews, be ready to:

  • Define MRO clearly.
  • Show how to inspect it (__mro__, mro()).
  • Explain diamond inheritance and C3 linearization at a high level.
  • Connect MRO to super() and mixin design in real backend/ML/GenAI systems.
Q16.HOW DO YOU OPTIMIZE PYTHON PERFORMANCE? [Input Token: 706 | Output Token: 3075] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition
    Optimization of Python performance means improving:

    • Execution speed (latency, throughput)
    • Memory usage
    • CPU/GPU utilization
    • I/O efficiency
      using better algorithms, data structures, libraries, and architecture.

  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews

    • Training/inference pipelines are often Python-heavy (NumPy, PyTorch, TensorFlow, LangChain).
    • Performance directly impacts:
      • Training time
      • Inference latency
      • Cost of serving LLMs / RAG systems.
    • Shows you understand how to go from “works” to “production-grade”.

  • Importance in Python/Rust Backend interviews

    • Python is often the orchestration layer; Rust handles critical paths.
    • Need to design services that:
      • Scale under load
      • Stay responsive (low latency APIs)
      • Efficiently use resources (CPU, memory, network).

Architecture / Concept Explanation

Think of Python performance optimization as layers:

  • 1. Algorithmic & Data-level

    • Choose better algorithms (O(n log n) vs O(n²)).
    • Use efficient data structures: list vs deque, dict vs list search, etc.
    • Use vectorized ops (numpy, pandas) instead of Python loops.

  • 2. Interpreter & Implementation-level

    • Avoid unnecessary Python overhead:
      • Minimize function call overhead in hot loops.
      • Use built-ins and C-extensions (NumPy, math, itertools).
    • Use PyPy or Cython for CPU-bound workloads when appropriate.

  • 3. Concurrency & Parallelism

    • I/O-bound: use asyncio, aiohttp, httpx, or threads.
    • CPU-bound: use multiprocessing (ProcessPoolExecutor), native extensions, or offload to Rust/C++.

  • 4. Memory & Object Management

    • Reduce allocations and temporary objects.
    • Use __slots__ to reduce per-object memory.
    • Reuse buffers (e.g., with NumPy arrays).

  • 5. System & Architecture Level

    • Caching (in-process functools.lru_cache, Redis).
    • Batch requests (model inference, DB calls).
    • Use profiling tools to find bottlenecks instead of guessing.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Application Layer

    • Python API server (FastAPI/Flask) or batch script.
    • Business logic, ML pipelines, RAG orchestration.

  • Performance-Critical Layer

    • NumPy/Pandas operations
    • PyTorch/TensorFlow ops
    • Rust/C++ extensions for tight loops or heavy computation.

  • Infra Layer

    • Web server: Uvicorn/Gunicorn
    • Caching: Redis/Memcached
    • Message queues: Kafka/RabbitMQ
    • Vector DB: Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus.

Technologies

  • Python

    • Web: FastAPI, Flask
    • Async: asyncio, aiohttp, httpx
    • ML: NumPy, Pandas, PyTorch, TensorFlow
    • Profiling: cProfile, line_profiler, py-spy, scalene
    • Optimization: Cython, Numba, multiprocessing, concurrent.futures

  • Rust

    • Performance-critical services:
      • actix-web / axum for APIs
      • pyo3 / maturin for Python bindings
    • Use Rust to implement heavy compute and expose to Python.

Data Flow & Processing Stages (Example: LLM/RAG API)

  • Request → Python API (FastAPI)
  • Preprocessing → tokenization, normalization (NumPy)
  • Embedding computation → GPU/CPU (PyTorch)
  • Vector DB query → network I/O (async)
  • Reranking / context building → Python logic
  • LLM call → external API / local model (I/O + compute)
  • Response formatting → JSON to client

Optimization targets:

  • Reduce Python loops in preprocessing.
  • Async I/O for vector DB + LLM calls.
  • Batch embedding & LLM calls.
  • Offload heavy computation to Rust or GPU.

Model Lifecycle & Performance

  • Training

    • Use GPUs efficiently (batch size, data loaders, pinned memory).
    • Parallel data loading (num_workers in PyTorch).
    • Mixed precision (FP16) to speed up and reduce memory.

  • Evaluation

    • Vectorized metric computation.
    • Use torch.no_grad() / model.eval().

  • Deployment

    • Use optimized runtimes: TensorRT, ONNX Runtime.
    • Serve with model servers (Triton, TorchServe, custom FastAPI + Gunicorn/Uvicorn).
    • Use batching and concurrency controls.

  • Monitoring

    • Track latency, throughput, error rate.
    • Profile periodically and under load (locust, k6).
    • Set alerts on tail latencies (p95, p99).

Scalability & Performance Considerations

  • Scalability

    • Horizontal scaling with multiple workers / replicas.
    • Stateless services; state in DB/Redis/vector DB.
    • Use load balancers (NGINX, Envoy).

  • Performance

    • Avoid global interpreter lock (GIL) limitations via:
      • Multiprocessing for CPU-bound tasks.
      • Native extensions (Rust).
    • Use connection pooling (DB, vector DB, external APIs).
    • Carefully tune thread/worker counts.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    A[Client Request] --> B[FastAPI Python Service]

    subgraph Python_App[Python Layer]
        B --> C[Preprocessing\n(Numpy, vectorized)]
        C --> D[Async I/O\nVector DB, LLM API]
        C --> E[CPU-bound Logic\nNumPy / Rust Extension]
    end

    D --> F[Vector DB / External Services]

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Measure

    • Use profilers (cProfile, line_profiler, py-spy, scalene) to find:
      • Hot functions
      • Hot lines
      • I/O vs CPU breakdown.

  2. Optimize

    • Algorithm & data structures.
    • Replace Python loops with vectorized NumPy / Pandas.
    • Use async for I/O-bound tasks; multiprocessing / Rust for CPU-bound.

  3. Validate & Iterate

    • Re-run benchmarks and load tests.
    • Ensure correctness and no regressions.
    • Deploy, monitor, and repeat.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

1. Profiling in Python

import cProfile
import pstats

def main():
    # your main pipeline
    run_pipeline()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with cProfile.Profile() as pr:
        main()
    stats = pstats.Stats(pr)
    stats.sort_stats(pstats.SortKey.TIME).print_stats(20)

2. Vectorization Example (Replace Python Loops)

import numpy as np

# Slow
def slow_dot(xs, ys):
    total = 0.0
    for x, y in zip(xs, ys):
        total += x * y
    return total

# Fast (vectorized)
def fast_dot(xs, ys):
    xs_arr = np.asarray(xs, dtype=np.float32)
    ys_arr = np.asarray(ys, dtype=np.float32)
    return float(np.dot(xs_arr, ys_arr))

3. Async I/O Example (LLM + Vector DB)

from fastapi import FastAPI
import httpx
import asyncio

app = FastAPI()

VECTOR_DB_URL = "http://vectordb/search"
LLM_URL = "http://llm/infer"

async def fetch_vector_results(client, query_vec):
    return await client.post(VECTOR_DB_URL, json={"vector": query_vec})

async def call_llm(client, prompt):
    return await client.post(LLM_URL, json={"prompt": prompt})

@app.post("/chat")
async def chat_endpoint(payload: dict):
    query = payload["query"]
    query_vec = embed_query(query)  # fast, vectorized embedding

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5.0) as client:
        vec_task = asyncio.create_task(fetch_vector_results(client, query_vec))
        # Other parallel I/O tasks can be added here
        vec_resp = await vec_task

        context = build_context(vec_resp.json())
        llm_resp = await call_llm(client, context + "\n\nUser: " + query)
        return llm_resp.json()

4. Offloading CPU-bound Work to Rust

Rust (using pyo3)

// Cargo.toml
// [dependencies]
// pyo3 = { version = "0.21", features = ["extension-module"] }

use pyo3::prelude::*;

#[pyfunction]
fn heavy_compute(xs: Vec<f64>) -> f64 {
    // Example: sum of squares
    xs.iter().map(|x| x * x).sum()
}

#[pymodule]
fn fastcore(py: Python, m: &PyModule) -> PyResult<()> {
    m.add_function(wrap_pyfunction!(heavy_compute, m)?)?;
    Ok(())
}

Build as a Python extension (via maturin), then in Python:

import fastcore

def compute_loss(xs):
    return fastcore.heavy_compute(xs)

5. Multiprocessing for CPU-bound Tasks

from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

def cpu_intensive_task(data):
    # e.g., feature extraction, scoring
    return heavy_calculation(data)

def process_batch(batch):
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
        results = list(executor.map(cpu_intensive_task, batch))
    return results

Advantages

  • Faster execution

    • Lower latency for APIs and inference.
    • Shorter training/evaluation cycles.

  • Better resource utilization

    • Less CPU & memory per request.
    • Lower cloud costs.

  • Scalability

    • Higher throughput with same hardware.
    • Easier to meet SLAs for LLM/RAG services.

  • Cleaner architecture

    • Clear separation of I/O-bound vs CPU-bound vs GPU-bound parts.
    • Easier to decide where to introduce Rust/C++.

Limitations

  • Complexity

    • Async, multiprocessing, and Rust bindings increase code complexity.
    • Harder debugging and testing.

  • Diminishing returns

    • Micro-optimizations may not matter vs algorithmic changes.
    • Over-optimization can hurt readability and maintainability.

  • GIL constraints

    • Threads don’t speed up CPU-bound pure Python code.
    • Need multiprocessing or native extensions.

  • Operational overhead

    • More moving parts: profiling, monitoring, tuning, build pipelines for Rust/Cython.

Interview Tips

  • Structure your answer

    • Always start with: “First profile, then optimize.”
    • Cover: algorithmic → implementation → concurrency → system-level.

  • Mention tools

    • Profiling: cProfile, line_profiler, py-spy, scalene.
    • Optimization: NumPy, Numba, Cython, Rust (pyo3), multiprocessing.

  • Differentiate I/O vs CPU-bound

    • I/O-bound → async, threads.
    • CPU-bound → multiprocessing, native extensions, GPU.

  • Talk about real patterns

    • Vectorization in ML.
    • Batching and caching in LLM/RAG.
    • Rust for tight loops and scoring functions.

  • Common interview questions

    • How to speed up a slow Python loop?
    • How does GIL affect multithreading?
    • When to use asyncio vs multiprocessing?
    • How to integrate Rust with Python?
    • How to optimize a FastAPI service under high load?

  • Tricky areas

    • Misusing threads for CPU-bound work.
    • Ignoring profiling and guessing bottlenecks.
    • Overusing micro-optimizations instead of algorithm changes.

Real-World Example

Use-case: High-throughput RAG-based Question Answering API

  • Initial state

    • Python FastAPI service.
    • Per-request:
      • Embed query with a local model (PyTorch).
      • Query vector DB (HTTP).
      • Build context in Python loops.
      • Call LLM API.
    • Observed:
      • p95 latency = 3 seconds.
      • CPU at 80%, vector DB calls sequential.

  • Optimizations

    • Profiling

      • Found context-building loop and embedding computation as hot spots.

    • Algorithm & Vectorization

      • Replaced Python loops in context building with NumPy-based scoring and sorting.

    • Async I/O

      • Used httpx.AsyncClient and asyncio.gather to parallelize:
        • Vector DB call
        • LLM call (in some flows)
        • Logging / analytics.

    • Batching

      • Batched embedding requests when multiple queries per user session.

    • Rust extension

      • Implemented similarity scoring and reranking in Rust (pyo3) for heavy ranking logic.

  • Result

    • p95 latency reduced from ~3s → ~800ms.
    • Throughput increased 3–4x on same hardware.
    • Service now meets SLA for interactive chat.

This style of answer (profiling-first, layered optimizations, concrete tools, and real example) is typically what interviewers look for when they ask, “How do you optimize Python performance?”

Q17.EXPLAIN PYTHON'S GARBAGE COLLECTION? [Input Token: 705 | Output Token: 2636] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:
    Python’s garbage collection (GC) is the mechanism that automatically reclaims memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable/needed by the program.
  • In AI/ML/GenAI interviews:
    • Memory management matters for:
      • Large tensors, model weights, and datasets
      • Long-running training/inference services
    • Understanding GC helps debug memory leaks and OOM errors during training/inference.
  • In Python/Rust backend interviews:
    • Python: GC + reference counting → latency spikes, memory fragmentation, leaks via reference cycles.
    • Rust: No GC; ownership/borrowing at compile time → good contrast to explain design choices.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

Python (CPython) uses two mechanisms:

  1. Reference Counting (Primary)

    • Every object has a reference count (ob_refcnt).
    • When a reference to an object is created: refcount++.
    • When a reference is removed: refcount--.
    • When refcount == 0 → object is immediately deallocated.

  2. Cyclic Garbage Collector (Generational GC)

    • Handles reference cycles (objects referencing each other) that reference counting alone cannot free.
    • Periodically scans container objects (lists, dicts, custom classes, etc.).
    • Uses generational GC:
      • Generation 0: youngest, most frequently collected
      • Generation 1: older
      • Generation 2: oldest, least frequently collected
    • Objects surviving collections are promoted to older generations.

  3. Generational Hypothesis

    • Most objects die young.
    • Frequent collection of young generation is cheap and effective.
    • Older generations collected less often to reduce overhead.

  4. Interaction with Native Extensions

    • Objects in C extensions (NumPy arrays, PyTorch tensors) may manage memory outside Python’s heap.
    • GC only knows about Python-level references, not external GPU/CPU buffers unless wrapped carefully.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Reference Counting Mechanism

    • Maintained by CPython interpreter.
    • Incremented/decremented on:
      • Variable assignment
      • Passing arguments
      • Returning values
      • Adding/removing from containers

  • Cyclic Garbage Collector

    • Implemented in gc module.
    • Tracks container objects that may participate in cycles.
    • Maintains:
      • gc.garbage: list of unreachable objects that can’t be collected safely (e.g., with __del__).

  • Generations

    • Default thresholds (can vary by version, configurable via gc.set_threshold):
      • Generation 0: collected when allocations - deallocations > threshold0
      • Generation 1: collected after some number of Gen0 collections
      • Generation 2: collected after some number of Gen1 collections

  • Python GC API (gc module)

    • gc.collect([generation])
    • gc.disable(), gc.enable()
    • gc.get_stats(), gc.get_threshold(), gc.set_threshold()
    • gc.get_objects(), gc.get_referrers(), gc.get_referents()

Data Flow and Processing Stages

  • Object Lifecycle

    • Creation → reference count increments.
    • Usage → references move around; counts change.
    • Dereference:
      • If no cycles: refcount hits 0 → immediate destruction.
      • If cycles: refcount never hits 0 → GC must detect and collect.

  • Cycle Detection Algorithm (Simplified)

    • GC roots: objects tracked by GC.
    • Mark objects reachable from roots.
    • Unmarked objects are unreachable → candidates for collection.
    • Special handling if objects define __del__ (finalizers).

API Endpoints / Contracts (Conceptual)

In a backend service, you don’t expose GC directly as HTTP, but you might:

  • Admin/Debug Endpoints
    • GET /admin/memory/summary → shows memory usage and GC stats.
    • POST /admin/gc/collect → triggers gc.collect() for debugging.

Model Lifecycle & GC in ML/GenAI

  • Training
    • Large temporary tensors created per batch.
    • Python GC + framework-specific memory management (e.g., PyTorch caching allocator).
  • Evaluation / Inference
    • Many short-lived request objects, prompts, embeddings.
    • GC must not introduce large latency spikes.
  • Deployment
    • Long-lived processes (FastAPI, Flask, gRPC).
    • Memory leaks accumulate over time if cycles or external resources are not freed.
  • Monitoring
    • Track:
      • Process RSS / heap size
      • Frequency & duration of GC pauses
      • Number of objects in each generation

Scalability Considerations

  • High-throughput services
    • Many small allocations → frequent GC.
    • Use:
      • Object pooling
      • Pre-allocation of buffers
      • Avoid unnecessary intermediate objects (e.g., large string concatenations).
  • Batching
    • Process requests in batches to reuse structures and reduce allocations.
  • Multiprocessing / Sharding
    • Spawn multiple worker processes to isolate memory and GC overhead.

Performance Considerations

  • Latency
    • GC cycles can cause stop-the-world pauses.
    • For low-latency inference, GC tuning may be needed.
  • Throughput
    • Excessive GC cycles reduce CPU available for actual work.
  • Optimization Techniques
    • Disable GC in critical tight loops (only if safe).
    • Avoid creating large reference cycles.
    • Use local variables and simple data structures.
    • Use slots in classes to reduce overhead when possible.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    A[Python Code<br/>Create Objects] --> B[Reference Counting]
    B -->|refcount == 0| C[Immediate Deallocation]
    B -->|refcount > 0<br/>possible cycles| D[Tracked by GC]
    D --> E[Generational GC<br/>Gen0, Gen1, Gen2]
    E -->|Periodically Triggered| F[Cycle Detection]
    F -->|Unreachable Objects| G[Collect & Free Memory]
    F -->|Objects with __del__ or issues| H[gc.garbage]
    G --> I[Free Python Heap Memory]
    I --> J[OS / Allocator Reuse]

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Object Creation

    • Python allocates memory and sets refcount = 1.
    • If object is a container, it’s added to GC’s tracked set.

  2. Program Execution

    • Variables, lists, dicts, closures hold references.
    • Reference counts are incremented/decremented as references are created/dropped.

  3. Collection

    • When refcount hits 0 → object is destroyed immediately.
    • Periodically, GC scans generations:
      • Finds unreachable cycles.
      • Frees them if safe.
    • Memory is returned to Python’s allocator (not always directly to OS).

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

Python Implementation (Reference Counting & GC Usage)

Basic Example

import gc

def create_cycle():
    a = {}
    b = {}
    a['b'] = b
    b['a'] = a
    # a and b reference each other → cycle

def main():
    gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_STATS)
    print("GC enabled:", gc.isenabled())

    create_cycle()

    # Force collection
    unreachable = gc.collect()
    print("Unreachable objects collected:", unreachable)
    print("Garbage list:", gc.garbage)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Tuning GC for an Inference Service (FastAPI)

from fastapi import FastAPI
import gc
import time

app = FastAPI()

# Example: relax GC thresholds for high-throughput service
gc.set_threshold(700, 10, 10)  # tweak based on profiling

@app.get("/infer")
def infer(prompt: str):
    start = time.time()
    # ... run model inference, build response ...
    response = {"answer": f"Echo: {prompt}"}
    # Optionally trigger GC on some heuristic (e.g., every N requests)
    # gc.collect(0)  # Only gen0
    latency = time.time() - start
    return {"latency_ms": latency * 1000, "response": response}

Rust Contrast (No GC, Ownership Model)

  • Rust:
    • Memory is managed at compile time via ownership and borrowing.
    • No runtime GC → no GC pauses.
    • Good to mention in interviews when asked to compare memory models.
struct Tensor {
    data: Vec<f32>,
}

fn main() {
    let t = Tensor { data: vec![0.0; 1024] };
    // `t` is automatically dropped when it goes out of scope
    // No GC, deterministic destruction
}
  • In a Python + Rust system:
    • Rust handles heavy computation and memory.
    • Python orchestrates, with GC overhead mostly on high-level logic.

Advantages

  • Automatic memory management
    • Reduces developer burden vs manual malloc/free.
  • Immediate reclamation via reference counting
    • Most objects freed as soon as they’re unused.
  • Cycle detection
    • Prevents memory leaks from reference cycles.
  • Generational GC
    • Efficient for workloads with many short-lived objects.

Limitations

  • Not real-time
    • GC can introduce unpredictable pauses.
  • Reference cycles with __del__
    • Can be tricky; such objects may end up in gc.garbage.
  • Memory fragmentation
    • Python’s allocator may hold onto memory; process RSS may not shrink.
  • C extensions
    • External memory (e.g., GPU tensors) may not be freed when expected unless explicitly released.
  • Overhead
    • Reference counting increments/decrements on every reference change.

Interview Tips

  • Key points to remember

    • CPython uses reference counting + cyclic GC.
    • GC is generational (Gen0, Gen1, Gen2).
    • GC handles reference cycles; ref counting alone cannot.
    • gc module allows inspection and tuning.

  • Common Interview Questions

    • How does Python’s garbage collection work?
    • What is the difference between reference counting and GC?
    • How does Python deal with reference cycles?
    • How can you debug memory leaks in a Python service?
    • How does Python’s GC impact latency in a web/ML service?
    • Compare Python’s GC with Rust’s memory model.

  • Tricky Areas

    • Objects with __del__ and cycles.
    • Why process memory may not shrink even after gc.collect().
    • Interaction with NumPy/PyTorch (they manage their own allocators).

Real-World Example

Scenario: Long-running LLM inference API (RAG system) built with Python.

  • Pipeline

    • Receive request → parse JSON.
    • Build prompt, retrieve embeddings from vector DB.
    • Call LLM (local or remote).
    • Construct response, log metadata.

  • GC Implications

    • Each request creates:
      • Strings (prompts, responses).
      • Python objects for metadata, traces.
      • Possibly large temporary lists/dicts.
    • If you:
      • Create reference cycles in request context objects.
      • Keep global caches without eviction.
      • Hold onto intermediate results in closures.
    • → Memory grows, GC runs more often, latency spikes.

  • Mitigation

    • Design request-scoped objects without cycles (e.g., DAG nodes with weak references where needed).
    • Use del for large temporary objects after use (especially large lists of embeddings).
    • Periodically call gc.collect() in low-traffic windows.
    • Monitor memory via Prometheus/Grafana; tune gc.set_threshold.

This level of understanding is usually sufficient to answer Python GC questions in both ML and backend system design interviews.

Q18.WHAT ARE PYTHON DESCRIPTORS? [Input Token: 704 | Output Token: 3110] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:
    Python descriptors are objects that define how attribute access (get, set, delete) is managed on another class through special methods: __get__, __set__, and __delete__.
  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:
    • Shows deep understanding of Python internals (important for building robust ML/GenAI libraries, custom layers, parameter management).
    • Used in frameworks for things like lazy loading, computed attributes, configuration fields, and model parameters.
  • Importance in Python/Rust backend interviews:
    • Demonstrates knowledge of advanced Python features used in ORMs (Django, SQLAlchemy), dependency injection, and configuration systems.
    • Useful for building clean, declarative APIs and domain models.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • Core idea:

    • A descriptor is any object that implements one or more of:
      • __get__(self, instance, owner)
      • __set__(self, instance, value)
      • __delete__(self, instance)
    • Descriptors live in the class body and control access to attributes on instances of that class.

  • Types:

    • Data descriptors: implement __get__ and __set__ (or __delete__)
      • Higher priority than instance __dict__
      • Examples: property, @dataclass fields, ORM columns
    • Non-data descriptors: implement only __get__
      • Lower priority than instance __dict__
      • Examples: functions becoming bound methods

  • How attribute access works:

    • When you do obj.attr:
      • Python checks type(obj).__dict__['attr']
      • If it finds an object with __get__, it calls that descriptor instead of returning the descriptor object directly.
    • When you do obj.attr = value:
      • Python checks if type(obj).__dict__['attr'] has __set__
      • If yes, calls descriptor’s __set__; otherwise writes to obj.__dict__.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Descriptor class:
    • Implements one or more of:
      • __get__(self, instance, owner)
      • __set__(self, instance, value)
      • __delete__(self, instance)
  • Owner class (the class using descriptors):
    • Has descriptor instances as class attributes.
  • Instances:
    • Access attributes that are controlled by descriptors.

Technologies / Contexts

  • Python:
    • Built-in descriptors: property, classmethod, staticmethod, functions (methods).
    • Libraries:
      • Django ORM: models.CharField, ForeignKey are descriptors.
      • SQLAlchemy: column definitions are descriptors.
      • Pydantic / dataclasses: fields often implemented via descriptor-like behavior.
  • Rust (conceptual parallel):
    • While Rust doesn’t have descriptors, similar patterns appear via:
      • Custom Deref implementations
      • Smart pointers
      • Getter/setter methods with traits

Data Flow & Processing Stages

  • Descriptor declaration:
    • Defined as a class with __get__/__set__.
    • Instantiated and assigned as a class attribute.
  • Attribute access:
    • Read (obj.attr) → descriptor.__get__(instance=obj, owner=type(obj))
    • Write (obj.attr = v) → descriptor.__set__(instance=obj, value=v)
    • Delete (del obj.attr) → descriptor.__delete__(instance=obj)
  • Storage:
    • Often descriptors store data in:
      • instance.__dict__ under a private name (e.g. '_attr')
      • External storage (DB, cache, vector DB, config store, etc.)

API Contract (Conceptual)

  • __get__(self, instance, owner):
    • instance:
      • The object instance when accessed via instance
      • None when accessed via class (Class.attr)
    • owner:
      • The owner class (Class)
    • Must return the attribute value.
  • __set__(self, instance, value):
    • Should validate/transform and then store value.
  • __delete__(self, instance):
    • Should remove the value or raise.

Model Lifecycle / Use in ML Systems

  • Training / configuration:
    • Descriptors can manage:
      • Hyperparameters (with validation)
      • Lazy-loading of large artifacts (e.g., embeddings, models)
  • Evaluation / inference:
    • Can implement read-only properties for metrics, model metadata.
  • Deployment / monitoring:
    • Can wrap access to configuration values that come from env/feature flags.

Scalability Considerations

  • Pros:
    • Centralized logic for attribute validation and transformation.
    • Helps prevent duplicated boilerplate across many model fields.
  • Cons:
    • Overuse can make code harder to understand.
    • Indirection can add micro-overhead in hot paths.

Performance Considerations

  • Attribute access via descriptors:
    • Slightly slower than direct __dict__ access due to method calls.
    • For performance-critical loops:
      • Cache descriptor results on the instance.
      • Use plain attributes for tight numeric loops.
    • For backend/ML services:
      • Overhead is usually negligible compared to I/O and model inference.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    subgraph OwnerClass[Owner Class]
        D[Descriptor\n(__get__, __set__)]
    end

    I[Instance of Owner Class] -->|access attr| A[Attribute Resolution]

    A -->|lookup in type(instance).__dict__| D
    D -->|__get__(instance, owner)| V[Returned Value]

    W[Write: instance.attr = value] -->|lookup descriptor| D
    D -->|__set__(instance, value)| S[Store in instance.__dict__ or external storage]

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Define descriptor class
    • Implement __get__, optionally __set__ and __delete__.
  2. Attach descriptor to owner class
    • Create descriptor instance as a class attribute.
  3. Use descriptor-controlled attribute
    • Access, assign, or delete the attribute through instances; Python automatically routes through descriptor methods.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

Python: Basic Descriptor Example

class PositiveFloat:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name  # attribute name (for storage key)

    def __get__(self, instance, owner):
        if instance is None:
            # Access via class: return descriptor itself or metadata
            return self
        return instance.__dict__.get(self.name, 0.0)

    def __set__(self, instance, value):
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError(f"{self.name} must be non-negative")
        instance.__dict__[self.name] = float(value)

    def __delete__(self, instance):
        if self.name in instance.__dict__:
            del instance.__dict__[self.name]


class ModelConfig:
    learning_rate = PositiveFloat("learning_rate")
    weight_decay = PositiveFloat("weight_decay")


cfg = ModelConfig()
cfg.learning_rate = 0.001  # triggers PositiveFloat.__set__
print(cfg.learning_rate)   # triggers PositiveFloat.__get__

Python: Descriptor for Lazy-Loaded LLM / Embeddings

class LazyResource:
    def __init__(self, loader_fn, attr_name):
        self.loader_fn = loader_fn
        self.attr_name = attr_name

    def __get__(self, instance, owner):
        if instance is None:
            return self
        if self.attr_name not in instance.__dict__:
            # Load resource on first access (e.g., LLM, embeddings)
            instance.__dict__[self.attr_name] = self.loader_fn()
        return instance.__dict__[self.attr_name]


def load_embeddings_model():
    # e.g., load sentence-transformers model
    from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
    return SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")


class EmbeddingService:
    embeddings_model = LazyResource(load_embeddings_model, "embeddings_model")


svc = EmbeddingService()
# Model is loaded only when first accessed:
emb = svc.embeddings_model.encode(["hello world"])

Python: Using Built-in Descriptor property

class TrainingRun:
    def __init__(self, loss_values):
        self._loss_values = loss_values

    @property
    def final_loss(self):
        # property is a descriptor
        return self._loss_values[-1]

    @final_loss.setter
    def final_loss(self, value):
        # example setter (not typical for final_loss, but for illustration)
        self._loss_values[-1] = value

Rust: Conceptual Analogy (No Direct Descriptors)

In Rust, you’d typically use explicit methods or traits instead of descriptors:

struct ModelConfig {
    learning_rate: f32,
}

impl ModelConfig {
    fn learning_rate(&self) -> f32 {
        self.learning_rate
    }

    fn set_learning_rate(&mut self, value: f32) {
        if value < 0.0 {
            panic!("learning_rate must be non-negative");
        }
        self.learning_rate = value;
    }
}
  • In Python, descriptors automate this getter/setter pattern.
  • In Rust, you keep it explicit for clarity and performance.

Advantages

  • Encapsulation of logic:
    • Centralizes validation, conversion, and side effects for attribute access.
  • Declarative APIs:
    • Clean class definitions with field-like syntax but rich behavior.
  • Reusability:
    • Same descriptor can be reused across many classes/fields.
  • Foundation of many frameworks:
    • Understanding descriptors helps understand Django, SQLAlchemy, Pydantic, etc.

Limitations

  • Complexity:
    • Harder to read for developers unfamiliar with descriptors.
  • Debugging difficulty:
    • Attribute access can have hidden behavior.
  • Performance overhead:
    • Extra function calls on attribute access (usually minor, but relevant in tight loops).
  • Misuse risk:
    • Over-engineering simple attributes into descriptors can hurt maintainability.

Interview Tips

  • Key points to remember:

    • Descriptor methods: __get__, __set__, __delete__.
    • Data vs non-data descriptors:
      • Data: have __set__/__delete__, override instance __dict__.
      • Non-data: only __get__, can be shadowed by instance attributes.
    • Built-in descriptors: property, functions, classmethod, staticmethod.
    • Descriptors must be defined as class attributes to work.

  • Common interview questions:

    • What is a descriptor and when would you use it?
    • Explain the difference between data and non-data descriptors.
    • How does property work under the hood?
    • How do descriptors relate to methods in Python?
    • Show how you’d implement type-checked or validated fields using descriptors.
    • How are descriptors used in ORMs like Django?

  • Tricky areas:

    • Access via class vs instance:
      • instance.attr → __get__(instance, owner)
      • Class.attr → __get__(None, owner) or descriptor object itself.
    • Interaction with __getattribute__ and __getattr__.
    • Shadowing behavior:
      • Data descriptors > instance __dict__ > non-data descriptors.

Real-World Example

Use-Case: Validated Configuration for an LLM Inference Service

  • Scenario:
    • You’re building a Python backend (FastAPI) serving LLM responses.
    • You want a configuration object with validated fields:
      • max_tokens, temperature, top_p, timeout.
    • You also want lazy loading of a vector store client.

Descriptor-Based Config

class BoundedFloat:
    def __init__(self, name, min_value=0.0, max_value=1.0):
        self.name = name
        self.min_value = min_value
        self.max_value = max_value

    def __get__(self, instance, owner):
        if instance is None:
            return self
        return instance.__dict__.get(self.name, self.min_value)

    def __set__(self, instance, value):
        if not (self.min_value <= value <= self.max_value):
            raise ValueError(f"{self.name} must be in [{self.min_value}, {self.max_value}]")
        instance.__dict__[self.name] = float(value)


class PositiveInt:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def __get__(self, instance, owner):
        if instance is None:
            return self
        return instance.__dict__.get(self.name, 0)

    def __set__(self, instance, value):
        if value <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f"{self.name} must be positive")
        instance.__dict__[self.name] = int(value)


class InferenceConfig:
    temperature = BoundedFloat("temperature", 0.0, 1.0)
    top_p = BoundedFloat("top_p", 0.0, 1.0)
    max_tokens = PositiveInt("max_tokens")
    timeout = PositiveInt("timeout")


cfg = InferenceConfig()
cfg.temperature = 0.7    # validated
cfg.top_p = 0.9          # validated
cfg.max_tokens = 512     # validated
cfg.timeout = 30         # validated
  • This pattern is similar to how ORMs define model fields.
  • In a real LLM/RAG backend:
    • Descriptors can validate:
      • Model names
      • Vector dimensions
      • Embedding batch sizes
    • Lazy descriptors can:
      • Initialize database/vector DB connections on first use.
      • Load models only when needed.

This understanding is often a strong signal in interviews that you know Python beyond the basics and can reason about framework internals and advanced patterns.

Q19.DIFFERENCE BETWEEN FLASK AND FASTAPI? [Input Token: 706 | Output Token: 3353] +

Topic Overview

  • Flask and FastAPI are popular Python web frameworks used to build APIs and backend services.
  • Flask: Minimal, flexible, WSGI-based framework.
  • FastAPI: Modern, async-first, high-performance framework built on ASGI with automatic OpenAPI docs.

Why important in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:

  • Most ML/LLM models are exposed via HTTP APIs.
  • Interviewers expect you to know:
    • How to deploy models behind REST/gRPC endpoints.
    • How to choose frameworks for low-latency inference and high throughput.
    • How to integrate with LLMs/RAG services and handle streaming.

Why important in Python/Rust backend interviews:

  • Shows understanding of:
    • Sync vs async architectures.
    • Performance, scalability, and maintainability trade-offs.
    • Choosing the right framework for microservices, model-serving, or LLM gateways.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

Flask

  • Type: WSGI, synchronous, micro-framework.
  • Philosophy:
    • Minimal core, many extensions.
    • You manually define structure and patterns.
  • Typical usage:
    • Simple REST APIs.
    • Legacy systems.
    • Small ML inference services with moderate traffic.

FastAPI

  • Type: ASGI, async-first, performance-focused.
  • Philosophy:
    • Use type hints for validation and docs.
    • Batteries-included for modern APIs (OpenAPI, JSON Schema).
  • Typical usage:
    • High-performance APIs.
    • LLM/RAG services needing concurrency and streaming.
    • Microservices in modern cloud-native stacks.

Key Conceptual Differences

  • Execution model:
    • Flask: Sync, blocking I/O (though can be used with gevent/gunicorn workers).
    • FastAPI: Async/await, non-blocking I/O, built on Starlette + Pydantic.
  • Type system & validation:
    • Flask: No built-in validation; use Marshmallow, pydantic, etc.
    • FastAPI: Request/response validation via Pydantic models from type hints.
  • Docs generation:
    • Flask: Manual or via extensions like flasgger.
    • FastAPI: Automatic OpenAPI/Swagger & ReDoc out-of-the-box.
  • Performance:
    • FastAPI: Significantly faster under I/O-bound loads due to async.
    • Flask: Adequate for smaller loads, but less suited for massive concurrency.

Technical Specifications

Components

Flask typical stack:

  • Framework: Flask (WSGI)
  • Server: gunicorn/uwsgi + Nginx
  • Validation: Flask-RESTful, Marshmallow, or custom.
  • Auth: Flask-JWT-Extended, Flask-Login.
  • Templates: Jinja2 (if needed).
  • ML/GenAI:
    • torch, transformers, langchain, llama-cpp-python etc.
    • Vector DB client (e.g., qdrant-client, pinecone-client).

FastAPI typical stack:

  • Framework: FastAPI (ASGI) + Starlette
  • Server: Uvicorn / Hypercorn + Nginx
  • Validation & models: Pydantic
  • Auth: OAuth2/JWT via FastAPI security utilities.
  • Docs: Swagger UI / ReDoc auto-generated.
  • ML/GenAI:
    • Same libraries as Flask, but easier async integration with:
      • External LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.)
      • Streaming responses (Server-Sent Events / websockets).

Data Flow and Processing Stages

Flask:

  • HTTP request → WSGI server → Flask routing → View function (sync) → Model inference → Response.

FastAPI:

  • HTTP request → ASGI server → FastAPI routing → Dependency injection → Async view (or sync) → Validation via Pydantic → Model inference → Response (possibly streaming).

API Endpoints and Contracts

  • In both:
    • Define routes like /predict, /chat, /embed.
    • Use JSON for request/response body.
  • FastAPI:
    • Contracts are explicit via type hints and Pydantic models.
    • OpenAPI schema generated automatically.
  • Flask:
    • Contracts implicit unless you document manually or via decorators.

Model Lifecycle (Training, Evaluation, Deployment, Monitoring)

Mostly framework-agnostic, but:

  • Training/Evaluation:
    • Offline in notebooks, scripts, or pipelines (Airflow, Prefect, Kubeflow).
  • Deployment:
    • Flask:
      • Wrap model in sync endpoints.
      • Use gunicorn workers to scale.
    • FastAPI:
      • Wrap model in async/sync endpoints.
      • Use uvicorn workers, horizontal scaling via Kubernetes.
  • Monitoring:
    • Use Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, or custom logging.
    • FastAPI integrates more naturally with modern observability stacks (ASGI middleware).

Scalability Considerations

  • Flask:

    • Scale via:
      • Multiple gunicorn workers.
      • Horizontal pods/VMs.
    • Limited concurrency per worker due to blocking I/O.
    • For heavy I/O (DB, vector DB, external LLM API), can become a bottleneck.

  • FastAPI:

    • Async I/O allows:
      • High concurrency with fewer workers.
      • Better utilization when calling external services (LLM APIs, vector DBs).
    • More suitable for:
      • Chatbots, RAG, LLM gateways with many concurrent requests.

Performance Considerations

  • Latency:
    • FastAPI often lower for I/O-bound workloads.
  • Throughput:
    • FastAPI can handle more concurrent connections.
  • CPU-bound workloads (e.g., local model inference):
    • Both limited by CPU/GPU, not framework.
    • Use:
      • Worker pools.
      • Background tasks.
      • Separate inference service (e.g., Rust or Triton) for heavy compute.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    subgraph Client
        U[User / Frontend / LLM App]
    end

    subgraph Backend
        direction TB
        A[Flask API\n(WSGI, sync)] ---|Option 1| B[(Model / LLM / RAG)]
        C[FastAPI API\n(ASGI, async)] ---|Option 2| B
    end

    U -->|HTTP Request| A
    U -->|HTTP Request| C
    B -->|JSON Response| A
    B -->|JSON/Streaming Response| C

Step-by-Step Flow

Flask Example Flow

  1. Client sends POST /predict with JSON payload.
  2. Flask route matches /predict and calls sync handler.
  3. Handler:
    • Parses request.json manually.
    • Runs model inference.
    • Returns JSON response.
  4. WSGI server sends response back to client.

FastAPI Example Flow

  1. Client sends POST /predict with JSON payload.
  2. FastAPI route matches /predict and:
    • Validates request body against Pydantic model.
    • Injects dependencies (DB, vector store clients, config).
  3. Handler (async or sync):
    • Calls model or external LLM/vector DB.
    • Returns Pydantic response model.
  4. ASGI server sends response; OpenAPI docs auto-updated.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

Flask Minimal Example (ML Inference Endpoint)

from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoTokenizer

app = Flask(__name__)

model_name = "distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_name)

@app.route("/predict", methods=["POST"])
def predict():
    data = request.get_json()
    text = data["text"]

    inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt")
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model(**inputs)
    probs = outputs.logits.softmax(dim=-1).tolist()[0]

    return jsonify({"label_probs": probs})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)

FastAPI Minimal Example (Same Inference Endpoint)

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoTokenizer

app = FastAPI()

model_name = "distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_name)

class PredictRequest(BaseModel):
    text: str

class PredictResponse(BaseModel):
    label_probs: list[float]

@app.post("/predict", response_model=PredictResponse)
def predict(req: PredictRequest):
    inputs = tokenizer(req.text, return_tensors="pt")
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model(**inputs)
    probs = outputs.logits.softmax(dim=-1).tolist()[0]
    return PredictResponse(label_probs=probs)

Async + External LLM (FastAPI)

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
import httpx

app = FastAPI()
OPENAI_API_KEY = "..."

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    prompt: str

class ChatResponse(BaseModel):
    answer: str

@app.post("/chat", response_model=ChatResponse)
async def chat(req: ChatRequest):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30) as client:
        resp = await client.post(
            "https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {OPENAI_API_KEY}"},
            json={
                "model": "gpt-4o-mini",
                "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": req.prompt}],
            },
        )
    data = resp.json()
    answer = data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
    return ChatResponse(answer=answer)

Rust Backend (for comparison / integration)

Use Axum or Actix-web to build high-performance inference or gateway services.

use axum::{routing::post, Json, Router};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::net::SocketAddr;

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct PredictRequest {
    text: String,
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct PredictResponse {
    label_probs: Vec<f32>,
}

async fn predict(Json(_req): Json<PredictRequest>) -> Json<PredictResponse> {
    // Call Python model over gRPC/HTTP or use Rust-native inference
    Json(PredictResponse {
        label_probs: vec![0.1, 0.9],
    })
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let app = Router::new().route("/predict", post(predict));
    let addr = SocketAddr::from(([0, 0, 0, 0], 8000));
    axum::Server::bind(&addr).serve(app.into_make_service()).await.unwrap();
}

Advantages

Flask

  • Simplicity:
    • Very easy to learn and bootstrap.
  • Ecosystem:
    • Huge number of extensions, tutorials, and examples.
  • Flexibility:
    • You decide structure and patterns.
  • Good for:
    • Small services, POCs, internal tools, simple ML endpoints.

FastAPI

  • Performance:
    • Async, high throughput; great for I/O-heavy LLM/RAG apps.
  • Developer productivity:
    • Type hints → validation + docs automatically.
  • Built-in docs:
    • Swagger UI and ReDoc without extra work.
  • Modern patterns:
    • Dependency injection, async, Pydantic models.
  • Good for:
    • Production APIs, microservices, LLM gateways, RAG backends.

Limitations

Flask

  • No native async:
    • Harder to handle many concurrent external calls (LLM APIs, vector DBs).
  • Manual validation/docs:
    • More boilerplate for large APIs.
  • Architecture drift:
    • Without conventions, large codebases can become messy.

FastAPI

  • Learning curve:
    • Requires understanding async, type hints, Pydantic, dependency injection.
  • Complexity:
    • Overkill for very small/simple scripts.
  • Async pitfalls:
    • Mixing sync CPU-heavy code in async endpoints can block event loop if not handled properly (need thread pools, etc.).

Interview Tips

  • Core comparison points to mention:
    • WSGI (Flask) vs ASGI (FastAPI).
    • Sync vs async.
    • Manual vs automatic validation/docs.
    • Performance and concurrency.
  • When asked “Which would you choose?”:
    • For modern production APIs, LLM/RAG services, high concurrency:
      • Prefer FastAPI.
    • For simple internal tools, legacy integration, small ML demos:
      • Flask is sufficient.
  • GenAI-specific points:
    • FastAPI is better for:
      • Streaming responses from LLMs (SSE/websockets).
      • High concurrency when calling external LLM APIs.
      • Managing multiple microservices (embedding service, vector DB service, reranker, etc.).
  • Tricky areas:
    • Don’t just say “FastAPI is faster” — explain why (async I/O, ASGI).
    • Mention OpenAPI auto-generation as a big advantage for FastAPI.
    • Mention that for CPU/GPU-bound inference, the framework is less important than:
      • Worker model.
      • Hardware acceleration.
      • Batch inference.

Real-World Example

RAG Backend: Flask vs FastAPI

Scenario: You build a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) backend:

  • Endpoints:
    • POST /embed → generate embeddings.
    • POST /retrieve → query vector DB.
    • POST /chat → retrieve + call LLM + return answer.

Flask-based RAG

  • Flow:
    • Sync handlers call:
      • Embedding model (local or remote).
      • Vector DB (e.g., Qdrant, Pinecone).
      • LLM API (OpenAI).
  • Issues:
    • Many concurrent users → threads blocked on I/O.
    • Harder to stream tokens to client.

FastAPI-based RAG

  • Flow:
    • Async handlers:
      • Use httpx.AsyncClient to call LLM APIs.
      • Use async clients for vector DB / databases.
    • Streaming:
      • Use StreamingResponse to stream tokens to client.
  • Benefits:
    • Higher concurrency.
    • Lower latency under load.
    • Auto-generated OpenAPI docs for all endpoints (useful for frontend and other services).

In interviews, tie your answer to such a concrete scenario and explain why FastAPI is typically preferred for modern GenAI/RAG/LLM backends, while Flask still has a place for simpler or legacy systems.

Q20.HOW DO YOU STRUCTURE LARGE PYTHON APPLICATIONS? [Input Token: 707 | Output Token: 3721] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition
    • Structuring large Python applications means organizing code, modules, packages, and services so the system is:
      • Maintainable
      • Testable
      • Scalable
      • Easy to onboard new engineers
  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews
    • Production ML/LLM systems are large, multi-component apps:
      • Data pipelines, model training, inference services, feature stores, vector DB clients, API layers
      • Interviewers want to see you can design clean architecture around ML/GenAI, not just write notebooks
  • Importance in Python/Rust backend interviews
    • Shows you understand:
      • Layered architecture, modularization, dependency management
      • Separation of concerns (domain vs infrastructure vs presentation)
      • How to evolve a monolith into services/microservices

Architecture / Concept Explanation

Common patterns for structuring large Python apps:

  • Package-based modularization
    • Break code into top-level packages:
      • api, services, domain, infrastructure, models, config, utils
    • Each package has clear responsibility and boundaries
  • Layered / Clean Architecture
    • Layers:
      • Domain layer: business logic, entities, value objects
      • Application / Service layer: use cases, orchestration, transactions
      • Infrastructure layer: DB, message queues, external APIs, vector DB clients, model registries
      • Presentation layer: REST/GraphQL/gRPC, CLI, UI
    • Dependency direction:
      • Outer layers depend on inner layers (not vice versa)
  • Configuration & environment separation
    • Different configs for dev, staging, prod
    • Use .env, config files, or environment variables
  • Explicit entrypoints
    • main.py or app.py for services
    • cli.py for CLI tools
    • worker.py for background jobs
  • ML/GenAI-specific structure
    • Separate:
      • data_pipeline/
      • training/
      • inference/
      • rag/ or retrieval/
      • evaluation/
      • monitoring/ (drift, quality)
    • Shared models/ and features/ across pipelines and services

Technical Specifications

Typical Components

  • Core packages
    • app/
      • api/ — FastAPI/Flask routes, request/response models
      • domain/ — business entities, domain services
      • services/ — application services/use cases
      • infrastructure/
        • db/ (SQLAlchemy, Redis, Mongo)
        • mq/ (Kafka, RabbitMQ)
        • vectorstore/ (Pinecone, Qdrant, Chroma)
        • llm_clients/ (OpenAI, vLLM, Ollama)
      • config/ — settings, environment management
      • auth/ — authn/authz, JWT, OAuth
      • utils/ — helper functions
  • ML / GenAI-specific
    • ml/
      • data/ — ingestion, preprocessing, feature engineering
      • models/ — training scripts, model definitions
      • evaluation/ — metrics, validation
      • pipelines/ — ETL, training, batch inference
    • genai/
      • embeddings/
      • retrievers/
      • prompts/
      • rag/ — RAG pipeline orchestration
      • agents/ — multi-step tools, planners

Technologies Used

  • Python
    • Web: FastAPI, Flask
    • ML: PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn
    • GenAI: LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack
    • Infra: SQLAlchemy, Pydantic, Celery, Redis, Kafka clients
    • Config: pydantic-settings, python-dotenv
  • Rust (for performance-critical parts)
    • Services: Axum, Actix Web
    • Data processing: Polars, custom pipelines
    • FFI: pyo3 to integrate Rust with Python for hot paths (e.g., vector ops, tokenization)

Data Flow & Processing Stages (Example: RAG API)

  • Flow
    • Client → API (FastAPI) → Service layer → RAG pipeline:
      • Embed query → retrieve from vector DB → call LLM → post-process → response
  • Stages
    • Request validation (Pydantic)
    • Auth & rate limiting
    • Routing to appropriate service (chat, search, summarization)
    • Service orchestrates:
      • Vector store queries
      • LLM calls
      • Caching
    • Logging & metrics

API Endpoints & Contracts (Example)

  • POST /v1/chat
    • Request:
      {
  "session_id": "abc123",
  "message": "Explain transformers",
  "context": "docs",
  "top_k": 5
}
    • Response:
      {
  "answer": "Transformers are...",
  "sources": [
    {"doc_id": "123", "score": 0.89},
    {"doc_id": "456", "score": 0.85}
  ],
  "latency_ms": 230
}

Model Lifecycle

  • Training
    • ml/pipelines/train_*.py scripts
    • Config-driven (YAML + Pydantic models)
  • Evaluation
    • ml/evaluation/ with metrics and benchmarks
    • For LLMs: prompt-based eval, human-in-the-loop, BLEU, ROUGE, custom metrics
  • Deployment
    • Export model (ONNX, TorchScript, safetensors)
    • Load in inference service (Python or Rust)
    • Serve via HTTP/gRPC
  • Monitoring
    • Metrics: latency, error rate, throughput
    • Model: drift, quality, prompt success rate, RAG retrieval quality
    • Logging: structured logs, traces

Scalability Considerations

  • Horizontal scaling:
    • Stateless API services behind load balancers
    • Separate inference workers, background jobs
  • Data & model:
    • External vector DB and RDBMS
    • Sharding/partitioning if needed
  • Architecture:
    • Start monolithic but modular
    • Extract hot or independent modules into microservices (e.g., embeddings service)

Performance Considerations

  • Use async I/O (FastAPI, asyncio) for:
    • LLM calls, DB, vector DB
  • Use Rust or C-extensions for:
    • Heavy compute, tokenization, custom vector ops
  • Caching:
    • Redis for:
      • Embeddings
      • RAG retrieval results
      • LLM responses
  • Batching:
    • Batch embeddings and LLM calls where possible
  • Profiling:
    • cProfile, PySpy, or Rust profiling tools

Example: Handling a RAG chat request in a well-structured large Python app.

  • Step 1: API receives request

Python: High-Level Structure

app/
