Example: FastAPI Endpoint

# app/api/routes_chat.py
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends
from pydantic import BaseModel
from app.services.chat_service import ChatService

router = APIRouter()

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    session_id: str
    message: str
    top_k: int = 5

class ChatResponse(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    sources: list[dict]
    latency_ms: int

@router.post("/v1/chat", response_model=ChatResponse)
async def chat_endpoint(
    payload: ChatRequest,
    chat_service: ChatService = Depends(ChatService.provide),
):
    result = await chat_service.handle_message(
        session_id=payload.session_id,
        message=payload.message,
        top_k=payload.top_k,
    )
    return ChatResponse(**result)

Example: Service Layer

# app/services/chat_service.py
from time import perf_counter
from app.genai.rag.pipeline import RagPipeline

class ChatService:
    def __init__(self, rag_pipeline: RagPipeline):
        self.rag_pipeline = rag_pipeline

    @classmethod
    def provide(cls):
        # In real code, use DI container/wiring
        from app.genai.rag.pipeline import RagPipeline
        pipeline = RagPipeline.provide()
        return cls(pipeline)

    async def handle_message(self, session_id: str, message: str, top_k: int):
        start = perf_counter()
        answer, sources = await self.rag_pipeline.answer_query(
            session_id=session_id,
            query=message,
            top_k=top_k,
        )
        latency_ms = int((perf_counter() - start) * 1000)
        return {"answer": answer, "sources": sources, "latency_ms": latency_ms}

Example: RAG Pipeline (Infrastructure + GenAI)

# app/genai/rag/pipeline.py
from app.infrastructure.vectorstore.qdrant_client import QdrantVectorStore
from app.infrastructure.llm_clients.openai_client import OpenAILLMClient
from app.genai.prompts.chat_prompts import build_rag_prompt

class RagPipeline:
    def __init__(self, vector_store: QdrantVectorStore, llm_client: OpenAILLMClient):
        self.vector_store = vector_store
        self.llm_client = llm_client

    @classmethod
    def provide(cls):
        vs = QdrantVectorStore.provide()
        llm = OpenAILLMClient.provide()
        return cls(vs, llm)

    async def answer_query(self, session_id: str, query: str, top_k: int):
        docs = await self.vector_store.search(query, top_k=top_k)
        prompt = build_rag_prompt(query=query, docs=docs)
        answer = await self.llm_client.generate(prompt)
        sources = [{"doc_id": d.id, "score": d.score} for d in docs]
        return answer, sources

Rust Integration Example

Use Rust for heavy vector operations, exposed to Python:

// src/lib.rs (Rust)
use pyo3::prelude::*;

#[pyfunction]
fn cosine_similarity(a: Vec<f32>, b: Vec<f32>) -> f32 {
    let dot: f32 = a.iter().zip(b.iter()).map(|(x, y)| x * y).sum();
    let norm_a = a.iter().map(|x| x * x).sum::<f32>().sqrt();
    let norm_b = b.iter().map(|x| x * x).sum::<f32>().sqrt();
    dot / (norm_a * norm_b)
}

#[pymodule]
fn fastvec(_py: Python, m: &PyModule) -> PyResult<()> {
    m.add_function(wrap_pyfunction!(cosine_similarity, m)?)?;
    Ok(())
}

# app/utils/vector_ops.py (Python)
from fastvec import cosine_similarity

def score_vectors(a: list[float], b: list[float]) -> float:
    return cosine_similarity(a, b)

Advantages

  • Maintainability
    • Clear separation of concerns, easier refactoring
  • Testability
    • Services and domain logic can be tested without infra
  • Scalability
    • Easy to split into microservices later
  • Team productivity
    • New engineers can find where things belong
  • Performance
    • Can optimize hotspots (e.g., Rust modules) without touching high-level architecture
  • ML/GenAI alignment
    • Distinct boundaries between training, inference, RAG, and API layers

Limitations

  • Initial complexity
    • More boilerplate, especially for small projects
  • Over-engineering risk
    • Too many layers for simple use cases
  • Requires discipline
    • Team must respect boundaries and avoid “god modules”
  • Onboarding
    • New devs need time to learn the structure and conventions

Interview Tips

  • Common questions
    • “How would you structure a large Python service-based application?”
    • “How do you organize a production ML/LLM system beyond notebooks?”
    • “How do you separate domain logic from infrastructure?”
    • “How would you evolve your monolith into microservices?”
    • “Where do you put RAG pipeline code vs API vs model code?”
  • Key points to mention
    • Package-based structure: api/, services/, domain/, infrastructure/, ml/, genai/
    • Clean architecture / hexagonal architecture
    • Dependency direction (outer → inner)
    • Config management and environment separation
    • Testing strategy:
      • Unit tests for domain/services
      • Integration tests for infra
      • End-to-end tests for APIs and pipelines
  • Tricky areas interviewers focus on
    • Avoiding circular imports and tight coupling
    • Handling shared utilities vs domain logic
    • Where to place:
      • Repository classes
      • DTOs / schemas
      • ML models and pipelines
    • How to structure RAG:
      • retrievers, embedders, vectorstore, llm_clients, pipelines
    • Deployment & CI/CD integration with this structure

Real-World Example

Use-case: Production RAG-based support chatbot for a SaaS product.

  • Structure

    • api/ — HTTP endpoints (chat, search, feedback)
    • services/ — ChatService, FeedbackService, UserService
    • genai/
      • rag/ — pipelines for support docs, product docs
      • prompts/ — system prompts per product
      • embeddings/ — embedding service abstraction
    • infrastructure/
      • vectorstore/ — Pinecone/Qdrant client
      • llm_clients/ — OpenAI, Anthropic, local LLM via vLLM
      • db/ — Postgres for users, sessions, feedback
      • cache/ — Redis for caching responses
    • ml/
      • training/ — fine-tuning classification model for intent detection
      • evaluation/ — RAG quality evaluation, answer correctness scoring
    • monitoring/

  • Benefits

    • Clear place for:
      • Adding new tools/agents

      • Adding non-LLM features (classic search, analytics)
    • Easier to split off:
      • A dedicated “embedding-service” microservice
      • A “batch-indexer” service for document ingestion

This is the level of structure and reasoning expected in senior Python/ML/GenAI or backend interviews.

Q21.EXPLAIN PYTHON PACKAGING AND DEPENDENCY? [Input Token: 704 | Output Token: 3212] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition

    • Python packaging: The process of organizing Python code into distributable units (packages, wheels) that can be installed via tools like pip.
    • Dependency management: Defining, resolving, and locking external libraries and their versions required by your project.

  • Why important in AI/ML/GenAI interviews

    • ML/GenAI projects rely on many libraries: numpy, pandas, torch, transformers, langchain, etc.
    • Reproducibility of experiments and deployments depends on correct dependency management.
    • Packaging is critical for:
      • Reusable model-serving services
      • Custom LLM tools/agents
      • RAG pipelines packaged as libraries or microservices

  • Why important in Python/Rust backend interviews

    • Backend services must:
      • Be easy to deploy (Docker, CI/CD)
      • Avoid dependency hell and version conflicts
    • Understanding packaging is key for:
      • Creating internal SDKs (Python client libraries)
      • Structuring microservices and monorepos
      • Interoperating Python services with Rust components (e.g., via pyo3, FFI)

Architecture / Concept Explanation

Core Concepts

  • Package:

    • A directory with an __init__.py (for classic packages) or modern namespace package.
    • Can be installed and imported (import my_package).

  • Distribution:

    • How your package is built for distribution:
      • Source distribution (sdist): .tar.gz or .zip containing source.
      • Built distribution (wheel): .whl file (pre-built, faster install).

  • Dependency specification:

    • Declaring required libraries and versions:
      • requirements.txt
      • pyproject.toml
      • setup.cfg / setup.py
      • Pipfile / Pipfile.lock
      • poetry.lock

  • Dependency resolution:

    • Tool (pip/Poetry/uv) finds compatible versions of all dependencies and their transitive dependencies.

  • Isolation:

    • Virtual environments: venv, conda, pipenv, poetry envs.
    • Avoids conflicts between projects.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Project structure

    • src/ or root package directory
    • Metadata files:
      • pyproject.toml (modern standard)
      • Optionally setup.cfg / setup.py (legacy/compat)
    • Dependency files:
      • requirements.txt
      • Lock file (poetry.lock, Pipfile.lock, uv.lock)

  • Tools

    • Build & packaging:
      • setuptools, hatchling, poetry, flit
    • Dependency management:
      • pip, pip-tools, poetry, pipenv, uv
    • Environment management:
      • venv, virtualenv, conda, pyenv

Typical Data/Config Flow

  • Source code → structured as a package → build system creates sdist/wheel → uploaded to PyPI/private index → installed via pip using dependency metadata → environment contains resolved versions.

Example pyproject.toml (modern Python packaging)

[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=68", "wheel"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "genai-rag-service"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "RAG microservice for LLM applications"
authors = [
  { name = "Your Name", email = "you@example.com" }
]
requires-python = ">=3.10"
dependencies = [
  "fastapi>=0.111",
  "uvicorn[standard]>=0.29",
  "pydantic>=2.7",
  "langchain>=0.2",
  "openai>=1.0",
  "faiss-cpu>=1.8",
  "numpy>=1.26,<2.0",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = [
  "pytest",
  "black",
  "ruff",
]

[project.scripts]
genai-rag-api = "genai_rag_service.api:main"

Dependency Resolution & Locking

  • Unpinned: fastapi>=0.111
  • Pinned: fastapi==0.111.0
  • Locking ensures:
    • Same versions in dev, staging, production.

Model Lifecycle Integration

  • For ML/GenAI projects:
    • Training dependencies:
      • torch, transformers, datasets, wandb
    • Inference dependencies:
      • onnxruntime, fastapi, uvicorn, langchain
    • May split into extras:
      • project.optional-dependencies["train"]
      • project.optional-dependencies["inference"]

Scalability & Performance Considerations

  • Slim dependencies:

    • Avoid heavy, unused libraries to reduce:
      • Docker image size
      • Cold-start time (serverless)
    • Use inference-only packages when possible (e.g., transformers with CPU-only builds).

  • GPU/CPU specific dependencies:

    • E.g., torch==2.3.0+cu121 vs torch==2.3.0+cpu
    • Often handled via:
      • Different requirements-*.txt files
      • Extras: genai[cu121], genai[cpu]

  • Private models & internal libs:

    • Host internal packages on:
      • Private PyPI (devpi, Artifactory, Nexus)
      • Git URLs (git+https://...)
    • Versioning is crucial for backward compatibility.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    A[Project Source Code\n(src/genai_rag_service)] --> B[pyproject.toml\nPackage Metadata & Dependencies]
    B --> C[Build System\n(setuptools/poetry)]
    C --> D[Distributions\nsdist, wheel]
    D --> E[Package Index\nPyPI / Private Repo]
    E --> F[pip / Poetry / uv\nDependency Resolver]
    F --> G[Virtual Environment\n(venv/conda)]
    G --> H[Backend Service\nFastAPI + LLM/RAG]
    H --> I[Deployed API\nDocker/K8s]

    F --> J[Resolved Dependencies\nExact versions]
    J --> G

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Project Setup

    • Create directory structure:
      • src/genai_rag_service/__init__.py
      • src/genai_rag_service/api.py
    • Create pyproject.toml with metadata and dependencies.

  2. Build & Distribute

    • Build wheel:
      • python -m build or poetry build
    • Upload to PyPI or internal registry:
      • twine upload dist/* or internal CI pipeline.

  3. Install & Run

    • In another project/service:
      • pip install genai-rag-service
    • Use entry point:
      • genai-rag-api (from [project.scripts]) starts FastAPI server with all dependencies resolved.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

High-Level Python Implementation (GenAI Service)

# Create virtual environment
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

# Install dependencies from pyproject (using pip + build backend)
pip install -e .

Example Project Structure

genai-rag-service/
  pyproject.toml
  src/
    genai_rag_service/
      __init__.py
      api.py
      rag_pipeline.py

rag_pipeline.py

# src/genai_rag_service/rag_pipeline.py
from langchain.embeddings import OpenAIEmbeddings
from langchain.vectorstores import FAISS
from langchain.llms import OpenAI

class RAGPipeline:
    def __init__(self, index_path: str):
        self.embeddings = OpenAIEmbeddings()
        self.vstore = FAISS.load_local(index_path, self.embeddings)
        self.llm = OpenAI(model="gpt-4o")

    def answer(self, query: str) -> str:
        docs = self.vstore.similarity_search(query, k=5)
        context = "\n\n".join(d.page_content for d in docs)
        prompt = f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {query}\nAnswer:"
        return self.llm(prompt)

api.py (FastAPI)

# src/genai_rag_service/api.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
from .rag_pipeline import RAGPipeline

app = FastAPI(title="GenAI RAG Service")
rag = RAGPipeline(index_path="/data/faiss_index")

class QueryRequest(BaseModel):
    query: str

class QueryResponse(BaseModel):
    answer: str

@app.post("/query", response_model=QueryResponse)
async def query_endpoint(req: QueryRequest):
    answer = rag.answer(req.query)
    return QueryResponse(answer=answer)

def main():
    import uvicorn
    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)

Rust Integration Example

  • Use Rust for performance-critical parts (e.g., vector search, custom ops).

Rust crate (vector search) + Python binding (pyo3)

// src/lib.rs in Rust crate `fast_vector_search`
use pyo3::prelude::*;

#[pyfunction]
fn cosine_similarity(a: Vec<f32>, b: Vec<f32>) -> f32 {
    let dot: f32 = a.iter().zip(b.iter()).map(|(x, y)| x * y).sum();
    let norm_a: f32 = a.iter().map(|x| x * x).sum::<f32>().sqrt();
    let norm_b: f32 = b.iter().map(|x| x * x).sum::<f32>().sqrt();
    dot / (norm_a * norm_b + 1e-8)
}

#[pymodule]
fn fast_vector_search(_py: Python, m: &PyModule) -> PyResult<()> {
    m.add_function(wrap_pyfunction!(cosine_similarity, m)?)?;
    Ok(())
}
  • Build as Python wheel using maturin or setuptools-rust.
  • In Python package:
from fast_vector_search import cosine_similarity
  • Packaging:
    • Rust crate builds a Python wheel with compiled extension.
    • Add to pyproject.toml dependencies as a normal package.

Advantages

  • Reproducibility

    • Same dependencies across local, CI, staging, production.

  • Modularity

    • Reusable GenAI components (RAG pipelines, embeddings services) as installable packages.

  • Maintainability

    • Clear versioning and change tracking via semantic versioning (1.2.3).

  • Deployment-friendly

    • Easy to:
      • Build Docker images
      • Run migrations
      • Spin up multiple microservices

  • Performance & Safety (with Rust)

    • Offload heavy computations to Rust crates while keeping Python ergonomics.

Limitations

  • Dependency hell

    • Conflicting transitive dependencies (e.g., torch vs jax vs tensorflow versions).

  • Platform-specific wheels

    • GPU builds, OS-specific binaries complicate deployment.

  • Complexity for monorepos

    • Multiple interdependent packages require careful versioning and tooling.

  • Large ML/GenAI stacks

    • Many heavy dependencies (CUDA, BLAS, etc.) increase:
      • Build times
      • Image sizes
      • Cold-start latency

Interview Tips

  • Common Questions

    • Explain pyproject.toml vs setup.py.
    • How do you manage dependencies across environments?
    • How do you ensure reproducible ML/GenAI experiments?
    • How do you structure a Python package for a microservice?
    • How do you handle GPU-specific dependencies?
    • How would you package a Rust-accelerated Python library?

  • Key Points to Remember

    • Use pyproject.toml for modern packaging.
    • Always use virtual environments.
    • Distinguish runtime vs dev dependencies.
    • Explain locking and why it's critical in production.
    • Mention private package indexes for internal ML models/tools.

  • Tricky Areas

    • Extras (project.optional-dependencies) and environment markers (e.g., ; sys_platform == 'linux').
    • Handling binary dependencies (e.g., faiss, torch).
    • Mixing Conda and pip (pitfalls).
    • Version constraints (~=, >=, <) and their implications.

Real-World Example

Use Case: Production RAG Microservice for Enterprise Docs

  • Goal:

    • Provide a REST API that:
      • Indexes internal documents
      • Answers queries via RAG using an LLM

  • Packaging & Dependencies:

    • Package name: enterprise-rag-service
    • Dependencies:
      • fastapi, uvicorn, pydantic
      • langchain, openai
      • faiss-cpu or qdrant-client
      • numpy, pandas
    • Dev dependencies:
      • pytest, httpx, black, ruff

  • Flow:

    1. Data team builds and tests RAG pipeline locally.
    2. Package is built into a wheel and published to internal PyPI.
    3. Backend team creates a deployment service that:
      • pip install enterprise-rag-service
      • Configures environment variables (OPENAI_API_KEY, DB URLs).
    4. CI/CD uses locked dependencies (poetry.lock) to ensure:
      • Same versions in all environments.
    5. For performance, they add a Rust-based vector similarity module:
      • Packaged as a Python extension wheel.
      • Included as a dependency in pyproject.toml.

This pattern demonstrates Python packaging + dependency management as a core skill for building robust, scalable AI/ML/GenAI backends.

Q22.WHAT IS PIP VS POETRY? [Input Token: 705 | Output Token: 3134] +

Topic Overview

  • pip:

    • The default Python package installer.
    • Installs packages from PyPI (and other indexes) into environments.
    • Works closely with virtualenv / venv and requirements.txt.

  • Poetry:

    • A higher-level dependency and project manager for Python.
    • Manages:
      • Dependencies
      • Virtual environments
      • Build and publish (packaging)
    • Uses pyproject.toml as a single source of truth.

  • Why important in AI/ML/GenAI interviews

    • Reproducible environments are critical for:
      • Training pipelines
      • RAG systems
      • Inference services
    • Interviewers want to see:
      • How you manage dependencies across experiments and services
      • How you ensure reproducibility and isolation

  • Why important in Python/Rust backend interviews

    • For Python backends: dependency management is foundational.
    • For Rust: similar concept to Cargo vs pip/Poetry in Python.
    • Shows you understand:
      • Packaging
      • Version pinning
      • Environment isolation
      • Deployment-friendly setups

Architecture / Concept Explanation

pip

  • What it does

    • Installs packages into:
      • Global Python environment, or
      • A virtual environment (venv, virtualenv, conda env, etc.)
    • Uses requirements.txt for dependency lists.

  • How it works (high-level)

    • You run pip install package-name.
    • pip:
      • Resolves the package version from PyPI (or custom index).
      • Downloads the wheel/source.
      • Installs into the current environment.
    • No built-in project-level:
      • Lock file
      • Build config
      • Publishing tools

Poetry

  • What it does

    • Manages the whole project:
      • Creates and manages a virtual environment.
      • Handles dependency resolution with a lock file.
      • Builds and publishes Python packages.
    • Uses pyproject.toml + poetry.lock.

  • How it works (high-level)

    • You run poetry init to create pyproject.toml.
    • Add dependencies via poetry add package-name.
    • Poetry:
      • Resolves dependency versions.
      • Writes exact versions to poetry.lock.
      • Creates/uses a dedicated virtualenv.
    • poetry install recreates the environment exactly from the lock file.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • pip-based setup

    • python / python3
    • pip
    • venv / virtualenv / conda
    • requirements.txt

  • Poetry-based setup

    • python / python3
    • poetry CLI
    • pyproject.toml (project + dependency metadata)
    • poetry.lock (exact resolved versions)
    • Poetry-managed virtualenv

Technologies Used

  • Python
    • pip: built into Python ≥ 3.4
    • Poetry: separate tool (pipx install poetry or pip install poetry)
  • ML/GenAI
    • Dependencies: torch, transformers, langchain, faiss-cpu, llama-index, etc.
  • Rust (analogy)
    • Cargo in Rust ≈ Poetry in Python (project + dependency + build manager).
    • pip + venv ≈ manually managing crates and builds (less integrated).

Data Flow / Processing Stages (Conceptual)

  • pip

    • Input: requirements.txt or CLI package names.
    • Process:
      • Resolve versions (basic resolver).
      • Install into current environment.
    • Output: Updated environment with packages.

  • Poetry

    • Input: pyproject.toml.
    • Process:
      • Resolve dependencies → poetry.lock.
      • Create/activate virtualenv.
      • Install exact versions from lock file.
    • Output: Reproducible, isolated environment + project metadata.

API Endpoints / Contracts (CLI Commands as “API”)

  • pip

    • pip install <pkg>
    • pip install -r requirements.txt
    • pip freeze > requirements.txt
    • pip uninstall <pkg>

  • Poetry

    • poetry init (create pyproject.toml)
    • poetry add <pkg> / poetry remove <pkg>
    • poetry install (install from poetry.lock)
    • poetry update (update dependencies + lock)
    • poetry run <cmd> (run inside env)
    • poetry build / poetry publish

Model Lifecycle (Training / Deployment / Monitoring)

  • With pip

    • Training:
      • Use requirements.txt to share environment.
    • Deployment:
      • Dockerfile installs from requirements.txt.
    • Monitoring:
      • Manual tracking of dependency changes.

  • With Poetry

    • Training:
      • poetry.lock ensures exact versions across machines.
    • Deployment:
      • Build wheel/sdist with poetry build.
      • Use poetry export to generate requirements.txt for Docker.
    • Monitoring:
      • Easier to version project + dependencies together.

Scalability Considerations

  • For large ML/GenAI projects:
    • pip
      • Harder to maintain complex dependency graphs.
      • Frequent “dependency hell”.
    • Poetry
      • Better dependency resolution.
      • Lock file improves consistency across:
        • Dev
        • CI
        • Prod

Performance Considerations

  • pip

    • Simple, fast for small/simple environments.
    • No extra layer, just installs.

  • Poetry

    • Additional overhead:
      • Dependency resolution.
      • Managing virtualenvs.
    • But:
      • Saves time in debugging version conflicts.
      • Helps reproducibility, which is critical in large ML/LLM systems.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    subgraph pip_flow[Using pip]
        A[Project Folder] --> B[requirements.txt]
        B --> C[pip install -r requirements.txt]
        C --> D[Virtualenv / System Python]
    end

    subgraph poetry_flow[Using Poetry]
        E[Project Folder] --> F[pyproject.toml]
        F --> G[poetry add / poetry install]
        G --> H[poetry.lock]
        G --> I[Poetry-managed Virtualenv]
    end

    style pip_flow fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
    style poetry_flow fill:#f0f9ff,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px

Step-by-Step Flow

Using pip

  • Step 1: Create virtual environment
    • python -m venv .venv
  • Step 2: Activate environment
    • Linux/macOS: source .venv/bin/activate
    • Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
  • Step 3: Install dependencies
    • pip install fastapi uvicorn torch transformers
    • Save: pip freeze > requirements.txt

Using Poetry

  • Step 1: Initialize project
    • poetry init (or poetry new my_project)
  • Step 2: Add dependencies
    • poetry add fastapi uvicorn torch transformers
  • Step 3: Install & run
    • poetry install
    • poetry run uvicorn app:app --reload

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

Python Example – pip-based FastAPI + LLM Service

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install fastapi uvicorn transformers torch
pip freeze > requirements.txt

# app.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

app = FastAPI()

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("gpt2")

@app.post("/generate")
async def generate(prompt: str):
    inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt")
    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_length=50)
    text = tokenizer.decode(outputs[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
    return {"output": text}

Python Example – Poetry-based FastAPI + LLM Service

poetry new llm_service
cd llm_service
poetry add fastapi uvicorn transformers torch

# pyproject.toml (partial)
[tool.poetry]
name = "llm_service"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "LLM inference service"
authors = ["You <you@example.com>"]

[tool.poetry.dependencies]
python = "^3.10"
fastapi = "^0.111.0"
uvicorn = "^0.30.0"
transformers = "^4.40.0"
torch = "^2.2.0"

poetry run uvicorn llm_service.app:app --reload

Rust Analogy

  • Cargo (Rust):

    • Cargo.toml (like pyproject.toml)
    • Cargo.lock (like poetry.lock)
    • cargo build, cargo run, cargo test

  • Poetry (Python) plays a similar role:

    • Project metadata + dependency management + build.

Advantages

pip

  • Built-in, no extra tool required.
  • Simple and widely known.
  • Works with any environment manager (venv, conda, etc.).
  • Good for:
    • Small scripts
    • Simple ML experiments
    • Quick prototypes

Poetry

  • Single source of truth (pyproject.toml).
  • Reproducible builds with poetry.lock.
  • Integrated:
    • Virtualenv management
    • Build & publish
  • Better for:
    • Production-grade services
    • Team projects
    • Complex ML/GenAI pipelines (RAG, multi-service setups)

Limitations

pip

  • No lock file by default (though pip-tools can help).
  • Weaker dependency resolution experience (conflicts harder to manage).
  • No project metadata / build configuration out-of-the-box.
  • Requires separate tools for:
    • Virtualenv management
    • Packaging

Poetry

  • Additional learning curve.
  • Slightly more overhead in:
    • Setup
    • Dependency resolution
  • Some environments (e.g., minimal Docker images) may prefer:
    • poetry export → requirements.txt → pip install
  • Not always pre-installed; needs bootstrap step.

Interview Tips

  • Common Questions

    • “Compare pip and Poetry.”
    • “How do you ensure reproducible environments for ML experiments?”
    • “How would you package and deploy a FastAPI/LLM service?”
    • “How is Poetry similar to Cargo in Rust?”

  • Key Points to Remember

    • pip = installer; Poetry = full project/dependency manager.
    • Poetry uses pyproject.toml + poetry.lock.
    • For production ML/GenAI systems:
      • Lock files are critical for reproducibility.
    • Poetry integrates:
      • Virtualenv
      • Build
      • Publish

  • Tricky Areas

    • How to deploy Poetry-based project in Docker:
      • Often use poetry export -f requirements.txt and then pip install.
    • Mixing tools:
      • Using pip inside Poetry env vs using poetry add.
    • Explaining when you’d still choose pip:
      • Very simple scripts
      • Constrained environments

Real-World Example

Use Case: RAG-based LLM API Service

  • Scenario
    • You build a Python backend that:
      • Uses FastAPI for HTTP API.
      • Uses langchain / llama-index for RAG.
      • Uses faiss or a vector DB client (e.g., qdrant-client, weaviate-client).
      • Uses transformers or OpenAI client.

With pip

  • requirements.txt:
fastapi==0.111.0
uvicorn[standard]==0.30.0
langchain==0.2.0
faiss-cpu==1.8.0
transformers==4.40.0
torch==2.2.0
  • Pros:
    • Simple to set up.
  • Cons:
    • Updating dependencies can break environment unexpectedly.
    • Harder to guarantee same versions across team.

With Poetry

  • pyproject.toml (partial):
[tool.poetry]
name = "rag_service"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "RAG-based LLM API"
authors = ["You <you@example.com>"]

[tool.poetry.dependencies]
python = "^3.10"
fastapi = "^0.111.0"
uvicorn = {extras = ["standard"], version = "^0.30.0"}
langchain = "^0.2.0"
faiss-cpu = "^1.8.0"
transformers = "^4.40.0"
torch = "^2.2.0"

  • Workflow:

    • Devs run poetry install → identical environment.
    • CI uses poetry install --no-dev → same environment.
    • Docker:
      • poetry export -f requirements.txt --output requirements.txt
      • pip install -r requirements.txt inside container.

  • Benefits:

    • Reproducible RAG pipeline behavior across:
      • Local dev
      • CI tests
      • Production inference cluster.

In interviews, a crisp summary:

  • pip: “Low-level package installer; I pair it with venv and requirements.txt.”
  • Poetry: “High-level project and dependency manager that gives me pyproject.toml, a lock file, virtualenv management, and build/publish tooling—similar to Cargo in Rust. I prefer it for production ML/GenAI backends where reproducibility and team collaboration matter.”
Q23.HOW DO YOU MANAGE ENVIRONMENT ISOLATION? [Input Token: 706 | Output Token: 2920] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:
    Environment isolation is the practice of separating runtime environments so that dependencies, configurations, and resources for one application or service do not interfere with others (e.g., Python virtualenvs, Docker containers, Kubernetes namespaces, microservice sandboxes).

  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:

    • Ensures reproducible experiments and stable training/inference.
    • Allows different models/pipelines to use different Python/Rust versions, CUDA versions, and library stacks.
    • Critical for RAG, LLM inference services, and multi-tenant ML platforms where different workloads must not conflict.

  • Importance in Python/Rust backend interviews:

    • Enables safe microservices, multi-version APIs, and zero-downtime deployments.
    • Needed for secure multi-tenant SaaS, resource isolation, and performance tuning.
    • Core to containerized deployments (Docker, Kubernetes) and CI/CD pipelines.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

Common layers of environment isolation:

  • Language-level isolation
    • Python: venv, conda, poetry environments.
    • Rust: cargo workspaces, separate binaries, feature flags.
  • Process/container-level isolation
    • Docker containers per service/model.
    • cgroups + namespaces (Linux) for CPU/memory/network isolation.
  • Orchestration-level isolation
    • Kubernetes namespaces, pods, node pools.
    • Separate staging / prod clusters.
  • Data/config isolation
    • Separate config files, env vars, secrets per environment.
    • Separate databases, buckets, vector indexes per environment.
  • Network/security isolation
    • VPCs, security groups, service meshes.
    • Per-tenant or per-env network policies.

For GenAI systems:

  • Different environments for:
    • Model training vs inference vs evaluation.
    • Experimentation (new model versions) vs production (stable versions).
  • Isolated:
    • Python environments for different model stacks.
    • GPU resources (MIG, node pools).
    • Vector DB indexes per environment or tenant.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Runtime & dependency isolation
    • Python: venv, conda, poetry
    • Rust: cargo + separate crates/binaries
    • Docker images per service/model
  • Orchestration & infra
    • Kubernetes (namespaces, deployments, services)
    • Helm or Kustomize for per-env configuration
  • Config & secrets
    • .env files, environment variables
    • Vault/Secrets Manager/K8s Secrets
  • Data layer
    • Separate:
      • Postgres databases/schemas
      • S3 buckets / GCS buckets
      • Vector DB collections (e.g., myapp_docs_dev, myapp_docs_prod)

Data Flow and Processing Stages (Example: RAG Service)

  • Client → API Gateway
    • Routes to dev, staging, or prod endpoints.
  • API Service (FastAPI / Actix)
    • Runs in its own container with isolated environment.
    • Reads config from environment variables / config maps.
  • Model Inference Service
    • Separate container with its own dependencies (transformers, CUDA).
  • Vector DB
    • Separate collections or clusters per environment.
  • Monitoring
    • Per-environment dashboards and alerting.

API Endpoints & Contracts (Example)

  • Versioned endpoints per environment:

    • Dev: https://api-dev.example.com/v1/chat
    • Staging: https://api-staging.example.com/v1/chat
    • Prod: https://api.example.com/v1/chat

  • Example request/response (same contract, different environments):

POST /v1/chat
{
  "user_id": "123",
  "message": "Explain RAG architecture",
  "context": "docs"
}

200 OK
{
  "answer": "...",
  "sources": [
    {"doc_id": "doc_42", "score": 0.89}
  ],
  "model_version": "gpt-neo-1.3b-rag-v4"
}

Model Lifecycle & Environment Isolation

  • Training
    • Runs in isolated training environment (separate cluster or node pool).
    • Uses different dependencies (e.g., heavy training libs).
  • Evaluation
    • Separate environment, can run multiple candidate models.
  • Staging
    • Deployed candidate model with shadow traffic or limited users.
  • Production
    • Stable model, tight SLOs, autoscaling.
  • Monitoring
    • Metrics/logs/traces separated by environment labels.

Scalability Considerations

  • Use Kubernetes namespaces per environment:
    • dev, staging, prod, experiments.
  • Use node pools:
    • GPU nodes for inference/training.
    • CPU nodes for routing, preprocessing.
  • Separate autoscaling policies per environment:
    • Aggressive scaling for prod, conservative for dev.

Performance Considerations

  • Avoid dependency bloat in production images:
    • Separate minimal inference images from heavy training/experimentation images.
  • Use multi-stage Docker builds to keep images small.
  • Isolate noisy workloads:
    • Training jobs on separate nodes from latency-sensitive inference.
  • Use cgroups/K8s resource requests/limits to prevent resource contention.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    subgraph Dev[Dev Environment]
      D_API[Dev API (FastAPI)]
      D_MODEL[Dev Model Service]
      D_VEC[Dev Vector DB]
    end

    subgraph Staging[Staging Environment]
      S_API[Staging API]
      S_MODEL[Staging Model Service]
      S_VEC[Staging Vector DB]
    end

    subgraph Prod[Prod Environment]
      P_API[Prod API]
      P_MODEL[Prod Model Service]
      P_VEC[Prod Vector DB]
    end

    Client[Client / Frontend]

    Client -->|dev.example.com| D_API
    Client -->|staging.example.com| S_API
    Client -->|api.example.com| P_API

    D_API --> D_MODEL --> D_VEC
    S_API --> S_MODEL --> S_VEC
    P_API --> P_MODEL --> P_VEC

Step-by-Step Flow

Example: Deploying a New RAG Model with Environment Isolation

  • Step 1: Local / Dev

    • Create Python virtualenv or poetry env.
    • Implement RAG pipeline (embedding model, vector DB client).
    • Run Dockerized service locally (e.g., docker-compose).

  • Step 2: Staging

    • Build Docker image tagged rag-service:v2-staging.
    • Deploy to Kubernetes staging namespace:
      • Namespace: rag-staging
      • Deployment: rag-api-staging
      • ConfigMap: points to staging vector index.
    • Run A/B tests or shadow traffic.

  • Step 3: Production

    • Promote image to rag-service:v2-prod.
    • Deploy to prod namespace with separate:
      • Resource limits.
      • Autoscaling rules.
      • Vector index (rag_docs_prod).
    • Monitor metrics and logs separately by environment.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

Python: Virtualenv + Docker + FastAPI

# Python environment isolation
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install fastapi uvicorn sentence-transformers

# Freeze dependencies
pip freeze > requirements.txt

# app/main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
import os

ENV = os.getenv("APP_ENV", "dev")  # dev / staging / prod

app = FastAPI(title=f"RAG Service ({ENV})")

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok", "env": ENV}

# Dockerfile
FROM python:3.11-slim AS base

WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY app ./app
ENV APP_ENV=prod
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080"]
  • Deploy same image with different APP_ENV and config in dev/staging/prod.

Rust: Cargo + Actix-Web + Docker

# Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "rag_service"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
actix-web = "4"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

// src/main.rs
use actix_web::{get, App, HttpResponse, HttpServer, Responder};
use std::env;

#[get("/health")]
async fn health() -> impl Responder {
    let env_name = env::var("APP_ENV").unwrap_or_else(|_| "dev".into());
    HttpResponse::Ok().json(serde_json::json!({
        "status": "ok",
        "env": env_name
    }))
}

#[actix_web::main]
async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let env_name = env::var("APP_ENV").unwrap_or_else(|_| "dev".into());
    println!("Starting RAG service in {} environment", env_name);

    HttpServer::new(|| App::new().service(health))
        .bind(("0.0.0.0", 8080))?
        .run()
        .await
}

# Dockerfile for Rust service
FROM rust:1.77 as builder
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY . .
RUN cargo build --release

FROM debian:bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app/target/release/rag_service .
ENV APP_ENV=prod
CMD ["./rag_service"]
  • Different Kubernetes deployments set different APP_ENV and config maps.

Advantages

  • Reproducibility
    • Same code + same env = same behavior.
  • Safety
    • Changes in dev/staging don’t break prod.
  • Dependency flexibility
    • Different services/models can use conflicting library versions.
  • Security
    • Limits blast radius; isolates secrets, data, and network.
  • Performance isolation
    • Prevents noisy neighbors (e.g., training jobs) from impacting latency-critical inference.

Limitations

  • Operational complexity
    • More environments to manage, monitor, and secure.
  • Resource cost
    • Multiple environments mean more infra usage.
  • Config drift
    • Dev/staging/prod can diverge if not managed with IaC and strong processes.
  • Debugging complexity
    • Bugs that appear only in certain environments (e.g., different GPUs, drivers).

Interview Tips

  • Key points to mention:
    • Use virtualenv/conda/poetry for Python dependency isolation.
    • Use Docker containers and Kubernetes namespaces for runtime and infra isolation.
    • Use separate configs, secrets, and data stores per environment.
    • For GenAI:
      • Isolate model versions, vector indexes, and GPU resources.
  • Common interview questions:
    • How do you manage different dependencies for different microservices?
    • How do you safely roll out a new model version?
    • How do you separate dev/staging/prod for an ML system?
    • How do you isolate multi-tenant workloads for a SaaS/LLM platform?
  • Tricky areas:
    • Handling migrations (DB/schema) across environments.
    • Ensuring config parity while allowing environment-specific overrides.
    • Balancing cost vs isolation (e.g., shared vs dedicated clusters).

Real-World Example

Multi-Environment RAG Chatbot Platform

  • Use case: Company provides a RAG-based internal knowledge chatbot.

  • Environments:

    • dev: For experimenting with new embedding models, chunking strategies.
    • staging: Mirrors prod data, used for load testing and evaluation.
    • prod: Serves employees with strict SLOs.

  • Isolation strategy:

    • Python:
      • rag-dev virtualenv with experimental libs.
      • rag-prod minimal env with pinned versions.
    • Docker/Kubernetes:
      • Namespaces: rag-dev, rag-staging, rag-prod.
      • Different autoscaling rules and resource limits.
    • Vector DB:
      • Collections: kb_dev, kb_staging, kb_prod.
    • Models:
      • embedding-dev: new model under test.
      • embedding-prod: stable, validated model.
    • API:
      • dev-chat.example.com, staging-chat.example.com, chat.example.com.

  • Outcome:

    • New RAG improvements are tested end-to-end in dev/staging.
    • Production remains stable and isolated from experimental changes.
    • Easy rollback by switching traffic back to previous deployment in prod.
Q24.WHAT IS WSGI? [Input Token: 705 | Output Token: 3121] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:
    WSGI (Web Server Gateway Interface) is a Python standard (PEP 3333) that defines a simple, universal interface between web servers (e.g., Gunicorn, uWSGI) and Python web applications/frameworks (e.g., Django, Flask).

  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:

    • Many ML/LLM services are exposed as HTTP APIs via Python backends.
    • Understanding WSGI helps you:
      • Deploy model inference services reliably.
      • Integrate with production web servers.
      • Reason about performance, concurrency, and scaling.

  • Importance in Python/Rust Backend interviews:

    • Core concept for Python web backend architecture.
    • Shows understanding of:
      • Server–application boundaries.
      • How frameworks like Flask/Django actually run.
      • Differences vs newer standards like ASGI (async).

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • WSGI is a protocol/contract, not a server or framework.

  • It defines:

    • How a server calls a Python application callable.
    • How the application:
      • Reads the request (from environ dict).
      • Sends the response (via start_response and return iterable).

  • Key concepts:

    • WSGI server:
      • Examples: Gunicorn, uWSGI, Waitress, mod_wsgi.
      • Handles:
        • HTTP parsing, sockets, concurrency (processes/threads).
        • Calls your WSGI app callable.
    • WSGI application:
      • A callable: app(environ, start_response) -> iterable.
      • Frameworks like Flask/Django expose this:
        • application = get_wsgi_application() (Django)
        • app = Flask(__name__) (Flask; app.wsgi_app under the hood).

  • Why WSGI exists:

    • Before WSGI: frameworks tied to specific servers.
    • With WSGI: plug-and-play:
      • Any WSGI-compliant app can run on any WSGI server.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • WSGI server:

    • Manages:
      • TCP connections
      • HTTP request/response parsing
      • Worker processes/threads
    • Calls the WSGI application for each request.

  • WSGI application callable:

    def application(environ, start_response):
    # environ: dict with request data
    # start_response: function to start HTTP response
    ...
    return [b"response body"]

  • Environment (environ):

    • A Python dict containing:
      • CGI-like variables:
        • REQUEST_METHOD, PATH_INFO, QUERY_STRING
        • CONTENT_TYPE, CONTENT_LENGTH
        • SERVER_NAME, SERVER_PORT
      • WSGI-specific keys:
        • wsgi.version, wsgi.url_scheme, wsgi.input, wsgi.errors
        • wsgi.multithread, wsgi.multiprocess, wsgi.run_once

  • start_response(status, response_headers, exc_info=None):

    • status: "200 OK", "404 Not Found", etc.
    • response_headers: list of (name, value) tuples.
    • Must be called before the first body bytes are yielded.

  • Response body:

    • An iterable yielding bytes:
      • return [b"Hello"]
      • Or a generator yielding bytes.

Technologies Used

  • Python frameworks:
    • Flask, Django, Pyramid, Bottle, Falcon (WSGI-based).
  • WSGI servers:
    • Gunicorn, uWSGI, Waitress, mod_wsgi, gevent (WSGI mode).
  • Infra tools:
    • Nginx / HAProxy as reverse proxies.
    • Systemd, Docker, Kubernetes for deployment.

Data Flow & Processing Stages

  • HTTP request → WSGI server → WSGI app:
    • Parse HTTP → build environ → call app(environ, start_response) → get body iterable → send HTTP response to client.

API Endpoints / Contracts (WSGI-Level)

  • WSGI defines one contract:
    • Callable signature: application(environ, start_response).
    • No routing, JSON, or REST semantics — those are done above WSGI in frameworks.

Model Lifecycle (in ML/GenAI context)

  • Training:
    • Offline; not WSGI-specific.
  • Serving / Inference:
    • Wrap model inference in a WSGI app:
      • Load model at process startup.
      • Expose /predict or /generate endpoints.
  • Deployment:
    • Use Gunicorn/uWSGI + Nginx.
    • Scale via processes/containers.
  • Monitoring:
    • Access logs at server (Nginx/Gunicorn).
    • Business metrics in app (latency, errors).

Scalability Considerations

  • Horizontal scaling:
    • Run multiple WSGI workers/processes.
    • Use a load balancer (Nginx, Kubernetes Service).
  • Vertical scaling:
    • More CPU/RAM per node.
  • Concurrency model:
    • Typically multi-process and/or multi-threaded.
    • Blocking I/O is OK; no native async (for that use ASGI).

Performance Considerations

  • Latency:
    • Preload models at worker start to avoid per-request load.
    • Use connection pooling for DB/vector DB.
  • Throughput:
    • Tune:
      • Number of workers.
      • Worker class (sync, gevent, etc. for I/O-bound).
  • Optimization:
    • Use uWSGI/Gunicorn with proper timeouts.
    • For heavy LLM inference, consider:
      • Separate inference server (e.g., vLLM, Triton) behind WSGI API.
      • Async (ASGI) for high-concurrency I/O.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    Client[User / Client] -->|HTTP Request| Nginx[Reverse Proxy (Nginx)]
    Nginx -->|Forward HTTP| WSGIServer[WSGI Server (Gunicorn/uWSGI)]
    subgraph PythonApp[Python Application]
        direction TB
        AppCallable[WSGI Application Callable<br/>application(environ, start_response)]
        Framework[Flask/Django App Logic]
        Model[ML/LLM Inference / Business Logic]

        AppCallable --> Framework --> Model
    end

    WSGIServer -->|Call with environ & start_response| AppCallable
    AppCallable -->|Iterable of bytes| WSGIServer
    WSGIServer -->|HTTP Response| Nginx --> Client

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Client sends request:

    • Browser / service sends HTTP GET /predict?text=....

  2. Reverse proxy (optional):

    • Nginx receives request.
    • Forwards to WSGI server (Gunicorn) at localhost:8000.

  3. WSGI server processes request:

    • Parses HTTP.
    • Builds environ dict.
    • Creates start_response function.
    • Calls application(environ, start_response).

  4. WSGI application handles logic:

    • Reads path, query, body from environ.
    • Routes to the correct handler (framework).
    • Executes business/ML logic (e.g., LLM inference).

  5. Response construction:

    • Application calls start_response("200 OK", headers).
    • Returns an iterable of bytes as body.

  6. Server sends response:

    • WSGI server iterates over body iterable.
    • Streams bytes back to client as HTTP response.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

High-Level Python Implementation (Pure WSGI)

# simple_wsgi_app.py
def application(environ, start_response):
    path = environ.get("PATH_INFO", "/")
    method = environ.get("REQUEST_METHOD", "GET")

    if path == "/":
        status = "200 OK"
        response_body = b"Hello, WSGI!"
    else:
        status = "404 Not Found"
        response_body = b"Not Found"

    headers = [
        ("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8"),
        ("Content-Length", str(len(response_body))),
    ]
    start_response(status, headers)
    return [response_body]

Running with a WSGI Server (Gunicorn)

gunicorn simple_wsgi_app:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 4

WSGI with a Framework (Flask Example)

from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/predict", methods=["POST"])
def predict():
    payload = request.get_json()
    text = payload["text"]
    # Call your ML/LLM model here
    prediction = {"label": "positive", "score": 0.95}
    return jsonify(prediction)

# app.wsgi_app is the WSGI callable Gunicorn will use
wsgi_app = app.wsgi_app

Run:

gunicorn my_flask_module:wsgi_app --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 4

Rust Side (Interoperating with WSGI)

  • Rust does not use WSGI; it has its own web stacks:
    • Actix-web, Axum, Warp, Rocket.
  • Interoperability patterns:
    • Option 1: Rust as a backend service; Python WSGI app calls Rust via:
      • HTTP (Rust service exposes REST/gRPC).
      • FFI (e.g., pyo3 / maturin to call Rust from Python).
    • Option 2: Rust as the main HTTP server:
      • Expose HTTP API directly from Rust.
      • Python ML/LLM service runs separately (WSGI/ASGI) and Rust calls it.

Example: Python WSGI app calling Rust microservice

import requests
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

RUST_SERVICE_URL = "http://rust-service:9000/score"

@app.route("/score", methods=["POST"])
def score():
    data = request.get_json()
    # Forward to Rust service
    resp = requests.post(RUST_SERVICE_URL, json=data, timeout=1.0)
    return jsonify(resp.json()), resp.status_code

wsgi_app = app.wsgi_app

Advantages

  • Standardized interface:
    • Any WSGI server ↔ any WSGI framework.
  • Mature ecosystem:
    • Battle-tested servers (Gunicorn, uWSGI) and frameworks.
  • Simplicity:
    • Very small core: just application(environ, start_response).
  • Production-ready:
    • Used widely in real-world deployments (Django/Flask apps).

Limitations

  • No native async support:
    • Designed pre-asyncio.
    • For high-concurrency async I/O, ASGI is preferred.
  • Low-level:
    • No routing, JSON, or sessions — frameworks must build on top.
  • Not ideal for streaming-heavy / websockets:
    • Harder to implement modern real-time patterns vs ASGI.

Interview Tips

  • Key points to remember:

    • WSGI is a specification, not a server or framework.
    • Signature: application(environ, start_response).
    • environ is a dict; start_response sets status & headers.
    • Distinguish WSGI server vs WSGI app vs framework.

  • Common interview questions:

    • What is WSGI and why do we need it?
    • How does a WSGI request/response cycle work?
    • Difference between WSGI and ASGI?
    • How does Flask/Django use WSGI under the hood?
    • How would you deploy a Flask/Django app in production?

  • Tricky areas:

    • Confusing WSGI with a web server (like Nginx).
    • Forgetting that WSGI itself is sync/blocking.
    • Mixing framework-level concepts (routing) with WSGI-level concepts (callable).

Real-World Example

Use Case: LLM Inference API using WSGI

  • Scenario:

    • You build an internal text classification or RAG service.
    • Expose it via HTTP for other microservices.

  • Architecture:

    • Nginx (reverse proxy, TLS termination).
    • Gunicorn (WSGI server, 4–8 workers).
    • Flask/Django app (WSGI application):
      • Loads an LLM or embedding model at startup.
      • Offers endpoints:
        • POST /embed → returns embeddings (for vector DB).
        • POST /generate → returns LLM completions.
    • Vector DB (e.g., Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate) for RAG.

  • Flow:

    1. Client sends POST /generate with query.
    2. WSGI app:
      • Uses embedding model → query vector.
      • Queries vector DB for top-k docs.
      • Constructs prompt and calls LLM (local or external).
    3. Returns generated answer as JSON.

  • Deployment:

    gunicorn llm_service.wsgi_app --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 4
    • Nginx forwards /api/ traffic to localhost:8000.

This pattern is extremely common in ML/GenAI backends, and understanding WSGI helps you reason about deployment, scaling, and performance of such services.

Q25.WHAT IS ASGI? [Input Token: 704 | Output Token: 3132] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:
    ASGI (Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface) is a Python standard for asynchronous web servers and applications. It’s the successor to WSGI, designed to support:

    • Async I/O
    • Long-lived connections (WebSockets)
    • HTTP/2, SSE, background tasks

  • Why important in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:

    • Modern LLM apps (chat, streaming responses, real-time dashboards) often require:
      • Streaming tokens to clients
      • WebSockets for interactive chat
      • High concurrency for inference APIs
    • ASGI is the foundation of frameworks like FastAPI, widely used for ML/GenAI microservices.

  • Why important in Python/Rust backend interviews:

    • Shows understanding of:
      • Async Python (async/await)
      • Modern web stack (FastAPI, Starlette, Django Channels)
      • High-performance APIs vs legacy WSGI apps
    • Relevant when designing high-throughput, low-latency backends for inference, RAG systems, etc.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • What ASGI is:

    • A specification (not a framework) that defines:
      • How a Python async application talks to an async server
      • A standard interface: scope, receive, send

  • Key ideas:

    • ASGI application is a callable:
      async def app(scope, receive, send):
    ...
    • Scope:
      • Metadata about the connection:
        • Type: "http", "websocket", "lifespan"
        • Path, headers, client IP, etc.
    • Receive:
      • Async callable to get events from the client/server:
        • HTTP request body chunks
        • WebSocket messages
        • Disconnect events
    • Send:
      • Async callable to send events back:
        • HTTP response headers/body
        • WebSocket messages
        • Close events

  • How it compares to WSGI:

    • WSGI:
      • Synchronous
      • HTTP-only
      • Request–response only
    • ASGI:
      • Asynchronous
      • Supports HTTP + WebSockets + other protocols
      • Supports long-lived connections and streaming

Technical Specifications

Components

  • ASGI Server:

    • Examples: Uvicorn, Hypercorn, Daphne
    • Responsibilities:
      • Handle TCP/HTTP/WebSocket
      • Convert network events into ASGI events (scope, receive, send)
      • Run the ASGI app coroutine

  • ASGI Application / Framework:

    • Examples:
      • FastAPI (built on Starlette)
      • Starlette
      • Django Channels (ASGI support)
      • Quart
    • Responsibilities:
      • Routing
      • Middleware
      • Request/response abstraction
      • Business logic

  • Middleware:

    • ASGI middleware wraps the app to:
      • Add logging, auth, CORS
      • Modify scope, receive, send

Technologies Used

  • Python:
    • asyncio, uvloop
    • Frameworks: FastAPI, Starlette, Django Channels
  • Rust:
    • Often used to build:
      • High-performance proxies/load balancers in front of ASGI
      • Async microservices that call ASGI-based Python inference APIs
    • Libraries: tokio, hyper, axum (Rust async web frameworks)

Data Flow and Processing Stages

  • Incoming request:
    • Client → ASGI server (Uvicorn) → ASGI app
  • Inside ASGI app:
    • Parse scope → route → handler
    • Handler may:
      • Call ML/LLM model
      • Query vector DB (RAG)
      • Stream tokens
  • Outgoing response:
    • Handler uses send (via framework abstractions) → ASGI server → client

API Endpoints and Contracts (Typical)

  • HTTP:

    • POST /predict
      • Request: JSON { "input": "...", "params": {...} }
      • Response: JSON { "output": "...", "latency_ms": 123 }
    • POST /chat/stream
      • Response: text/event-stream or chunked HTTP for token streaming

  • WebSocket:

    • GET /ws/chat
      • Contract:
        • Client sends: { "message": "Hi", "session_id": "..." }
        • Server streams back: tokens or messages over WebSocket

Model Lifecycle (in ASGI-based ML Service)

  • Training:
    • Offline; models stored in object storage (S3, GCS)
  • Loading:
    • On app startup (lifespan scope)
    • Load model into memory/GPU
  • Inference:
    • ASGI endpoint calls model:
      • CPU/GPU, possibly via separate worker
  • Evaluation & Monitoring:
    • Logging latency, errors, token throughput
    • Prometheus metrics from ASGI app
  • Deployment:
    • ASGI app packaged in Docker
    • Served by Uvicorn/Gunicorn (uvicorn workers) behind Nginx/Envoy
  • Scaling:
    • Horizontal scaling via Kubernetes, autoscaling on QPS/latency

Scalability Considerations

  • Concurrency:
    • ASGI + async allows:
      • Many concurrent connections
      • Efficient I/O (DB calls, vector DB queries, external APIs)
  • Streaming:
    • WebSockets/SSE for streaming LLM tokens
  • Separation of concerns:
    • Python ASGI for orchestration + inference
    • Rust microservices for high-throughput preprocessing or gateway

Performance Considerations

  • Latency:
    • Use uvloop with Uvicorn
    • Offload heavy CPU-bound work to:
      • ThreadPool / ProcessPool
      • Separate inference workers
  • Throughput:
    • Use async DB clients
    • Connection pooling
    • Efficient serialization (ujson/orjson)
  • Backpressure:
    • Handle slow clients in streaming endpoints
    • Timeouts, cancellation, rate limits

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    Client[Client (Browser / Mobile / Service)] -->|HTTP/WebSocket| ASGIServer[ASGI Server\n(Uvicorn/Hypercorn)]
    ASGIServer -->|scope, receive, send| ASGIApp[ASGI App\n(FastAPI/Starlette)]
    ASGIApp -->|Async calls| ModelService[Model / LLM Service]
    ASGIApp -->|Async calls| VectorDB[Vector DB\n(Pinecone, Qdrant, PGVector)]
    ASGIApp -->|Async I/O| OtherAPIs[Other Services\n(Auth, Cache, DB)]
    ModelService --> ASGIApp
    VectorDB --> ASGIApp
    OtherAPIs --> ASGIApp
    ASGIApp --> ASGIServer --> Client

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Connection Established

    • Client sends HTTP/WebSocket request.
    • ASGI server (Uvicorn) accepts the connection and builds a scope dict.

  2. ASGI App Handling

    • Server calls: await app(scope, receive, send)
    • ASGI app (e.g., FastAPI) routes based on scope["path"] and method.
    • Handler runs:
      • Async DB calls
      • LLM inference
      • Vector search
      • Potentially streams response chunks.

  3. Response / Streaming

    • App uses send (via framework) to send:
      • HTTP response headers + body
      • Or WebSocket messages
    • When done, connection is closed or kept alive (HTTP/2, WebSocket).

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

High-Level Python ASGI Implementation (Bare ASGI)

# minimal_asgi_app.py
import json

async def app(scope, receive, send):
    assert scope["type"] == "http"

    # Wait for request body
    event = await receive()
    body = event.get("body", b"")
    data = json.loads(body or b"{}")

    response = {"message": "Hello from ASGI", "input": data}

    await send({
        "type": "http.response.start",
        "status": 200,
        "headers": [
            (b"content-type", b"application/json"),
        ],
    })
    await send({
        "type": "http.response.body",
        "body": json.dumps(response).encode("utf-8"),
    })

Run with Uvicorn:

uvicorn minimal_asgi_app:app --reload

FastAPI ASGI App for LLM Inference

# app.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    prompt: str

@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(req: ChatRequest):
    # Call to LLM (sync or async)
    # For demo, just echo
    return {"response": f"Echo: {req.prompt}"}

Run:

uvicorn app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

Streaming Tokens via WebSocket (Python)

# ws_app.py
from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket

app = FastAPI()

@app.websocket("/ws/chat")
async def chat_ws(ws: WebSocket):
    await ws.accept()
    try:
        while True:
            data = await ws.receive_text()
            # Fake streaming tokens
            for token in ["Hello", ",", " world", "!"]:
                await ws.send_text(token)
            # In real app, stream from LLM
    except Exception:
        await ws.close()

Rust Integration Pattern

  • Pattern:
    • Rust service as:
      • API gateway / load balancer
      • Preprocessing or postprocessing service
    • Calls Python ASGI service via HTTP/JSON or gRPC.
// Simplified Rust client using reqwest to call ASGI/LLM service
use reqwest::Client;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ChatRequest {
    prompt: String,
}

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct ChatResponse {
    response: String,
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let client = Client::new();
    let req = ChatRequest {
        prompt: "Hello".into(),
    };

    let res = client
        .post("http://localhost:8000/chat")
        .json(&req)
        .send()
        .await?
        .json::<ChatResponse>()
        .await?;

    println!("LLM says: {}", res.response);
    Ok(())
}

Advantages

  • Modern async support:
    • Efficient I/O, high concurrency.
  • Supports WebSockets and streaming:
    • Ideal for LLM token streaming, real-time dashboards, chat apps.
  • Ecosystem:
    • FastAPI, Starlette, Django Channels, etc.
  • Backward-compatible:
    • Can wrap WSGI apps inside ASGI (via adapters).
  • Simple interface:
    • scope, receive, send is minimal yet powerful.

Limitations

  • Complexity:
    • Async programming introduces:
      • Event loop management
      • Concurrency bugs (race conditions)
  • CPU-bound workloads:
    • Async won’t speed up heavy CPU-bound ML inference directly.
    • Need separate workers / multiprocessing / GPU services.
  • Learning curve:
    • Understanding ASGI events, scopes, and async patterns is non-trivial.
  • Debugging:
    • Harder than synchronous WSGI apps in some cases.

Interview Tips

  • Key points to remember:

    • ASGI is a spec, not a framework.
    • It is the async successor to WSGI.
    • Core signature: async def app(scope, receive, send).
    • Supports HTTP + WebSockets + lifespan.
    • Foundation of FastAPI and modern Python web stack.

  • Common interview questions:

    • What is ASGI and how is it different from WSGI?
    • Why is ASGI important for real-time applications (e.g., chat, LLM streaming)?
    • How does an ASGI server interact with an ASGI app?
    • How would you design a high-throughput LLM inference API with ASGI?
    • How do you handle CPU-bound tasks in an ASGI app?

  • Tricky areas:

    • Mixing sync and async code:
      • When to use run_in_threadpool.
    • WebSocket lifecycle:
      • Connect, receive, send, close.
    • Backward compatibility:
      • Using WSGI apps under ASGI (e.g., WSGIMiddleware in Starlette/FastAPI).

Real-World Example

  • Use case: RAG-based Chatbot with Streaming Responses

    • Architecture:

      • ASGI app (FastAPI):
        • /chat (HTTP) for non-streaming responses.
        • /ws/chat (WebSocket) for token streaming.
      • LLM backend:
        • Local model (PyTorch) or remote (OpenAI, Anthropic).
      • Vector DB:
        • Qdrant / Pinecone / PGVector for document search.
      • Rust gateway (optional):
        • Rate limiting, auth, request routing.

    • Flow:

      1. Client connects via WebSocket to /ws/chat.
      2. ASGI app receives user question.
      3. ASGI app:
        • Runs vector search (async call to vector DB).
        • Builds prompt with retrieved context.
        • Calls LLM and streams tokens as they arrive.
      4. Tokens are sent over WebSocket using ASGI send.
      5. Client renders streaming chat UI.

    • This pattern is standard for production-grade GenAI apps and heavily relies on ASGI capabilities.

Q26.HOW DOES FLASK HANDLE REQUESTS INTERNALLY? [Input Token: 706 | Output Token: 3514] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:
    How Flask internally processes an HTTP request from the moment it hits the server socket until a response is returned to the client.
  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:
    • Many ML/GenAI systems expose models via HTTP APIs (Flask/FastAPI).
    • Understanding request handling is key to building RAG APIs, model inference endpoints, and webhooks for pipelines.
  • Importance in Python/Rust Backend interviews:
    • Tests understanding of WSGI, middleware, routing, threading, and request context.
    • Useful for debugging performance, concurrency, and production deployment (uWSGI, Gunicorn, etc.).

Architecture / Concept Explanation

Flask is a WSGI-based micro web framework. It doesn’t handle sockets itself in production; a WSGI server calls Flask with the request environment.

High-level internal flow:

  • 1. WSGI Server → Flask App

    • A WSGI server (e.g., Gunicorn, uWSGI, Waitress, or Flask’s dev server using werkzeug.serving) receives the HTTP request.
    • It constructs a WSGI environ dict and a start_response callable.
    • It calls the Flask app object: response_iterable = app(environ, start_response).

  • 2. Flask App as a WSGI Application

    • Flask.__call__ delegates to wsgi_app.
    • wsgi_app:
      • Creates request and application contexts.
      • Dispatches to the correct view function via the URL map.
      • Handles before/after request hooks, error handlers, and teardown.

  • 3. Request Context & Globals

    • Builds a Request object from environ.
    • Pushes RequestContext to a thread-/greenlet-local stack.
    • Enables flask.request, flask.g, flask.session as proxies to the current context.

  • 4. Routing

    • Uses werkzeug.routing.Map and Rule to match PATH_INFO and HTTP method.
    • Finds the correct view function and extracts URL parameters.

  • 5. View Function Execution

    • Executes before_request and before_app_request hooks.
    • Calls the matched view function.
    • View returns something convertible to a Response:
      • str, dict (if using jsonify or Flask>=2 convenience), tuple, or Response object.

  • 6. Response Creation

    • Wraps the return value using make_response.
    • Runs after_request hooks to modify response (headers, cookies, etc.).
    • Converts Response into a WSGI iterable and calls start_response.

  • 7. Teardown

    • Executes teardown_request and teardown_appcontext handlers.
    • Pops request and app contexts, cleaning up thread-local state.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Flask core
    • Flask (WSGI app)
    • Request, Response
    • RequestContext, AppContext
    • URL routing: url_map, Rule, MapAdapter
  • Werkzeug (under the hood)
    • WSGI utilities
    • Request/response wrappers
    • Routing and URL building
  • Context Globals
    • flask.request, flask.session, flask.g, flask.current_app

Data Flow & Processing Stages

  1. HTTP Layer

    • TCP connection → HTTP request.
    • Handled by web/WSGI server (Gunicorn/uWSGI/Dev server).

  2. WSGI Layer

    • Server builds environ (headers, path, query, body, etc.).
    • Calls app(environ, start_response).

  3. Flask WSGI App

    • Flask.__call__ → Flask.wsgi_app(environ, start_response).

  4. Context Setup

    • Create Request from environ.
    • Push AppContext and RequestContext.

  5. Routing & Dispatch

    • Match route:
      • adapter = self.url_map.bind_to_environ(environ)
      • endpoint, values = adapter.match()
    • Lookup view function: view = self.view_functions[endpoint].

  6. View Execution

    • Run:
      • before_request / before_app_request
      • View function
      • after_request / after_app_request

  7. Response & WSGI Return

    • Build Response object.
    • Call start_response(status, headers).
    • Return body iterable.

  8. Teardown & Cleanup

    • Run teardown callbacks.
    • Pop contexts.

Technologies & Libraries

  • Python
    • Flask (core framework)
    • Werkzeug (WSGI, routing, request/response)
  • WSGI Servers
    • Gunicorn, uWSGI, Waitress, Hypercorn
  • For ML/GenAI APIs
    • PyTorch / TensorFlow for models
    • LangChain, LlamaIndex for RAG
    • Vector DBs (e.g., Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, FAISS)
  • Infra
    • Nginx/Envoy as reverse proxy
    • Docker/Kubernetes for deployment

API Endpoints & Contracts

Example typical Flask endpoint contract:

  • Endpoint: POST /v1/llm/generate
  • Request:
    • JSON body: { "prompt": "string", "max_tokens": 256, "temperature": 0.7 }
  • Response:
    • JSON: { "completion": "string", "latency_ms": 123, "model": "my-llm" }

Flask internally:

  • Matches /v1/llm/generate → generate() view.
  • Parses JSON via request.get_json().
  • Returns jsonify(...) → Response.

Model Lifecycle Integration (in an ML/GenAI backend)

  • Training

    • Offline; not handled by Flask itself.
    • Flask may expose endpoints to trigger training jobs.

  • Evaluation

    • Endpoints to run evaluation or fetch metrics.

  • Deployment

    • Flask app loads model at startup:
      • model = load_model() in global or app factory.
    • Endpoints call model’s predict / generate.

  • Monitoring

    • Middleware for logging:
      • Latency, status codes, errors.
    • Metrics exporters (Prometheus, OpenTelemetry).

Scalability Considerations

  • Flask itself is single-process, single-thread by default (dev server).
  • For production:
    • Use multi-worker WSGI server (Gunicorn with --workers).
    • Optionally async workers (gevent/eventlet) for I/O-bound tasks.
  • Scaling ML/GenAI inference:
    • Use model server processes per worker.
    • Offload heavy tasks to:
      • Background workers (Celery/RQ)
      • Separate inference microservice (possibly Rust for performance).
  • Use reverse proxy (Nginx) for:
    • Load balancing
    • TLS termination
    • Static file offload

Performance Considerations

  • Latency
    • Minimize per-request overhead in before_request/after_request.
    • Pre-load models and vector indexes on startup, not per request.
  • Throughput
    • Increase WSGI workers.
    • Use batching for model inference if possible.
  • Optimization
    • Use ujson/orjson for JSON.
    • Avoid heavy global locks.
    • Use connection pooling for DB/vector DB.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    Client[Client (Browser / LLM Client)] -->|HTTP Request| WebServer[Nginx / Load Balancer]
    WebServer -->|WSGI| WSGIServer[Gunicorn / uWSGI]
    WSGIServer -->|environ, start_response| FlaskApp[Flask WSGI App]

    subgraph FlaskAppInternal[Flask Internal Flow]
        A[Create App & Request Context] --> B[Routing via url_map]
        B --> C[Run before_request Hooks]
        C --> D[Execute View Function]
        D --> E[Create Response Object]
        E --> F[Run after_request Hooks]
        F --> G[Teardown & Pop Contexts]
    end

    FlaskApp --> FlaskAppInternal
    FlaskAppInternal -->|status, headers, body iterable| WSGIServer
    WSGIServer -->|HTTP Response| WebServer --> Client

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. WSGI Entry

    • WSGI server receives request and calls app(environ, start_response).

  2. Context + Routing

    • Flask builds Request, pushes contexts, matches route to view.

  3. View → Response → Cleanup

    • Runs hooks, executes view, builds Response, returns via WSGI, then tears down contexts.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

High-Level Python Implementation (Flask)

from flask import Flask, request, jsonify, g

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.before_request
def before():
    # Example: attach request ID or start timer
    g.start_time = request.headers.get("X-Request-Start")

@app.route("/v1/llm/generate", methods=["POST"])
def generate():
    data = request.get_json()
    prompt = data["prompt"]
    # Imagine: call to ML/LLM inference
    completion = run_model_inference(prompt)
    return jsonify({"completion": completion})

@app.after_request
def after(response):
    # Example: set headers, logging, etc.
    response.headers["X-Powered-By"] = "Flask"
    return response

def run_model_inference(prompt: str) -> str:
    # Placeholder: call to model or external service
    return f"Echo: {prompt}"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Dev server; not for production
    app.run(debug=True)

Internally, each request goes through:

  • WSGI → app(environ, start_response) → wsgi_app
  • Contexts → routing → before_request → generate() → after_request.

Rust Side (For High-Performance Microservice)

In real systems, you might:

  • Use Flask as API gateway or orchestration layer.
  • Use Rust (e.g., Actix-web, Axum) for heavy or latency-critical parts.

Example: Rust microservice for vector search; Flask calls it:

// Simplified Rust Axum handler
use axum::{routing::post, Router, Json};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct SearchRequest {
    query: String,
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct SearchResponse {
    results: Vec<String>,
}

async fn search_handler(Json(req): Json<SearchRequest>) -> Json<SearchResponse> {
    // Perform vector search / heavy compute
    let results = vec![format!("Result for '{}'", req.query)];
    Json(SearchResponse { results })
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let app = Router::new().route("/search", post(search_handler));
    axum::Server::bind(&"0.0.0.0:8080".parse().unwrap())
        .serve(app.into_make_service())
        .await
        .unwrap();
}

Flask then calls this service inside a view:

import requests
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/v1/search", methods=["POST"])
def search():
    payload = request.get_json()
    resp = requests.post("http://rust-service:8080/search", json=payload, timeout=2)
    return jsonify(resp.json())

Advantages

  • Simplicity
    • Clear WSGI-based architecture.
    • Easy to understand lifecycle: request → context → view → response.
  • Extensibility
    • Hooks: before_request, after_request, teardown_request.
    • Blueprints for modularization.
  • Compatibility
    • Works with any WSGI server.
    • Integrates well with ML/GenAI stacks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, LangChain).
  • Fine-grained control
    • Direct access to environ, headers, and low-level request handling if needed.

Limitations

  • Synchronous by default
    • Not ideal for high-concurrency long-polling or streaming without extra tools.
  • Global context pattern
    • Relies on context-local proxies (request, g), which can be misused.
  • Scaling
    • Requires external WSGI servers and process management.
  • Less modern than ASGI frameworks
    • FastAPI/Starlette provide async-first design and better for streaming LLM responses.

Interview Tips

  • Key points to remember

    • Flask is a WSGI application; it does not handle sockets directly.
    • Request flow: WSGI → wsgi_app → context → routing → hooks → view → response → teardown.
    • Explain request/app context and flask.request, flask.g.
    • Mention Werkzeug as the underlying toolkit.

  • Common interview questions

    • How does Flask handle a request internally from WSGI call to response?
    • What are request context and application context in Flask?
    • How does Flask’s routing work (URL map, endpoint, view function)?
    • How would you handle global state or DB connections per request?
    • How to integrate Flask with a model inference pipeline?

  • Tricky areas

    • Difference between dev server and production deployment (Gunicorn/uWSGI).
    • Thread-safety and the role of context-local proxies.
    • How before_request, after_request, and teardown_request differ.

Real-World Example

Use-case: A RAG-based LLM API using Flask.

  • Flow:

    1. Client calls POST /v1/rag/query with a user question.
    2. Flask receives request via WSGI server.
    3. before_request:
      • Start latency timer, attach request ID.
    4. View function:
      • Parse JSON (request.get_json()).
      • Use vector DB client to retrieve relevant docs.
      • Call LLM (local model or external API) with prompt + retrieved context.
      • Construct JSON response.
    5. after_request:
      • Add latency metrics header.
      • Log request + response metadata.
    6. Teardown:
      • Close any per-request resources (DB sessions, tracing spans).

  • Code sketch:

from flask import Flask, request, jsonify, g
import time

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.before_request
def start_timer():
    g.start_time = time.time()

@app.route("/v1/rag/query", methods=["POST"])
def rag_query():
    payload = request.get_json()
    query = payload["query"]

    # 1) Retrieve docs from vector DB (pseudo-code)
    docs = vector_db_search(query)

    # 2) Build prompt with retrieved docs
    prompt = build_rag_prompt(query, docs)

    # 3) Call LLM inference (local or remote)
    answer = llm_generate(prompt)

    return jsonify({"answer": answer, "docs": docs})

@app.after_request
def add_timing_header(response):
    if hasattr(g, "start_time"):
        latency = time.time() - g.start_time
        response.headers["X-Latency-ms"] = str(int(latency * 1000))
    return response

Understanding how Flask internally handles this request—from WSGI to context, routing, and hooks—helps you design robust, scalable ML/GenAI APIs and answer system-design questions confidently.

Q27.WHAT ARE PYTHON TYPE HINTS? [Input Token: 705 | Output Token: 2875] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:

    • Python type hints (a.k.a. type annotations) are optional syntax to declare the expected types of variables, function parameters, and return values.
    • Introduced in PEP 484, enhanced by later PEPs (PEP 563, 585, 604, 649, etc.).

  • Why important in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:

    • Production ML/GenAI systems are large and complex; type hints:
      • Reduce bugs in data pipelines, model interfaces, and inference services.
      • Make contracts between components (e.g., feature extractors, vector DB clients, LLM wrappers) explicit.
    • They are often required in modern codebases using mypy, pyright, or pydantic.

  • Why important in Python/Rust backend interviews:

    • Rust is strongly typed; interviewers often check if you can bring similar rigor to Python using type hints.
    • Essential for:
      • Clean API contracts (FastAPI, gRPC).
      • Large microservices and distributed systems.
      • Refactoring safely and enabling better IDE support.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • Core idea

    • Add metadata about types without changing Python’s runtime semantics.
    • Static type checkers analyze these hints to find errors before runtime.

  • How it works conceptually

    • You annotate:
      • Function params: def f(x: int) -> str: ...
      • Variables: count: int = 0
      • Classes: attributes, methods, generics.
    • Tools (mypy, pyright, IDE) read annotations and:
      • Validate type consistency.
      • Provide autocompletion and refactor support.

  • In ML/GenAI systems

    • Type hints clarify:
      • Input/output schemas for:
        • Data preprocessing functions.
        • Feature engineering pipelines.
        • Embedding functions and vector search clients.
        • RAG pipelines and LLM wrappers.
      • Shapes and types of tensors (using typing, numpy.typing, or custom TypedDict/Protocol).

  • In backend services

    • Frameworks like FastAPI use type hints to:
      • Auto-generate OpenAPI schemas.
      • Validate request/response bodies.
      • Integrate with Pydantic models for runtime validation.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Language features

    • typing module: List, Dict, Tuple, Union, Optional, Callable, TypeVar, Generic, Protocol, TypedDict, Literal, etc.
    • Python 3.9+: built-in generics: list[int], dict[str, int].
    • Python 3.10+: X | Y union operator.
    • Python 3.11+: typing.Self, better error messages, etc.

  • Static analysis tools

    • mypy, pyright, pyre, pytype.
