Advantages

  • Reduced hallucinations

    • Answers grounded in retrieved documents rather than pure parametric memory.

  • Up-to-date knowledge

    • No need to retrain LLM for new data; just update index.

  • Data privacy & control

    • Keep proprietary data in your own vector DB; use LLM as stateless compute.

  • Cost-effective vs fine-tuning

    • Typically cheaper/faster than frequent fine-tuning cycles.

  • Explainability

    • Can return source documents and citations.

  • Multi-tenant / domain-specific

    • Use metadata filters to isolate tenants or domains.

Limitations

  • Garbage in, garbage out

    • If retrieval returns irrelevant or low-quality docs, the LLM answer degrades.

  • Context window limits

    • Only a subset of retrieved docs can fit into the prompt.

  • Latency

    • Extra steps (embedding + vector search) add latency vs plain LLM.

  • Index maintenance

    • Need pipelines to ingest, chunk, embed, and reindex data.

  • Complexity

    • More moving parts: vector DB, LLM service, embedding service, orchestration.

  • Security / access control

    • Must enforce document-level permissions at retrieval time.

Interview Tips

  • Common questions

    • What is RAG and why is it needed?
    • Compare RAG vs fine-tuning:
      • When to use which? Can they be combined?
    • Explain the RAG architecture end-to-end.
    • How to evaluate a RAG system?
    • How to reduce hallucinations in RAG?
    • How do you scale a RAG system to millions of documents?
    • How would you implement RAG with Python + FastAPI or Rust + Axum?

  • Key points to remember

    • RAG = retrieve first, then generate.
    • Separate indexing pipeline from query-time pipeline.
    • Emphasize:
      • Chunking strategy
      • Embedding choice
      • Retrieval quality
      • Prompt design
    • Mention vector DBs and ANN.

  • Tricky areas interviewers focus on

    • Handling access control / multi-tenancy in retrieval.
    • Dealing with stale data and reindexing.
    • Combining:
      • Keyword + vector search (hybrid)
      • Rerankers for better retrieval quality
    • How to log and monitor RAG performance in production.

Real-World Example

  • Use case: Internal enterprise knowledge assistant

  • Scenario

    • Company wants a chatbot for:
      • HR policies
      • Engineering docs
      • Runbooks
      • Confluence pages, Google Docs, GitHub READMEs

  • RAG setup

    • Indexing

      • Crawl Confluence / GitHub / GDrive
      • Normalize and chunk documents
      • Embed chunks with bge-large-en or OpenAI embeddings
      • Store in Qdrant / Pinecone with metadata:
        • {tenant_id, department, doc_type, updated_at}

    • Query-time

      • User asks: “How do I request parental leave?”
      • Backend:
        • Embeds the query
        • Retrieves top-k HR policy chunks
        • Builds prompt: instructions + retrieved policy text + question
        • Calls LLM (e.g., GPT-4o or local Llama 3) to generate answer
        • Returns answer + links to original HR docs

  • Benefits

    • No need to fine-tune on all internal docs.
    • When policies change:
      • Re-index those docs only.
    • Users see:
      • Concise answer
      • Source references for verification.
Q49.HOW DO EMBEDDINGS WORK? [Input Token: 704 | Output Token: 3103] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition
    • Embeddings are dense numerical vectors that represent data (text, images, code, users, items, etc.) in a continuous vector space where semantic similarity ≈ geometric closeness.
  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews
    • Core to:
      • RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
      • Semantic search
      • Recommendation systems
      • Clustering & classification
      • Fine-tuning & alignment tasks
  • Importance in Python/Rust backend interviews
    • Used in:
      • Building vector search APIs
      • Integrating LLMs with vector databases
      • Designing low-latency embedding pipelines
      • Implementing personalization and recommendations

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • High-level idea

    • Map input objects (e.g., sentences) to fixed-size vectors (e.g., 768-dim).
    • Similar objects → vectors close in space (cosine similarity, dot product).
    • Dissimilar objects → vectors far apart.

  • How embeddings are learned (conceptually)

    • Start with a neural network (e.g., Transformer).
    • Train it on tasks where similar inputs should have similar outputs, e.g.:
      • Next word prediction (language modeling).
      • Contrastive tasks (e.g., sentence pairs that should/shouldn’t match).
    • The hidden layer activations (or a pooled representation) are used as the embedding.

  • Usage pattern

    • Offline or online:
      • Compute embeddings for documents/items.
      • Store in a vector store (FAISS, Milvus, pgvector, Qdrant, Pinecone).
    • At query time:
      • Embed the query.
      • Find nearest neighbors in vector space.
      • Use those neighbors for:
        • Search results
        • RAG context for LLM
        • Recommendations

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Model
    • Text: BERT, SBERT, OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, all-MiniLM-L6-v2
    • Image: CLIP, ViT-based encoders
    • Code: CodeBERT, OpenAI code embeddings
  • Services
    • Embedding service (Python/Rust microservice)
    • Vector database (Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, pgvector)
    • Application backend (FastAPI/Actix Web) calling both
  • Pipelines
    • Ingestion pipeline: chunk → embed → upsert to vector DB
    • Query pipeline: query → embed → vector search → rank → return / feed to LLM

Technologies Used

  • Python
    • sentence-transformers, transformers, torch, faiss, langchain, llama-index
    • Web: FastAPI, Flask
  • Rust
    • Web: actix-web, axum
    • Vector search: qdrant-client, tantivy, hnsw_rs
    • Calling Python/LLM: reqwest, pyo3 (if embedding in Rust via Python)

Data Flow and Processing Stages

  1. Input preprocessing
    • Text normalization: lowercasing, remove control chars, optional stemming/lemmatization.
    • Chunking long docs into manageable segments (e.g., 512–1000 tokens).
  2. Embedding generation
    • Tokenize text → IDs → model → last hidden states → pooled vector.
  3. Vector storage
    • Store vectors + metadata (id, text, tags) in vector DB.
  4. Similarity search
    • Given query vector, compute nearest neighbors using:
      • Cosine similarity
      • Dot product
      • L2 distance
    • Often with ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor) indexes (HNSW, IVF, PQ).
  5. Post-processing
    • Re-ranking, filtering, scoring.
    • For RAG: build prompt from retrieved docs.

API Endpoints and Contracts (Example)

  • Embedding service

    • POST /embed
      • Request:
        {
  "texts": ["hello world", "how do embeddings work?"],
  "model": "all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
}
      • Response:
        {
  "embeddings": [
    [0.0123, -0.23, ...],
    [0.045, 0.11, ...]
  ],
  "dim": 384
}

  • Vector search service

    • POST /search
      • Request:
        {
  "query": "how to implement RAG with Python",
  "top_k": 5
}
      • Response:
        {
  "results": [
    {
      "id": "doc_123",
      "score": 0.87,
      "text": "RAG combines a retriever with a generator..."
    }
  ]
}

Model Lifecycle

  • Training
    • Pretrained models on large corpora (self-supervised).
    • Optional fine-tuning on:
      • Domain-specific pairs (Q–A, duplicate detection).
      • Contrastive learning (positive/negative pairs).
  • Evaluation
    • Metrics: MRR, nDCG, Recall@k, Spearman correlation (STS).
  • Deployment
    • Package model as:
      • Python service (FastAPI + Torch)
      • ONNX/TensorRT service for speed
      • Rust wrapper calling a model server
  • Monitoring
    • Latency, throughput, GPU utilization.
    • Drift: embedding distribution changes, drop in retrieval quality.

Scalability Considerations

  • Horizontal scaling of embedding service:
    • Multiple replicas behind a load balancer.
    • Batch requests to maximize GPU utilization.
  • Vector DB scaling
    • Sharding by collection or ID ranges.
    • Use ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF) for large-scale search (millions+ vectors).
  • Caching
    • Cache frequent embeddings (e.g., identical queries) using Redis.

Performance Considerations

  • Latency
    • Use smaller, distilled models for real-time embeddings.
    • Quantization (INT8) + ONNX/TensorRT.
  • Throughput
    • Batch queries (e.g., batch size 32–128).
    • Async I/O in Python/Rust.
  • Memory
    • Dimensionality reduction (PCA) or product quantization.
    • Store vectors in float16 instead of float32 when acceptable.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    subgraph Client
        Q[User Query / Document]
    end

    subgraph Backend
        Q --> P[Preprocessor]
        P --> E[Embedding Model Service]
        E -->|vector| VDB[(Vector Database)]
        VDB --> R[Rank & Filter]
        R --> APP[App / LLM / API Response]
    end

    subgraph Offline Ingestion
        D[Raw Documents] --> C[Chunker]
        C --> E2[Embedding Model Service]
        E2 -->|vectors + metadata| VDB
    end

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Training (conceptual)
    • Collect large corpus of text (and optionally pairs).
    • Train a neural network so that:
      • Similar texts → similar embeddings.
      • Dissimilar texts → distant embeddings.
  2. Indexing
    • For each document:
      • Preprocess and chunk.
      • Compute embedding.
      • Store in vector database with metadata.
  3. Querying
    • Receive user query.
    • Compute query embedding.
    • Perform nearest neighbor search in vector DB.
    • Return top-k results or pass them to LLM (RAG).

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

Python: Embedding + Vector Search (FAISS + FastAPI)

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import faiss
import numpy as np

app = FastAPI()
model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

# Example index
dim = 384
index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(dim)  # cosine via normalized dot product
documents = []  # store texts

class EmbedRequest(BaseModel):
    texts: list[str]

class SearchRequest(BaseModel):
    query: str
    top_k: int = 5

@app.post("/embed")
def embed(req: EmbedRequest):
    embeddings = model.encode(req.texts, normalize_embeddings=True)
    return {"embeddings": embeddings.tolist(), "dim": embeddings.shape[1]}

@app.post("/index")
def index_docs(req: EmbedRequest):
    global documents
    embeddings = model.encode(req.texts, normalize_embeddings=True)
    index.add(np.array(embeddings, dtype="float32"))
    documents.extend(req.texts)
    return {"count": len(documents)}

@app.post("/search")
def search(req: SearchRequest):
    q_emb = model.encode([req.query], normalize_embeddings=True).astype("float32")
    scores, ids = index.search(q_emb, req.top_k)
    results = [
        {"text": documents[i], "score": float(scores[0][j])}
        for j, i in enumerate(ids[0])
    ]
    return {"results": results}

Rust: Calling a Vector DB (Qdrant) from Backend

use actix_web::{post, web, App, HttpServer, Responder};
use qdrant_client::prelude::*;

#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]
struct SearchReq {
    query_embedding: Vec<f32>,
    top_k: usize,
}

#[post("/search")]
async fn search(body: web::Json<SearchReq>) -> impl Responder {
    let client = QdrantClient::from_url("http://localhost:6333").build().unwrap();

    let search_result = client
        .search_points(&SearchPoints {
            collection_name: "docs".into(),
            vector: body.query_embedding.clone(),
            limit: body.top_k as u64,
            ..Default::default()
        })
        .await
        .unwrap();

    web::Json(search_result.result)
}

#[actix_web::main]
async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    HttpServer::new(|| App::new().service(search))
        .bind(("0.0.0.0", 8080))?
        .run()
        .await
}
  • In Rust, you typically:
    • Call an embedding API (Python/LLM provider) to get vectors.
    • Use Rust to handle high-performance search, routing, and orchestration.

Advantages

  • Semantic understanding
    • Captures meaning beyond exact keywords (e.g., “car” ≈ “automobile”).
  • Unified representation
    • Same framework for text, images, code, users, items.
  • Enables powerful systems
    • RAG, recommendation, de-duplication, anomaly detection.
  • Efficient retrieval
    • ANN indexes allow sub-second search over millions of items.

Limitations

  • Context & length
    • Single embedding may not capture very long documents → need chunking.
  • Domain specificity
    • General models may perform poorly on specialized domains (legal, medical).
  • Static vs dynamic meaning
    • Standard embeddings don’t adapt to user-specific context unless designed.
  • Approximate search
    • ANN may miss some nearest neighbors (recall vs speed trade-off).
  • Privacy
    • Embeddings can sometimes leak information about original data.

Interview Tips

  • Key points to remember
    • Embeddings = dense vectors where distance ≈ semantic similarity.
    • Common similarity metrics: cosine, dot product, L2.
    • Used heavily in RAG: retrieve docs via embeddings → feed to LLM.
    • Indexing via ANN structures (HNSW, IVF, PQ).
  • Common interview questions
    • How do embeddings differ from one-hot or TF-IDF?
    • Cosine similarity vs dot product – when and why?
    • How to build a semantic search system with embeddings?
    • How to scale vector search to millions of documents?
    • How to choose embedding dimension and model?
    • How to evaluate embedding quality?
  • Tricky areas
    • Handling multi-lingual embeddings.
    • Chunking strategy for documents in RAG.
    • Normalization of embeddings and its impact on similarity.
    • Trade-off between model size, latency, and quality.

Real-World Example

RAG-based Documentation Assistant

  • Use-case

    • A chatbot that answers questions about your company’s internal docs.

  • How embeddings are used

    1. Ingestion
      • Parse docs (PDF, Confluence, Markdown).
      • Chunk into ~500–1000 token segments.
      • Compute embeddings using a text embedding model.
      • Store {id, text, metadata, embedding} in a vector database.
    2. Query
      • User asks: “How do I request production access?”
      • Backend:
        • Embeds the query.
        • Searches vector DB for top-k similar chunks.
        • Builds a prompt: includes question + retrieved chunks.
        • Sends to LLM (e.g., GPT-4, LLaMA) for answer synthesis.
    3. Response
      • LLM responds using only relevant chunks → grounded, accurate answers.

  • Python stack

    • FastAPI + sentence-transformers + Qdrant/Pinecone + langchain for RAG orchestration.

  • Rust stack

    • Rust backend (Actix/Axum) for:
      • High-performance routing.
      • Calling embedding API + vector DB.
      • Streaming responses from LLM to frontend.

This is the typical way embeddings “work” in modern GenAI systems: they transform unstructured data into a searchable, comparable numeric space that powers retrieval, similarity, and downstream intelligent behavior.

Q50.WHAT ARE VECTOR DATABASES? [Input Token: 704 | Output Token: 3596] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition

    • A vector database is a database optimized for storing, indexing, and querying high-dimensional vector embeddings (numerical representations of text, images, audio, etc.) using similarity search (e.g., cosine similarity, Euclidean distance).
    • It enables operations like: “find the most similar documents to this query embedding” efficiently at scale.

  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews

    • Core component of RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) systems.
    • Essential for semantic search, recommendation systems, document retrieval, and context injection for LLMs.
    • Interviewers expect you to understand how embeddings + vector DBs enable LLM applications without full fine-tuning.

  • Importance in Python/Rust Backend interviews

    • Part of modern backend architectures for LLM-powered APIs, chatbots, and search services.
    • Requires understanding of:
      • Indexing and query performance
      • Consistency with traditional relational/NoSQL stores
      • Integration with microservices and inference pipelines

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • Core idea

    • Convert data (text, images, code) into embeddings using ML models.
    • Store these embeddings as vectors in a specialized DB.
    • Query by embedding a user query and performing nearest neighbor search in vector space.

  • Key concepts

    • Embedding model: Maps input → dense vector (e.g., 768-dim float array).
    • Similarity metric: Cosine similarity, dot product, L2 distance.
    • Index structures: IVF, HNSW, PQ, Annoy, etc. for Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search.
    • Hybrid search: Combine vector similarity with keyword/metadata filters.

  • Typical workflow

    • Ingestion:
      • Chunk documents → embed → store {id, vector, metadata}.
    • Query:
      • Embed query → similarity search → retrieve top-k items → use in downstream task (e.g., feed to LLM).

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Models

    • Embedding model (e.g., text-embedding-3-large, bge-large, sentence-transformers).
    • Optional reranker model (e.g., cross-encoder) for better ranking.

  • Services

    • Vector DB service: e.g., Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, pgvector (Postgres extension), Chroma.
    • Embedding service: Python microservice wrapping a model (local or external API).
    • Application backend: Python (FastAPI) or Rust (Axum/Actix) service orchestrating the flow.

  • Pipelines

    • Ingestion pipeline: data → chunking → embedding → upsert to vector DB.
    • Query pipeline: query → embed → vector search → optional rerank → return results or call LLM.

Technologies Used

  • Python
    • Frameworks: FastAPI, Flask
    • ML libraries: PyTorch, Transformers, sentence-transformers
    • LLM tooling: LangChain, LlamaIndex
    • Vector DB clients: qdrant-client, weaviate-client, pymilvus, pinecone-client, psycopg2 + pgvector
  • Rust
    • Web frameworks: Axum, Actix Web
    • Vector ops: ndarray, nalgebra, or FFI bindings to C++ libs (e.g., Faiss) or gRPC to external vector DB.
    • gRPC/REST clients to vector DBs.

Data Flow and Processing Stages

  • Ingestion
    • Input: raw documents (PDF, HTML, markdown, code)
    • Steps:
      • Preprocess & chunk
      • Generate embeddings
      • Store in vector DB: id, vector, metadata (e.g., source, tags, timestamps)
  • Query
    • Input: user query text
    • Steps:
      • Embed query
      • Query vector DB using similarity search
      • Filter by metadata (e.g., tenant, time range)
      • Optional rerank using cross-encoder
      • Return structured results

API Endpoints and Contracts (Example)

  • Ingestion API (Python FastAPI)
POST /documents
Request:
{
  "id": "doc_123",
  "text": "Some content ...",
  "metadata": {"source": "kb", "lang": "en"}
}

Response:
{
  "status": "ok",
  "id": "doc_123"
}
  • Search API
POST /search
Request:
{
  "query": "How do I reset my password?",
  "top_k": 5,
  "filters": {"source": "kb"}
}

Response:
{
  "results": [
    {
      "id": "doc_123",
      "score": 0.89,
      "text": "To reset your password...",
      "metadata": {"source": "kb"}
    },
    ...
  ]
}

Model Lifecycle

  • Training
    • Often use pretrained embedding models; may fine-tune on domain data for better similarity.
  • Evaluation
    • Metrics: Recall@K, MRR, NDCG, semantic similarity accuracy.
    • Manual eval: Are retrieved passages relevant to queries?
  • Deployment
    • Deploy embedding model as a service (GPU/CPU).
    • Deploy vector DB cluster.
    • Wire into backend APIs.
  • Monitoring
    • Query latency, QPS, index size, recall quality.
    • Drift: changes in data distribution or embedding model versions.
  • Versioning
    • Keep track of:
      • Embedding model version
      • Index version
      • Migration strategy when changing models (re-embedding vs dual-index).

Scalability Considerations

  • Sharding and replication
    • Distribute vectors across nodes (by ID or hash).
    • Replicate for HA and read scaling.
  • Index strategies
    • Use ANN indices (HNSW, IVF-PQ) for large-scale (millions+ vectors).
    • Control trade-off: recall vs latency via index parameters.
  • Batching
    • Batch embedding and upserts for ingestion.
  • Horizontal scaling
    • Stateless embedding services + autoscaling.
    • Vector DB that supports horizontal scaling (Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Pinecone).

Performance Considerations

  • Latency
    • Use ANN instead of exact search.
    • Optimize embedding model (quantization, distillation, GPU).
  • Throughput
    • Batch queries when possible.
    • Use async I/O in Python/Rust.
  • Memory
    • Quantization (e.g., 8-bit, 4-bit) to reduce memory footprint.
    • Use PQ (Product Quantization) or HNSW with compressed vectors.
  • Index build time
    • Background index building for large ingestions.
    • Incremental vs full rebuild strategies.

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Ingestion

    • Receive documents via API or batch.
    • Chunk into smaller passages (e.g., 200–1000 tokens).
    • Generate embeddings for each chunk.
    • Upsert {id, vector, metadata} into the vector DB.

  2. Query

    • Receive user query via API.
    • Generate query embedding using the same embedding model.
    • Perform similarity search in the vector DB with filters.

  3. Post-processing / Consumption

    • Optionally rerank results.
    • Combine retrieved text with user query as context.
    • Pass to LLM (for RAG) or return directly as search results.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

High-level Implementation in Python (FastAPI + Qdrant)

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient
from qdrant_client.http.models import VectorParams, Distance

app = FastAPI()

# Initialize embedding model
model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

# Initialize Qdrant
qdrant = QdrantClient(host="localhost", port=6333)
COLLECTION = "docs"

# Create collection (once)
qdrant.recreate_collection(
    collection_name=COLLECTION,
    vectors_config=VectorParams(size=384, distance=Distance.COSINE),
)

class Document(BaseModel):
    id: str
    text: str
    metadata: dict | None = None

class SearchRequest(BaseModel):
    query: str
    top_k: int = 5
    filters: dict | None = None

@app.post("/documents")
def add_document(doc: Document):
    embedding = model.encode([doc.text])[0].tolist()
    qdrant.upsert(
        collection_name=COLLECTION,
        points=[{
            "id": doc.id,
            "vector": embedding,
            "payload": {"text": doc.text, **(doc.metadata or {})}
        }]
    )
    return {"status": "ok", "id": doc.id}

@app.post("/search")
def search(req: SearchRequest):
    query_vec = model.encode([req.query])[0].tolist()
    res = qdrant.search(
        collection_name=COLLECTION,
        query_vector=query_vec,
        limit=req.top_k,
        query_filter=None  # map req.filters to qdrant filter here
    )
    return {
        "results": [
            {
                "id": p.id,
                "score": p.score,
                "text": p.payload.get("text"),
                "metadata": {k: v for k, v in p.payload.items() if k != "text"}
            }
            for p in res
        ]
    }

}

Integration with RAG (Python + LangChain)

from langchain_community.vectorstores import Qdrant
from langchain_community.embeddings import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(model_name="sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o")

vectorstore = Qdrant(
    client=qdrant,
    collection_name=COLLECTION,
    embeddings=embeddings
)

retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 5})

def answer_question(question: str):
    docs = retriever.get_relevant_documents(question)
    context = "\n\n".join(d.page_content for d in docs)
    prompt = f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}\nAnswer:"
    return llm.invoke(prompt).content

Advantages

  • Semantic search: Finds conceptually similar content, not just keyword matches.
  • Foundation for RAG: Efficiently provides context to LLMs without fine-tuning.
  • Scalable similarity search: Designed for millions to billions of vectors.
  • Metadata filtering: Combine semantic similarity with structured filters (tenants, tags, time).
  • Model-agnostic: Works with any embedding model (text, image, multimodal).

Limitations

  • Approximate results: ANN trades exactness for speed; recall < 100%.
  • Index maintenance: Re-embedding and re-indexing when changing models is costly.
  • Operational complexity: Requires managing another specialized database.
  • Consistency with source DB: Must keep vector DB in sync with primary data store.
  • Security/tenancy: Need careful design for multi-tenant isolation and access control.

Interview Tips

  • Common questions

    • What is a vector database? How is it different from SQL/NoSQL DBs?
    • Explain how you’d build a RAG system using a vector DB.
    • How do you choose similarity metrics (cosine vs dot vs L2)?
    • What is ANN? Describe HNSW / IVF at a high level.
    • How do you handle multi-tenancy and authorization in a vector DB?
    • When would you use pgvector vs a dedicated vector DB (Qdrant/Milvus/Pinecone)?

  • Key points to remember

    • Always mention embeddings + ANN + similarity metrics.
    • Emphasize RAG, semantic search, and metadata filters.
    • Mention scaling strategies (sharding, replication, index choices).
    • Clarify that vector DBs complement traditional DBs, not replace them.

  • Tricky areas interviewers focus on

    • Handling model upgrades (re-embedding strategy).
    • Latency vs recall trade-offs in ANN.
    • Security & multi-tenancy: per-tenant collections vs filters.
    • Hybrid search: combining BM25 (keyword) with vector search.

Real-World Example

  • Use-case: RAG-based Customer Support Chatbot

    • Problem

      • Company has thousands of support articles, FAQs, and tickets.
      • Wants an LLM chatbot that answers user queries using internal docs.

    • Solution using vector DB

      • Ingestion:
        • Extract and chunk all support docs.
        • Generate embeddings for each chunk using a domain-tuned embedding model.
        • Store in Qdrant/Pinecone with metadata (product, language, last_updated).
      • Query:
        • User asks: “How do I reset my password if I lost my phone?”
        • Backend:
          • Embed query.
          • Vector search with filters (e.g., product = “mobile app”).
          • Retrieve top-k relevant chunks.
          • Build a prompt: include chunks as context.
          • Call LLM (e.g., GPT-4) to generate answer grounded in retrieved docs.
      • Benefits:
        • High-quality, up-to-date answers without fine-tuning the LLM.
        • Can update knowledge by re-ingesting docs into vector DB.
Q51.EXPLAIN COSINE SIMILARITY? [Input Token: 703 | Output Token: 3118] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:
    • Cosine similarity measures how similar two vectors are by computing the cosine of the angle between them in a high-dimensional space.
    • It ranges from -1 to 1 (for centered vectors), but in many ML/GenAI cases (non-negative embeddings) it’s effectively 0 to 1.
  • Why important in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:
    • Core to embeddings, vector search, RAG, semantic search, recommendation systems, document similarity, clustering.
    • Used heavily with LLM embeddings (OpenAI, SentenceTransformers, etc.).
  • Why important in Python/Rust Backend interviews:
    • Backend services implementing semantic search APIs, RAG pipelines, personalization, or nearest neighbor search often rely on cosine similarity.
    • You’ll need to know how to compute it efficiently and integrate it with vector DBs, caches, and microservices.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • Core idea:

    • Represent objects (texts, images, users, items) as vectors in a high-dimensional space.
    • Cosine similarity measures orientation (angle), not magnitude.
    • Two vectors are similar if they point in the same direction, regardless of length.

  • Mathematical definition:
    For vectors a and b in ℝⁿ: [ \text{cosine_similarity}(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{|a|\ |b|} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i^2}\ \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_i^2}} ]

  • Interpretation:

    • 1 → vectors are identical in direction (max similarity).
    • 0 → vectors are orthogonal (no similarity).
    • -1 → vectors point in opposite directions (max dissimilarity; rare in typical embedding spaces).

  • Why cosine vs Euclidean:

    • Euclidean distance is sensitive to magnitude.
    • Cosine focuses on direction, which is more robust for:
      • TF-IDF vectors
      • Text embeddings
      • Normalized feature vectors

  • In LLM / RAG context:

    • Convert text → embedding vector.
    • Compare embeddings using cosine similarity to find semantically related content.
    • Used by vector databases (e.g., Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus) as a primary similarity metric.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Models:
    • Embedding models (e.g., OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, SentenceTransformers, bge, E5).
  • Services:
    • Embedding service: converts text/documents into vectors.
    • Similarity service: computes cosine similarity or uses vector DB.
    • Search / RAG API: exposes endpoints for querying similar items.
  • Pipelines:
    • Ingestion pipeline: raw text → cleaned → embedded → stored.
    • Query pipeline: query text → embedded → similarity search → ranked results.

Technologies

  • Python:
    • numpy, scipy, torch, sklearn.metrics.pairwise.cosine_similarity
    • Web: FastAPI, Flask
  • Rust:
    • ndarray, nalgebra for vector ops
    • Web: axum, actix-web
  • Vector DBs:
    • Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, pgvector (Postgres extension)
  • Infra tools:
    • Docker, Kubernetes, Redis (cache), Prometheus/Grafana (monitoring)

Data Flow & Processing Stages

  • Offline / Ingestion:
    • Input documents → text pre-processing → embedding model → vector store with metadata.
  • Online / Query:
    • User query → embed → cosine similarity search against stored vectors → top-k results → optional reranking → response.

API Endpoints (Example)

  • POST /embed
    • Request: { "texts": ["hello world", "foo bar"] }
    • Response: { "embeddings": [[...], [...]] }
  • POST /similarity
    • Request: { "vector": [...], "candidates": [[...], [...]] }
    • Response: { "scores": [0.91, 0.73] }
  • POST /semantic-search
    • Request: { "query": "LLM for customer support", "top_k": 5 }
    • Response: list of documents with similarity scores.

Model Lifecycle

  • Training:
    • Train or fine-tune embedding model (e.g., contrastive learning).
  • Evaluation:
    • Evaluate on similarity benchmarks (e.g., STS, retrieval tasks).
  • Deployment:
    • Containerized embedding service + vector DB backend.
  • Monitoring:
    • Track latency, throughput, similarity distribution, drift in embeddings.

Scalability Considerations

  • High dimensional vectors (e.g., 768, 1536 dims)
  • Use ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor) indexes:
    • HNSW, IVF, PQ, ScaNN, FAISS, etc.
  • Sharding and replication in vector DBs.
  • Pre-normalize vectors to unit length to speed up cosine computations.

Performance Considerations

  • Precompute L2 norms or store normalized vectors.
  • Use batch operations for similarity computation.
  • Use BLAS / SIMD-optimized libraries (NumPy, PyTorch, Rust blas).
  • For large-scale, offload similarity search to specialized vector DBs.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    A[Input Text / Document] --> B[Embedding Model<br/>LLM / Encoder]
    B --> C[Vector Representation<br/>R^d]
    C --> D[Vector Store / Index]
    E[User Query Text] --> F[Query Embedding Model]
    F --> G[Query Vector<br/>R^d]
    G --> H[Cosine Similarity Computation]
    D --> H
    H --> I[Top-k Similar Documents<br/>Ranked by Cosine Similarity]

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Vector Representation

    • Convert items (documents, queries, users, products) into d-dimensional vectors via an embedding model.

  2. Normalization & Storage

    • Normalize vectors to unit length (optional but common).
    • Store them in a vector database or an index structure.

  3. Similarity Computation

    • For a query vector:
      • Compute cosine similarity with stored vectors.
      • Retrieve top-k most similar vectors.
      • Use similarity scores for ranking, recommendations, or context selection in RAG.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

Python Example (Cosine Similarity)

import numpy as np

def cosine_similarity(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> float:
    # Ensure 1D vectors
    a = a.ravel()
    b = b.ravel()
    dot = np.dot(a, b)
    norm_a = np.linalg.norm(a)
    norm_b = np.linalg.norm(b)
    if norm_a == 0 or norm_b == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(dot / (norm_a * norm_b))

# Batch version
def cosine_similarity_matrix(query: np.ndarray, candidates: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    # query: (d,), candidates: (N, d)
    query_norm = query / (np.linalg.norm(query) + 1e-9)
    cand_norm = candidates / (np.linalg.norm(candidates, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9)
    return cand_norm @ query_norm  # shape: (N,)

Python + FastAPI Microservice

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
import numpy as np

app = FastAPI()

class SimilarityRequest(BaseModel):
    vector: list[float]
    candidates: list[list[float]]

class SimilarityResponse(BaseModel):
    scores: list[float]

@app.post("/similarity", response_model=SimilarityResponse)
def similarity(req: SimilarityRequest):
    v = np.array(req.vector, dtype=np.float32)
    cands = np.array(req.candidates, dtype=np.float32)
    scores = cosine_similarity_matrix(v, cands)
    return SimilarityResponse(scores=scores.tolist())

Rust Example (Cosine Similarity)

use ndarray::{Array1};
use std::f32;

fn cosine_similarity(a: &Array1<f32>, b: &Array1<f32>) -> f32 {
    let dot = a.dot(b);
    let norm_a = a.dot(a).sqrt();
    let norm_b = b.dot(b).sqrt();
    if norm_a == 0.0 || norm_b == 0.0 {
        return 0.0;
    }
    dot / (norm_a * norm_b)
}

fn main() {
    let a = Array1::from(vec![1.0, 2.0, 3.0]);
    let b = Array1::from(vec![4.0, 5.0, 6.0]);
    let sim = cosine_similarity(&a, &b);
    println!("cosine similarity = {}", sim);
}

Rust + Axum (High-level Sketch)

use axum::{routing::post, Json, Router};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use ndarray::Array1;

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct SimilarityRequest {
    vector: Vec<f32>,
    candidates: Vec<Vec<f32>>,
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct SimilarityResponse {
    scores: Vec<f32>,
}

fn cosine_similarity(a: &Array1<f32>, b: &Array1<f32>) -> f32 {
    let dot = a.dot(b);
    let norm_a = a.dot(a).sqrt();
    let norm_b = b.dot(b).sqrt();
    if norm_a == 0.0 || norm_b == 0.0 {
        return 0.0;
    }
    dot / (norm_a * norm_b)
}

async fn similarity_handler(Json(req): Json<SimilarityRequest>) -> Json<SimilarityResponse> {
    let v = Array1::from(req.vector);
    let scores = req.candidates
        .into_iter()
        .map(|c| cosine_similarity(&v, &Array1::from(c)))
        .collect();
    Json(SimilarityResponse { scores })
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let app = Router::new().route("/similarity", post(similarity_handler));
    axum::Server::bind(&"0.0.0.0:8080".parse().unwrap())
        .serve(app.into_make_service())
        .await
        .unwrap();
}

Advantages

  • Scale-invariant:
    • Insensitive to magnitude; focuses on direction.
  • Works well for sparse and dense vectors:
    • TF-IDF, bag-of-words, modern embeddings.
  • Simple & efficient:
    • Just dot products and norms; easily vectorized.
  • Standard in semantic similarity:
    • Widely supported by vector DBs and ML libraries.

Limitations

  • Ignores magnitude:
    • In some tasks, vector length contains meaningful information (e.g., confidence).
  • Not a true distance metric (in some definitions):
    • 1 - cosine_similarity is often used as a distance, but triangle inequality may not hold.
  • Sensitive to embedding quality:
    • Poor embeddings → meaningless similarity.
  • High-dimensional challenges:
    • Curse of dimensionality; requires ANN indexes for large-scale systems.

Interview Tips

  • Key points to remember:
    • Formula: cos(a, b) = (a · b) / (||a|| * ||b||).
    • Intuition: angle between vectors, not length.
    • Why used with embeddings and TF-IDF.
    • Relationship to dot product when vectors are normalized:
      • If ||a|| = ||b|| = 1, then cosine_similarity(a, b) = a · b.
  • Common interview questions:
    • Compare cosine similarity vs Euclidean distance.
    • Why is cosine similarity preferred in text similarity / RAG?
    • How to compute cosine similarity efficiently for millions of vectors?
    • How does cosine similarity integrate with FAISS / vector DBs?
    • What happens if vectors are not normalized?
  • Tricky areas:
    • Handling zero vectors (norm = 0).
    • Understanding range and interpretation of values.
    • Explaining how cosine similarity is used in semantic search vs keyword search.

Real-World Example

  • Use-case: RAG-based QA System with Semantic Search

    • Goal: Given a user question, retrieve the most relevant documents from a knowledge base.

    • Flow:

      1. Ingestion:
        • Split documents into chunks (e.g., 512–1000 tokens).
        • Use an embedding model to convert each chunk into a vector.
        • Store vectors + metadata in a vector database using cosine similarity as the metric.
      2. Query:
        • User asks: "How do I handle rate limiting in the API?"
        • Embed the query into a vector.
        • Run cosine similarity search against stored vectors to get top-k chunks.
      3. RAG:
        • Pass the retrieved chunks + question into an LLM.
        • LLM generates an answer grounded in high-similarity context.

    • Why cosine similarity here:

      • It captures semantic similarity between question and document chunks.
      • Robust to different wording but similar meaning (e.g., rate limiting vs throttling).

This is the level of understanding and implementation detail typically expected in strong AI/ML + backend interviews.

Q52.HOW DO YOU BUILD AN LLM PIPELINE? [Input Token: 708 | Output Token: 3969] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition

    • An LLM pipeline is an end-to-end system that takes user input, processes it through multiple stages (preprocessing, retrieval, reasoning, generation, postprocessing), and returns a response from a Large Language Model (LLM).
    • It often includes components like prompting, retrieval (RAG), tools, safety filters, logging, and monitoring.

  • Why it is important in AI/ML/GenAI interviews

    • Shows you understand how to operationalize LLMs, not just call an API.
    • Tests knowledge of RAG, prompt engineering, vector databases, orchestration, observability, and safety.
    • Many questions are framed as “Design a production LLM system for X”.

  • Why it is important in Python/Rust Backend interviews

    • LLM apps are latency-sensitive, stateful, and often multi-service.
    • Requires understanding of API design, concurrency, streaming, caching, and scaling in Python/Rust.
    • Backend engineers are expected to know how to wrap LLMs into robust microservices.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

Typical production LLM pipeline (RAG + tools) includes:

  • 1. Ingestion / Indexing (offline)

    • Fetch data from sources (DBs, PDFs, APIs, S3, etc.).
    • Chunk documents, clean text.
    • Generate embeddings and store in vector database (e.g., Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate).

  • 2. Online Request Handling

    • Receive user query via HTTP/WebSocket.
    • Authenticate user, rate-limit, log request.

  • 3. Preprocessing & Intent Understanding

    • Normalize text (lowercase, remove control chars).
    • Detect language, classify intent (Q&A, code-gen, summarization).
    • Decide whether to use RAG, tools, or direct LLM.

  • 4. Retrieval (RAG)

    • Embed user query.
    • Perform similarity search in vector DB to get relevant chunks.
    • Optionally do hybrid search (BM25 + vector).

  • 5. Prompt Construction / Orchestration

    • Build a system prompt (role, rules, tools).
    • Add retrieved context.
    • Add user query and any conversation history.
    • Optionally call a router model or planner to decide tool usage.

  • 6. LLM Inference

    • Call LLM (OpenAI, Anthropic, local LLaMA, etc.).
    • Use streaming for partial tokens.
    • Optionally use tool calling / function calling to fetch external data.

  • 7. Postprocessing

    • Parse structured outputs (JSON, SQL, code).
    • Apply safety filters (toxicity, PII detection).
    • Reformat for client (markdown, HTML, JSON).

  • 8. Logging, Metrics & Feedback

    • Log prompts, responses, latency, errors.
    • Store feedback (thumbs up/down, corrections) for evaluation & fine-tuning.
    • Monitor costs, throughput, quality.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Models

    • LLM: GPT-4, Claude, LLaMA, Mistral, etc.
    • Embedding model: text-embedding-3-large, bge, instructor.
    • Optional small models: intent classifier, router, safety classifier.

  • Services

    • API Gateway / Backend: FastAPI (Python), Axum/Actix (Rust).
    • Vector DB: Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, Chroma.
    • Relational/NoSQL DB: Postgres, Redis, DynamoDB.
    • Task Queue: Celery/RQ (Python), Tokio + Redis (Rust) for async jobs.

  • Pipelines

    • Ingestion pipeline: ETL -> embeddings -> vector DB.
    • Online inference pipeline: request -> retrieval -> LLM -> response.
    • Evaluation pipeline: replay logs, compute metrics, compare models.

Technologies (Python)

  • Backend
    • FastAPI, Uvicorn, Gunicorn.
    • Pydantic for schemas.
  • ML / LLM
    • PyTorch, Transformers, vLLM.
    • LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack for RAG orchestration.
  • Infra
    • Docker, Kubernetes, Redis, Postgres.
    • Prometheus/Grafana, OpenTelemetry.

Technologies (Rust)

  • Backend
    • Axum, Actix-web, Warp.
    • Serde for JSON.
  • LLM Integration
    • Call out to Python microservice via HTTP/GRPC.
    • Or call external APIs directly from Rust (reqwest).
  • Infra
    • Tokio for async.
    • Tonic for gRPC.

Data Flow & Processing Stages

  • Ingestion
    • Raw data → chunker → embedder → vector DB.
  • Online
    • HTTP request → auth → preprocessor → embedder → vector DB search → prompt builder → LLM → postprocessor → response.

Example API Endpoints & Contracts

  • POST /v1/chat

    • Request
      {
  "user_id": "u123",
  "messages": [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Explain RAG with code examples"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Previous reply..."}
  ],
  "use_rag": true,
  "top_k": 5
}
    • Response
      {
  "answer": "RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is...",
  "sources": [
    {"doc_id": "doc_42", "score": 0.89},
    {"doc_id": "doc_77", "score": 0.74}
  ],
  "usage": {
    "prompt_tokens": 1234,
    "completion_tokens": 256,
    "total_tokens": 1490
  },
  "latency_ms": 812
}

  • POST /v1/ingest

    • Upload documents, trigger embedding + indexing.

Model Lifecycle

  • Training / Fine-tuning
    • Collect conversation logs and labeled data.
    • Fine-tune domain-specific models (e.g., instruction-tuning, LoRA).
  • Evaluation
    • Use held-out test sets, human eval, and LLM-as-judge.
  • Deployment
    • Containerize model server (vLLM, TGI).
    • Deploy behind load balancer.
  • Monitoring
    • Track latency, error rate, token usage, quality metrics.
  • Iteration
    • Improve prompts, retrieval, and model choice based on metrics.

Scalability Considerations

  • Horizontal scaling
    • Multiple LLM workers behind load balancer.
    • Separate ingestion and inference services.
  • Caching
    • Prompt+response cache (Redis).
    • Embedding cache.
  • Sharding
    • Shard vector DB by tenant or domain.
  • Concurrency
    • Async I/O (Python: async/await; Rust: Tokio).
  • Queueing
    • Rate-limiting, backpressure for heavy requests.

Performance Considerations

  • Latency
    • Use streaming responses.
    • Use smaller models for simple tasks, larger only when needed.
    • Optimize retrieval (HNSW, IVF, ANN indices).
  • Throughput
    • Batch embedding and LLM calls when possible.
    • Use high-throughput inference engines (vLLM, TGI).
  • Cost
    • Use router to choose between cheap and expensive models.
    • Cache frequent queries.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    subgraph Offline[Offline Ingestion]
        A[Raw Data\n(PDFs, DB, APIs)] --> B[Chunk & Clean Text]
        B --> C[Embedding Model]
        C --> D[Vector DB]
    end

    subgraph Online[Online Inference]
        E[Client\n(Web/Mobile)] --> F[API Gateway\nFastAPI/Axum]
        F --> G[Preprocess & Intent Classifier]
        G --> H[Embed Query]
        H --> D
        D --> I[Retriever\nTop-k Chunks]
        I --> J[Prompt Builder\n(System + Context + User)]
        J --> K[LLM Inference\n(OpenAI / Local)]
        K --> L[Postprocess\n(Safety, Formatting)]
        L --> E
    end

    subgraph Observability[Logging & Monitoring]
        F --> M[Request Logs]
        K --> N[LLM Metrics\nLatency, Tokens]
        L --> O[Feedback Store\nRatings, Corrections]
    end

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Ingestion (offline)

    • Load documents → chunk → embed → store in vector DB.

  2. Handling a user query

    • User sends query to backend → validate, log, preprocess.

  3. Retrieval & generation

    • Embed query → retrieve top-k chunks → build prompt → call LLM → postprocess → send response + sources.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

High-Level Python Implementation (FastAPI + RAG)

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import List
import httpx
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient
from qdrant_client.http import models as qmodels

app = FastAPI()
qdrant = QdrantClient(host="qdrant", port=6333)

class Message(BaseModel):
    role: str
    content: str

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    user_id: str
    messages: List[Message]
    use_rag: bool = True
    top_k: int = 5

OPENAI_API_KEY = "..."

async def embed_text(text: str) -> List[float]:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
        resp = await client.post(
            "https://api.openai.com/v1/embeddings",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {OPENAI_API_KEY}"},
            json={"model": "text-embedding-3-large", "input": text},
        )
        resp.raise_for_status()
        return resp.json()["data"][0]["embedding"]

async def retrieve_context(query: str, top_k: int) -> List[str]:
    embedding = await embed_text(query)
    search_result = qdrant.search(
        collection_name="docs",
        query_vector=embedding,
        limit=top_k,
        search_params=qmodels.SearchParams(hnsw_ef=128)
    )
    return [hit.payload["text"] for hit in search_result]

async def call_llm(prompt: str) -> str:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=60) as client:
        resp = await client.post(
            "https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {OPENAI_API_KEY}"},
            json={
                "model": "gpt-4o-mini",
                "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
                "temperature": 0.2,
                "stream": False,
            },
        )
        resp.raise_for_status()
        return resp.json()["choices[0]"]["message"]["content"]

def build_prompt(contexts: List[str], messages: List[Message]) -> str:
    system = (
        "You are a helpful assistant. "
        "Use the provided context to answer accurately. "
        "If context is insufficient, say you don't know.\n\n"
    )
    ctx_str = "\n\n".join(f"[DOC {i+1}]\n{c}" for i, c in enumerate(contexts))
    conv_str = "\n".join(f"{m.role.upper()}: {m.content}" for m in messages)
    return system + "CONTEXT:\n" + ctx_str + "\n\nCONVERSATION:\n" + conv_str

@app.post("/v1/chat")
async def chat(req: ChatRequest):
    user_msg = [m for m in req.messages if m.role == "user"][-1]
    contexts = await retrieve_context(user_msg.content, req.top_k) if req.use_rag else []
    prompt = build_prompt(contexts, req.messages)
    answer = await call_llm(prompt)
    return {
        "answer": answer,
        "sources": contexts,
    }

This is simplified: in production you’d add auth, rate-limiting, safety filters, streaming, and error handling.

Rust Backend Calling Python LLM Service

Use Rust for high-performance API and Python for model logic:

// Cargo.toml dependencies:
// axum = "0.7"
// serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] }
// tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
// reqwest = { version = "0.11", features = ["json", "rustls-tls"] }

use axum::{routing::post, Json, Router};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::net::SocketAddr;

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Message {
    role: String,
    content: String,
}

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct ChatRequest {
    user_id: String,
    messages: Vec<Message>,
    use_rag: Option<bool>,
    top_k: Option<u32>,
}

#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct LlmResponse {
    answer: String,
    sources: Vec<String>,
}

async fn chat_handler(Json(req): Json<ChatRequest>) -> Json<LlmResponse> {
    let client = reqwest::Client::new();
    let resp = client
        .post("http://python-llm-service:8000/v1/chat")
        .json(&req)
        .send()
        .await
        .expect("LLM service error");

    let llm_resp: LlmResponse = resp.json().await.expect("Invalid JSON");
    Json(llm_resp)
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let app = Router::new().route("/v1/chat", post(chat_handler));
    let addr = SocketAddr::from(([0, 0, 0, 0], 8080));
    println!("Listening on {}", addr);
    axum::Server::bind(&addr)
        .serve(app.into_make_service())
        .await
        .unwrap();
}

Pattern: Rust for fast, safe API + Python microservice for LLM & ML logic.

Advantages

  • Modularity
    • Clear separation: ingestion, retrieval, LLM, API, monitoring.
  • Scalability
    • Each component can scale independently.
  • Cost-efficiency
    • Use RAG + smaller models instead of blindly calling large models.
  • Extensibility
    • Easy to add tools (search, DB queries, calculators).
  • Observability
    • Centralized logging and metrics for quality and cost.

Limitations

  • Complexity
    • Many moving parts: vector DB, model servers, orchestrators.
  • Latency
    • Embedding + retrieval + LLM can be slow without optimization.
  • Data freshness
    • RAG requires frequent re-ingestion for up-to-date knowledge.
  • Safety
    • Hard to fully prevent hallucinations or unsafe outputs.
  • Operational overhead
    • Requires robust DevOps (K8s, monitoring, incident response).

Interview Tips

  • Common Questions

    • “Design a RAG-based LLM system for X domain.”
    • “How would you reduce latency in your LLM pipeline?”
    • “How do you ensure the LLM uses retrieved context?”
    • “How do you log, monitor, and evaluate an LLM system?”
    • “How would you handle multi-tenant data isolation in vector DB?”

  • Key Points to Mention

    • RAG pattern: embeddings + vector search + context injection.
    • Prompt design: system vs user vs context; guardrails.
    • Streaming for UX and lower perceived latency.
    • Caching: embeddings, responses, retrieval results.
    • Safety & compliance: PII, toxic content, access control.
    • A/B testing: compare prompts/models using offline logs.

  • Tricky Areas Interviewers Focus On

    • Handling hallucinations and source attribution.
    • Multi-turn conversation state and memory.
    • Scaling vector DB and ensuring relevance.
    • Fallback strategies when LLM or vector DB fails.
    • Cost control and model selection strategy.

Real-World Example

Use-case: Enterprise Knowledge Base Assistant (RAG)

  • Goal

    • Employees ask questions about internal docs (policies, architecture, APIs).
    • System answers with citations to internal documents.

  • Pipeline

    • Ingestion
      • Crawl Confluence, Git repos, Google Drive.
      • Chunk docs (e.g., 512–1024 tokens).
      • Generate embeddings (e.g., bge-large) and store in Qdrant.
    • Online
      • Frontend (React) calls Rust or Python backend /v1/chat.
      • Backend:
        • Auth via SSO / OAuth.
        • Embed query, search vector DB with user-specific filters (ACL).
        • Build prompt with top-k chunks + user question.
        • Call LLM (GPT-4 or local LLaMA) with RAG prompt.
        • Return answer + list of source docs/links.
    • Monitoring
      • Track which answers users correct.
      • Use these to improve prompts and fine-tune a smaller domain model.

  • Why this example is good for interviews

    • Touches RAG, auth, multi-tenant data, vector DB, LLM orchestration, and monitoring.
    • Very close to what many companies actually want to build.

For interview prep, practice:

  • Explaining this architecture in 2–3 minutes.
  • Drawing a simplified version of the Mermaid diagram on a whiteboard.
  • Writing a minimal FastAPI RAG service from memory.
Q53.WHAT IS HALLUCINATION IN LLMS? [Input Token: 708 | Output Token: 3326] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition

    • In LLMs, hallucination is when the model produces confident, fluent output that is factually wrong, logically inconsistent, or unsupported by input/context.
    • Examples:
      • Citing non-existent papers/APIs
      • Inventing fake error messages
      • Misstating numbers, dates, or entities with high confidence

  • Why important in AI/ML/GenAI interviews

    • Directly impacts trust, safety, and product reliability
    • Central to RAG, evaluation, guardrails, and enterprise LLM discussions
    • Interviewers test if you know how to detect, reduce, and handle hallucinations in production

  • Why important in Python/Rust backend interviews

    • Affects how you design LLM APIs, validation layers, RAG pipelines, and safety mechanisms
    • You must know where hallucinations can appear in the pipeline and how to architect mitigations (e.g., retrieval, verification, constraints)

Architecture / Concept Explanation

What causes hallucinations?

  • Model-level causes

    • LLMs are next-token predictors, not truth engines
    • They optimize for likelihood of text, not factual correctness
    • Training data noise: misinformation, outdated info, biased data
    • Distribution shift: deployment domain differs from training domain

  • Prompt / context causes

    • Underspecified prompts: too vague, missing constraints
    • Lack of context: model guesses when it doesn’t know
    • Overly broad questions: “Explain X” when X is obscure
    • Misleading prompts: user assumptions baked into prompt

  • System / architecture causes

    • Weak or wrong retrieval in RAG (irrelevant or missing docs)
    • No post-verification or fact-checking layers
    • Missing “I don’t know” handling or confidence calibration
    • Poor prompt templates or tool invocation logic

Types of hallucinations (interview-friendly)

  • Factual hallucination
    • Wrong facts: dates, names, APIs, formulas, citations
  • Logical/Reasoning hallucination
    • Steps look plausible but logic is wrong (math, code reasoning)
  • Contextual hallucination
    • Output contradicts or ignores given context/documents
  • Anchoring hallucination
    • Model sticks to incorrect user premise (“Given that the sun orbits the earth…”)
  • Citation hallucination
    • Fabricated references, URLs, or research papers

Technical Specifications

Components in a typical LLM system where hallucination matters

  • Models

    • Base LLM (e.g., GPT, LLaMA, Mistral)
    • Instruction-tuned / chat-tuned models
    • Fine-tuned domain models (finance, medical, code)

  • Services / Pipelines

    • Prompt builder (templates, system prompts)
    • RAG pipeline (retriever + vector DB + ranker)
    • Tooling / function calling (APIs, DB, calculators)
    • Post-processing (validators, critics, re-rankers)
    • Guardrails (safety, policy filters)

  • Backend layers

    • API gateway (FastAPI / Actix-web / Axum)
    • LLM orchestration (LangChain, LlamaIndex, custom)
    • Vector DB (PGVector, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus)
    • Cache (Redis, in-memory)
    • Monitoring & logging (Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, custom logs)

Data Flow & Processing Stages (with hallucination risk points)

  1. User Input
    • Risk: Ambiguous or misleading questions
  2. Prompt Construction
    • Risk: Missing constraints (“don’t guess”), poor instructions
  3. Retrieval (RAG)
    • Risk: Irrelevant or missing documents → model invents details
  4. LLM Inference
    • Core hallucination risk: model fills gaps based on priors
  5. Post-Processing
    • Risk: No verification; blindly returning model output
  6. Response Delivery
    • Risk: No metadata (confidence, sources, citations)

API Endpoints / Contracts (example)

  • POST /v1/chat

    • Request:
      • messages: chat history
      • enable_rag: bool
      • max_hallucination_mode: enum ("strict" | "normal" | "creative")
    • Response:
      • answer: string
      • sources: list of documents/URLs
      • hallucination_risk: score or label
      • verification_status: "verified" | "not_verified" | "partial"

  • POST /v1/verify

    • Takes answer + context_docs and returns a consistency score.

Model Lifecycle & Hallucination

  • Training
    • Use instruction tuning with “I don’t know” examples
    • RLHF / DPO with rewards for truthfulness and source grounding
  • Evaluation
    • Use hallucination metrics:
      • Faithfulness scores (e.g., with LLM-as-judge)
      • Context-consistency benchmarks
      • Domain-specific factual QA tests
  • Deployment
    • Enable RAG for knowledge-heavy tasks
    • Configure tool use for up-to-date or numeric info
  • Monitoring
    • Log and analyze:
      • User corrections (“That’s wrong because…”)
      • Escalations to humans
      • LLM-judge disagreement rates
  • Continuous Improvement
    • Collect hallucination examples → fine-tune or update prompts
    • Improve retrieval quality and tool coverage

Scalability & Performance Considerations

  • Scalability

    • RAG adds: vector search + additional LLM calls (e.g., verifier)
    • Tool-based verification adds extra API calls (DB, services)
    • Use:
      • Batching for verification calls
      • Caching for repeated Q&A and retrieval results
      • Streaming responses while running background verification

  • Performance

    • Trade-off: Lower hallucinations vs higher latency
    • Techniques:
      • Use smaller verifier model (e.g., 7B) alongside main model
      • Restrict max tokens and temperature
      • Use structured outputs (JSON schemas) to reduce free-form errors

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    U[User Query] --> P[Prompt Builder<br/>System + User + Context]
    P -->|Optional: Query| R[Retriever<br/>Vector DB / Search]
    R --> C[Context Docs]
    P --> L[LLM Inference]
    C --> L
    L --> V[Verifier / Critic LLM<br/>+ Rules / Tools]
    V -->|OK| A[Final Answer]
    V -->|Low Confidence| H[Handle Hallucination<br/>Ask Clarification / Say 'I don't know']
    H --> A
    A --> U2[User]

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. User Query
    • User asks a question (possibly ambiguous or domain-specific).
  2. Prompt Construction & Retrieval
    • Build a structured prompt with:
      • System instructions (“If unsure, say you don’t know”)
      • Retrieved documents (RAG) and constraints
  3. LLM Inference & Verification
    • LLM generates answer
    • Optional verifier (LLM or rule-based) checks:
      • Consistency with context
      • Logical correctness
    • System either:
      • Returns answer with citations
      • Or asks for clarification / admits uncertainty

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

Python: RAG + Hallucination Mitigation (FastAPI + LangChain)

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
from langchain.chat_models import ChatOpenAI
from langchain.vectorstores import PGVector
from langchain.embeddings import OpenAIEmbeddings
from langchain.chains import RetrievalQA

app = FastAPI()

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    query: str
    strict_mode: bool = True

# Setup LLM + retriever
llm = ChatOpenAI(model_name="gpt-4o", temperature=0.1)
embeddings = OpenAIEmbeddings()
vectorstore = PGVector(
    connection_string="postgresql://...",
    collection_name="docs",
    embedding_function=embeddings,
)
retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 5})

qa_chain = RetrievalQA.from_chain_type(
    llm=llm,
    retriever=retriever,
    chain_type="stuff"
)

@app.post("/v1/chat")
async def chat(req: ChatRequest):
    system_prompt = (
        "You are a factual assistant. "
        "Use only the provided context. "
        "If the answer is not in the context, say 'I don't know'."
        if req.strict_mode else
        "You are a helpful assistant. Prefer factual answers, "
        "but you may speculate if needed and clearly label speculation."
    )

    # Wrap with system prompt
    query = f"{system_prompt}\n\nQuestion: {req.query}"

    result = qa_chain({"query": query})
    answer = result["result"]
    sources = [d.metadata for d in result["source_documents"]]

    return {
        "answer": answer,
        "sources": sources,
        "hallucination_mode": "strict" if req.strict_mode else "normal"
    }

Python: Simple Verifier (LLM-as-judge)

from langchain.prompts import PromptTemplate
from langchain.chains import LLMChain

judge_prompt = PromptTemplate.from_template(
    """
You are a strict fact-checker.
Given the context and an answer, decide if the answer is supported.

CONTEXT:
{context}

ANSWER:
{answer}

Respond with one word: SUPPORTED or UNSUPPORTED.
"""
)

judge_chain = LLMChain(llm=llm, prompt=judge_prompt)

def verify_answer(answer: str, docs: list[str]) -> str:
    context = "\n\n".join(docs)
    verdict = judge_chain.run(context=context, answer=answer).strip()
    return verdict

Rust: Backend Skeleton with Hallucination Controls (Axum)

use axum::{routing::post, Json, Router};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct ChatRequest {
    query: String,
    strict_mode: Option<bool>,
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ChatResponse {
    answer: String,
    sources: Vec<String>,
    hallucination_mode: String,
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let app = Router::new().route("/v1/chat", post(chat_handler));
    axum::Server::bind(&"0.0.0.0:8000".parse().unwrap())
        .serve(app.into_make_service())
        .await
        .unwrap();
}

async fn chat_handler(Json(req): Json<ChatRequest>) -> Json<ChatResponse> {
    let strict = req.strict_mode.unwrap_or(true);

    // Pseudo-code: call Python microservice or Rust LLM client
    // let (answer, sources) = call_llm_with_rag(req.query, strict).await?;

    let answer = if strict {
        "I don't know based on the provided knowledge.".to_string()
    } else {
        "Here is a possible answer (not fully verified).".to_string()
    };

    let res = ChatResponse {
        answer,
        sources: vec![],
        hallucination_mode: if strict { "strict".into() } else { "normal".into() },
    };

    Json(res)
}

Advantages

  • Explicit modeling of hallucination risk
    • Better trust and user satisfaction
  • RAG + verification significantly reduces factual hallucinations
  • Strict prompts (“don’t guess”) help in enterprise & regulated domains
  • Tool use (DB, calculators, search) replaces guessing with grounded data
  • Enables graded modes: creative vs factual vs strict

Limitations

  • Cannot fully eliminate hallucinations
    • LLM still a probabilistic model over text
  • Latency overhead
    • RAG + verifier + tools = more network and compute
  • Complexity
    • More components: retrievers, judges, rules → harder to maintain
  • Verifier models can also hallucinate
    • LLM-as-judge is not perfectly reliable
  • Domain coverage
    • If knowledge base is incomplete, RAG cannot fix missing facts

Interview Tips

  • Key points to mention
    • Hallucination = confidently wrong or unsupported outputs
    • Root cause: next-token prediction, not truth optimization
    • Main mitigations:
      • RAG (grounding on external knowledge)
      • Tool use (search, DB, calculators)
      • Prompting (“If unsure, say you don’t know”)
      • Verification (LLM-as-judge, rules, domain validators)
  • Common interview questions
    • “What is hallucination and why does it happen in LLMs?”
    • “How would you design a system to reduce hallucinations?”
    • “How does RAG help with hallucinations? What are its limits?”
    • “How would you detect hallucinations automatically?”
    • “How do you handle hallucinations in a medical/financial chatbot?”
  • Tricky areas
    • Don’t claim hallucinations can be fully eliminated
    • Distinguish hallucination vs outdated info vs bias
    • Mention trade-off: creativity vs factual strictness
    • Talk about evaluation: LLM-as-judge, human eval, test suites

Real-World Example

Enterprise RAG Chatbot for Internal Documentation

  • Use-case
    • Employee Q&A assistant over Confluence, Git repos, Notion, API docs
  • Hallucination Risks
    • Model invents:
      • Non-existent internal APIs
      • Wrong config flags
      • Deprecated endpoints as current
  • Mitigation Architecture
    • RAG:
      • Embed docs → store in PGVector / Qdrant
      • Retrieve top-k relevant docs per query
    • Strict system prompt:
      • “Answer only from provided docs. If docs don’t contain the answer, say you don’t know.”
    • Verifier:
      • LLM-as-judge checks answer vs retrieved docs
    • Backend controls (Python + Rust):
      • Python: LLM orchestration (LangChain, RAG, verification)
      • Rust: high-performance API gateway, rate limiting, auth
    • Response:
      • Always include:
        • Cited documents and links
        • Verification status (supported / unsupported / partial)

This pattern (RAG + strict prompts + verification + citations) is the standard, interview-ready answer for “How do you handle hallucinations in LLM systems?”.

Q54.HOW DO YOU REDUCE HALLUCINATIONS? [Input Token: 706 | Output Token: 3827] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:
    Reducing hallucinations means decreasing the frequency and severity of incorrect, fabricated, or unjustified outputs produced by LLMs (e.g., making up facts, APIs, references, or code that doesn’t work).
  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:
    • Core challenge in LLM apps, RAG, agents, and chatbots
    • Shows understanding of prompting, retrieval, evaluation, and system design
    • Often asked: “How do you make LLMs more reliable?”
  • Importance in Python/Rust backend interviews:
    • Impacts API design, validation layers, observability, and safety
    • You must know how to architect services (RAG, guardrails, monitoring) to ensure reliable outputs in production.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

To reduce hallucinations, you combine model-level, prompt-level, and system-level techniques:

  • 1. Model & Data Level

    • Use stronger base models (e.g., GPT-4, Claude, Llama 3) that hallucinate less
    • Fine-tune on domain-specific, high-quality data
    • Use instruction-tuning and RLHF/RLAIF to enforce honesty and refusal when unsure

  • 2. Prompt Engineering & Constraints

    • Explicitly instruct the model:
      • “If you don’t know, say you don’t know”
      • “Only answer using the provided context”
    • Use structured outputs (JSON schemas) and chain-of-thought (internally) to encourage reasoning
    • Use few-shot examples showing correct behavior and refusal patterns

  • 3. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

    • Retrieve relevant documents from vector DBs or search before answering
    • Force the model to ground answers in retrieved context
    • Use citation-style prompts: “Cite sources as [doc_id:line]”

  • 4. Post-Generation Verification

    • Self-checking: ask the same or another model to verify the answer
    • Fact-checking pipelines:
      • Re-query search / RAG to validate claims
      • Use tools/agents for external verification (databases, APIs)
    • Rule-based and ML-based guardrails for safety and consistency

  • 5. System & Backend Design

    • Add confidence estimation and abstention (“I’m not sure”)
    • Implement fallback strategies:
      • Return partial answers
      • Ask clarifying questions
      • Escalate to human
    • Logging, evaluation, and feedback loops to continuously improve

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Models
    • Base LLM (e.g., GPT-4, Llama 3, Mistral)
    • Optional: smaller LLM for verification / critique
  • Services
    • RAG service (retrieval + reranking)
    • Guardrail/validation service
    • Prompt orchestration service
  • Pipelines
    • Query → Retrieval → Generation → Verification → Response
  • Backend Layers
    • API gateway (FastAPI / Actix-Web / Axum)
    • Orchestrator (Python service, Rust microservice)
    • Vector DB service (e.g., Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, pgvector)
    • Monitoring (Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, Sentry)

Technologies Used

  • Python
    • Web: FastAPI, Flask
    • LLM: langchain, llama_index, transformers, vllm
    • RAG: langchain, chromadb, qdrant-client, faiss
    • Validation: pydantic, guardrails-ai
  • Rust
    • Web: axum, actix-web
    • LLM clients: reqwest + HTTP to external LLMs, or bindings to local models
    • Vector DB: gRPC/HTTP clients to Qdrant/Milvus
    • Concurrency: tokio
  • Infra
    • Vector DB: Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, Postgres + pgvector
    • Caching: Redis
    • Observability: Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry

Data Flow and Processing Stages

  1. Input
    • User query: natural language question / task
  2. Pre-processing
    • Normalization, language detection, user/session context
  3. Retrieval (RAG)
    • Embed query → vector search → retrieve top-k docs
    • Optional reranking (e.g., cross-encoder)
  4. Prompt Construction
    • System prompt (rules)
    • Context (retrieved docs)
    • User query
  5. Generation
    • LLM generates answer grounded in context
  6. Verification & Guardrails
    • Self-check / critique step
    • Schema validation (JSON, enums)
    • Rule-based checks (PII, policy)
  7. Response
    • Return answer (+ citations, confidence score)
    • Log traces for monitoring

API Endpoints & Contracts (Example)

  • POST /v1/answer
    • Request:
      {
  "query": "What are the side effects of drug X?",
  "top_k": 5,
  "max_tokens": 512,
  "require_citations": true
}
    • Response:
      {
  "answer": "Drug X commonly causes nausea and headache...",
  "citations": [
    {"doc_id": "guidelines_2023", "score": 0.94},
    {"doc_id": "paper_1234", "score": 0.89}
  ],
  "confidence": 0.87,
  "grounded": true,
  "abstained": false
}

Model Lifecycle

  • Training / Fine-tuning
    • Collect domain data
    • Fine-tune or LoRA adapters for:
      • Factual QA in your domain
      • Refusal behavior when no evidence
  • Evaluation
    • Automatic: factual QA benchmarks, hallucination metrics
    • Human: expert review, red-teaming
  • Deployment
    • Containerized LLM or API-based provider
    • Blue-green / canary releases
  • Monitoring
    • Track:
      • Hallucination incidents (tagged by feedback)
      • Refusal rate
      • Latency, token usage
    • Feedback loop to improve prompts and retrieval

Scalability Considerations

  • Stateless LLM orchestration services
  • Horizontal scaling of:
    • Vector DB
    • LLM inference (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, distributed inference)
  • Caching:
    • Query → answer cache
    • Embedding cache
  • Batch retrieval and generation for throughput

Performance Considerations

  • Latency
    • Use smaller models for retrieval/reranking
    • Stream responses
    • Pre-compute and cache embeddings
  • Throughput
    • Batch requests
    • Use Rust for high-throughput retrieval and orchestration
  • Cost vs hallucination trade-off
    • Sometimes need larger models or extra verification steps → more cost but fewer hallucinations

Step-by-Step Flow

  • Step 1: Retrieve Context (RAG)
    • Embed query → search vector DB → get top-k relevant documents
  • Step 2: Constrained Generation
    • Build a prompt that:
      • Includes retrieved context
      • Explicitly instructs the model to only answer from context or say “I don’t know”
    • Generate answer with LLM
  • Step 3: Verify & Respond
    • Run a verification step:
      • Check if answer is grounded in citations
      • Validate JSON schema / safety rules
    • Return answer with citations and confidence; abstain if not reliable

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

High-Level Python Implementation (FastAPI + RAG + Guardrails)

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
from langchain.embeddings import OpenAIEmbeddings
from langchain.vectorstores import Qdrant
from langchain.chat_models import ChatOpenAI
from langchain.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate

app = FastAPI()

embeddings = OpenAIEmbeddings()
vectorstore = Qdrant(
    url="http://qdrant:6333",
    collection_name="docs",
    embeddings=embeddings
)
llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o", temperature=0.1)

class QueryRequest(BaseModel):
    query: str
    top_k: int = 5

class AnswerResponse(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    citations: list
    confidence: float
    grounded: bool
    abstained: bool

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a factual assistant. Use ONLY the provided context.
If the answer is not in the context, say: "I don't know based on the provided data."
Always cite sources as [doc_id].
"""

@app.post("/v1/answer", response_model=AnswerResponse)
async def answer(req: QueryRequest):
    # 1. Retrieve relevant docs
    docs = vectorstore.similarity_search(req.query, k=req.top_k)

    context = "\n\n".join(
        f"[{d.metadata.get('doc_id', 'unknown')}]: {d.page_content}"
        for d in docs
    )

    # 2. Build prompt
    prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
        ("system", SYSTEM_PROMPT),
        ("human", "Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}")
    ]).format(context=context, question=req.query)

    # 3. Generate answer
    llm_resp = await llm.ainvoke(prompt)
    answer_text = llm_resp.content

    # 4. Simple heuristic grounding check
    grounded = any(f"[{d.metadata.get('doc_id', 'unknown')}]" in answer_text for d in docs)
    abstained = "I don't know based on the provided data" in answer_text

    # In real systems: add more advanced verification + scoring
    return AnswerResponse(
        answer=answer_text,
        citations=[d.metadata.get("doc_id", "unknown") for d in docs],
        confidence=0.8 if grounded and not abstained else 0.4,
        grounded=grounded,
        abstained=abstained
    )

High-Level Rust Implementation (Axum + Retrieval Orchestrator)

use axum::{routing::post, Json, Router};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::net::SocketAddr;

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct QueryRequest {
    query: String,
    top_k: Option<u32>,
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct AnswerResponse {
    answer: String,
    citations: Vec<String>,
    confidence: f32,
    grounded: bool,
    abstained: bool,
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let app = Router::new().route("/v1/answer", post(answer_handler));

    let addr = SocketAddr::from(([0, 0, 0, 0], 8080));
    axum::Server::bind(&addr)
        .serve(app.into_make_service())
        .await
        .unwrap();
}

async fn answer_handler(Json(req): Json<QueryRequest>) -> Json<AnswerResponse> {
    // 1. Call vector DB (e.g., Qdrant) to retrieve docs
    let docs = retrieve_docs(&req.query, req.top_k.unwrap_or(5)).await;

    // 2. Build system prompt + context
    let context = docs.iter()
        .map(|d| format!("[{}]: {}", d.doc_id, d.content))
        .collect::<Vec<_>>()
        .join("\n\n");

    let system_prompt = r#"
You are a factual assistant. Use ONLY the provided context.
If the answer is not in the context, say: "I don't know based on the provided data."
Always cite sources as [doc_id].
"#;

    let user_prompt = format!(
        "Context:\n{}\n\nQuestion: {}",
        context, req.query
    );

    // 3. Call external LLM API (e.g., OpenAI, local gateway)
    let answer_text = call_llm(system_prompt, &user_prompt).await;

    // 4. Simple grounding/abstention check
    let grounded = docs.iter().any(|d| answer_text.contains(&format!("[{}]", d.doc_id)));
    let abstained = answer_text.contains("I don't know based on the provided data");

    Json(AnswerResponse {
        answer: answer_text,
        citations: docs.iter().map(|d| d.doc_id.clone()).collect(),
        confidence: if grounded && !abstained { 0.8 } else { 0.4 },
        grounded,
        abstained,
    })
}

}

}

async fn call_llm(_system: &str, _user: &str) -> String {
