            .route("/v1/llm/infer", web::post().to(llm_infer))
    })
    .bind(("0.0.0.0", 8080))?
    .run()
    .await
}

Advantages

  • Clear responsibility boundaries:
    • Avoids confusion between provider vs. customer duties.
  • Scalability with security:
    • IAM, VPC, and managed services scale with infra.
  • Compliance-friendly:
    • Easier to meet SOC2/GDPR/HIPAA with structured controls.
  • Better risk management:
    • Layered security (defense in depth).
  • Suitable for AI/ML/GenAI:
    • Protects data, models, and inference endpoints.

Limitations

  • Complexity:
    • IAM policies, network rules, and encryption setups can be hard to manage.
  • Misconfiguration risk:
    • Public S3 buckets, overly permissive roles, open security groups.
  • Vendor lock-in:
    • Security tooling and policies often tied to specific cloud providers.
  • Operational overhead:
    • Continuous monitoring, key rotation, audits, and policy updates.
  • Performance overhead:
    • Extra hops, encryption, and logging can add latency if not tuned.

Interview Tips

  • Key points to remember:

    • Clearly explain the shared responsibility model.
    • Mention IAM, network security, encryption, logging as core pillars.
    • Tie your answer to real workloads: APIs, ML pipelines, LLM inference.

  • Common interview questions:

    • Explain the cloud shared responsibility model.
    • How would you secure an LLM inference API in the cloud?
    • How do you secure S3/GCS buckets and databases?
    • How do you handle secrets and API keys?
    • How do you secure a RAG system (vector DB + LLM)?

  • Tricky areas:

    • Confusing authN vs. authZ.
    • Overlooking internal threats (insider access).
    • Ignoring egress controls (data exfiltration).
    • Not mentioning least privilege and zero trust.

Real-World Example

Secure RAG-based Enterprise Assistant on AWS

  • Use case:

    • An internal chatbot that answers questions using company documents.

  • Security model application:

    • IAM:
      • Each microservice (ingestion, embedding, retrieval, LLM) has its own IAM role.
      • Users authenticated via SSO (Cognito/Okta) and mapped to roles.
    • Network:
      • All services in private subnets.
      • API Gateway + WAF in public subnet.
      • Vector DB and RDS only accessible from VPC.
    • Data:
      • Documents stored in S3, encrypted with KMS.
      • Embeddings stored in a vector DB with encryption at rest.
    • Application:
      • Python FastAPI backend exposes /chat endpoint.
      • Rust microservice for high-performance embedding generation.
    • Monitoring:
      • CloudWatch/Prometheus logs and metrics.
      • Alerts on unusual access patterns or spikes.

This is a textbook example of applying a cloud security model to a modern GenAI/RAG system.

Q159.WHAT IS IAM? [Input Token: 703 | Output Token: 3546] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:
    IAM (Identity and Access Management) is a framework of policies, processes, and technologies that ensures the right entities (users, services, machines) have the right access to the right resources at the right time, and that access is auditable and controllable.

  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:

    • Models, datasets, and prompts are sensitive assets.
    • IAM is critical for:
      • Securing training data (e.g., PII, proprietary data).
      • Controlling access to model endpoints (LLM inference APIs, vector DBs).
      • Multi-tenant GenAI platforms where different customers share infrastructure.

  • Importance in Python/Rust Backend interviews:

    • Backend services must enforce authN/authZ correctly.
    • Microservices, APIs, and workers need service-level identities and roles.
    • Integration with cloud IAM (AWS IAM, GCP IAM, Azure AD) is a common requirement.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • Core Concepts:

    • Identity: Who/what you are (user, service account, machine).
    • Authentication (AuthN): Verifying identity (password, OAuth, JWT, mTLS).
    • Authorization (AuthZ): Deciding what an identity can do (RBAC, ABAC, policies).
    • Accountability: Logging, auditing, and traceability of access.

  • IAM Working (High-level):

    • A client (user or service) tries to access a resource (API, DB, model).
    • The system:
      • Authenticates the client.
      • Retrieves policies/roles attached to the identity.
      • Evaluates permissions against the requested action/resource.
      • Allows or denies access and logs the decision.

  • Typical IAM Components:

    • Identity Provider (IdP): Manages identities and authentication (e.g., Keycloak, Auth0, AWS Cognito, Okta).
    • Policy Store / Engine: Stores and evaluates access policies (e.g., AWS IAM policies, OPA, Casbin).
    • Resource Server: The actual backend/ML service enforcing IAM checks.
    • Audit & Logging: Tracks who accessed what and when.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Models & Services (GenAI context):

    • LLM Inference Service (e.g., FastAPI + PyTorch/Transformers).
    • Vector Database (e.g., Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, pgvector).
    • Model Registry (e.g., MLflow, SageMaker Model Registry).
    • Data Lake / Feature Store (e.g., S3, BigQuery, Feast).

  • IAM Layer:

    • User identities: Human users (engineers, analysts, customers).
    • Service identities: Microservices, batch jobs, model training pipelines.
    • Roles: e.g., admin, ml-engineer, viewer, inference-client.
    • Policies:
      • Allow ml-engineer to deploy models.
      • Allow inference-client to call /v1/llm/infer.
      • Deny access to PII vector collections except for data-privacy-team.

Technologies Used

  • Python-side:

    • Web: FastAPI, Flask, Django (with DRF).
    • Auth: PyJWT, Authlib, python-jose, fastapi-security.
    • Policy: OPA (via HTTP), Casbin (Python binding).

  • Rust-side:

    • Web: Axum, Actix-web, Rocket.
    • Auth/JWT: jsonwebtoken, oauth2, tower-http middlewares.
    • Policy: Casbin-rs, custom policy evaluators.

  • Cloud IAM:

    • AWS IAM: Roles, policies, STS, IAM users, IAM roles for services.
    • GCP IAM: Service accounts, roles, IAM policies.
    • Azure: Azure AD, Managed Identities, RBAC.

Data Flow and Processing Stages (GenAI Backend Example)

  • Request Path:

    • User → API Gateway → AuthN (JWT/OAuth2) → Backend (FastAPI/Axum) → IAM policy check → LLM/Vector DB → Response.

  • IAM Data Flow:

    • Token → Identity → Roles → Policies → Decision (Allow/Deny) → Log.

API Endpoints and Contracts (Example)

  • Auth endpoints (handled by IdP or auth service):

    • POST /auth/login
      • Input: { "username": "...", "password": "..." }
      • Output: { "access_token": "...", "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 3600 }
    • POST /auth/refresh
    • GET /auth/me – returns current user, roles, permissions.

  • Protected ML endpoints:

    • POST /v1/llm/infer
      • Headers: Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
      • Body: { "prompt": "...", "model_id": "gpt-xyz" }
      • Backend checks:
        • Is token valid?
        • Does role allow llm:infer on model_id?
    • POST /v1/rag/query
      • Requires permission: rag:query on collection_id.

Model Lifecycle and IAM

  • Training:
    • IAM controls who can:
      • Access raw data buckets.
      • Launch training jobs (e.g., on SageMaker, Vertex AI).
      • Access GPU clusters.
  • Evaluation:
    • IAM restrictions on evaluation datasets (test sets with sensitive data).
  • Deployment:
    • Only ml-admin or CI/CD service role can:
      • Register new model version.
      • Promote model to production endpoint.
  • Monitoring:
    • IAM for access to logs, traces, prompt/response logs (to protect privacy).

Scalability Considerations

  • Token verification:
    • Use JWT with public key verification (no DB lookup).
    • Cache public keys (JWKS) from IdP.
  • Policy evaluation:
    • Use in-memory or distributed cache for policies.
    • Offload complex policy evaluation to policy engine (e.g., OPA sidecar).
  • Multi-tenant:
    • Tenant-aware roles and resource scoping.
    • Namespace resources by tenant (e.g., tenantA:collection:123).

Performance Considerations

  • Latency:
    • Avoid per-request DB lookups for auth; prefer JWT + cached policy.
    • Use middleware to short-circuit unauthorized requests early.
  • Throughput:
    • Stateless auth (JWT) allows horizontal scaling.
  • Security:
    • Short-lived tokens, refresh tokens, mTLS between services.
    • Principle of least privilege for service roles.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    U[User / Service Client] -->|HTTP Request + JWT| GW[API Gateway]

    GW -->|Forward Request| B[Backend Service (FastAPI / Axum)]

    B -->|Verify Token| IdP[Identity Provider (Auth0/Keycloak/Cognito)]
    IdP -->|JWKS / Public Keys| B

    B -->|Who is this?| IAM[Policy Engine (IAM / OPA / Casbin)]
    IAM -->|Allow / Deny| B

    B -->|Authorized| LLM[LLM / RAG Service]
    B -->|Authorized| VDB[Vector DB / Data Store]

    LLM --> B
    VDB --> B
    B -->|Response| U

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Authentication:
    • Client obtains an access token (JWT) from IdP via login or client credentials.
  2. Authorization:
    • Client calls backend API with Authorization: Bearer <token>.
    • Backend:
      • Verifies token signature and expiry.
      • Extracts identity, roles, claims (e.g., sub, roles, tenant).
      • Evaluates policies (RBAC/ABAC) via IAM/policy engine.
  3. Access & Audit:
    • If allowed:
      • Backend executes business logic (LLM inference, RAG query, DB operations).
      • Logs request, identity, and decision for audit.
    • If denied:
      • Returns 403 Forbidden or 401 Unauthorized.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

Python (FastAPI + JWT + Casbin Example)

from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer
from jose import jwt, JWTError
import casbin

app = FastAPI()
security = HTTPBearer()

JWT_PUBLIC_KEY = "..."  # from IdP JWKS
JWT_ALGO = "RS256"

# Casbin enforcer (RBAC/ABAC)
e = casbin.Enforcer("model.conf", "policy.csv")

def get_current_user(token=Depends(security)):
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token.credentials, JWT_PUBLIC_KEY, algorithms=[JWT_ALGO])
        return {
            "sub": payload["sub"],
            "roles": payload.get("roles", []),
            "tenant": payload.get("tenant"),
        }
    except JWTError:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED, detail="Invalid token")

def authorize(user, obj, act):
    # Example: subject = user_id or role
    # Here we use role-based check
    for role in user["roles"]:
        if e.enforce(role, obj, act):
            return True
    raise HTTPException(status_code=status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN, detail="Forbidden")

@app.post("/v1/llm/infer")
def infer_llm(request: dict, user=Depends(get_current_user)):
    model_id = request.get("model_id", "default")
    # Authorization: can this user perform 'infer' on this model?
    authorize(user, f"model:{model_id}", "infer")

    prompt = request["prompt"]
    # Call LLM inference pipeline (omitted)
    result = {"output": f"LLM response to: {prompt}"}
    return result

Rust (Axum + JWT + Casbin-rs Example)

use axum::{
    routing::post,
    Router, Json, extract::State,
};
use jsonwebtoken::{decode, DecodingKey, Validation, Algorithm};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use casbin::{Enforcer, DefaultModel, FileAdapter};

#[derive(Clone)]
struct AppState {
    enforcer: Enforcer,
    jwt_decoding_key: DecodingKey,
}

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
struct Claims {
    sub: String,
    roles: Vec<String>,
    exp: usize,
}

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
struct InferRequest {
    prompt: String,
    model_id: Option<String>,
}

async fn infer_llm(
    State(state): State<AppState>,
    Json(req): Json<InferRequest>,
    // In practice, extract token from headers via middleware
) -> Result<Json<serde_json::Value>, (axum::http::StatusCode, String)> {
    let token = "..."; // Extract from Authorization header
    let token_data = decode::<Claims>(
        token,
        &state.jwt_decoding_key,
        &Validation::new(Algorithm::RS256),
    ).map_err(|_| (axum::http::StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED, "Invalid token".into()))?;

    let claims = token_data.claims;
    let model_id = req.model_id.unwrap_or_else(|| "default".to_string());

    // Authorization check
    let mut allowed = false;
    for role in claims.roles {
        if state.enforcer.enforce((role, format!("model:{}", model_id), "infer")).unwrap_or(false) {
            allowed = true;
            break;
        }
    }
    if !allowed {
        return Err((axum::http::StatusCode::FORBIDDEN, "Forbidden".into()));
    }

    let response = serde_json::json!({
        "output": format!("LLM response to: {}", req.prompt)
    });
    Ok(Json(response))
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let m = DefaultModel::from_file("model.conf").await.unwrap();
    let a = FileAdapter::new("policy.csv");
    let enforcer = Enforcer::new(m, a).await.unwrap();

    let state = AppState {
        enforcer,
        jwt_decoding_key: DecodingKey::from_rsa_pem(include_bytes!("public.pem")).unwrap(),
    };

    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/v1/llm/infer", post(infer_llm))
        .with_state(state);

    axum::Server::bind(&"0.0.0.0:8080".parse().unwrap())
        .serve(app.into_make_service())
        .await
        .unwrap();
}

Advantages

  • Security:
    • Centralized control over who can access what.
    • Reduces risk of data leakage, model misuse, and privilege escalation.
  • Compliance:
    • Supports audit trails for GDPR, HIPAA, SOC2, etc.
  • Scalability & Manageability:
    • Role-based and policy-based access scales better than per-user permissions.
    • Easy to onboard/offboard users and services.
  • Multi-tenancy:
    • Critical for SaaS GenAI platforms serving multiple customers.

Limitations

  • Complexity:
    • Designing fine-grained policies can be difficult and error-prone.
  • Performance Overhead:
    • Policy evaluation and token verification add latency if not optimized.
  • Operational Burden:
    • Requires ongoing policy management, key rotation, and audit review.
  • Misconfiguration Risk:
    • Overly permissive roles or incorrect policies can undermine security.

Interview Tips

  • Common Questions:

    • What is IAM and how is it different from authentication/authorization?
    • Explain RBAC vs ABAC vs PBAC (policy-based access control).
    • How would you secure an LLM inference API in production?
    • How do you use AWS IAM roles for services (e.g., EC2, Lambda, ECS, SageMaker)?
    • How do you implement multi-tenant access control for a RAG system?

  • Key Points to Remember:

    • Separate AuthN and AuthZ clearly.
    • Emphasize least privilege and zero trust principles.
    • Mention JWT, OAuth2, OIDC, and policy engines (OPA/Casbin).
    • Highlight auditing and compliance for enterprise contexts.

  • Tricky Areas:

    • Designing tenant-aware IAM (e.g., tenant isolation in vector DB).
    • Handling service-to-service auth (mTLS, service accounts, IAM roles).
    • Token lifetimes, refresh tokens, and key rotation strategies.

Real-World Example

  • Use Case: Enterprise RAG/LLM Platform

    • Scenario:

      • A company offers a RAG-based knowledge assistant to multiple customers.
      • Each customer has private documents stored in a vector DB.
      • LLM inference is served via a central API.

    • IAM Requirements:

      • Each customer’s users can only query their own document collections.
      • Admins can configure ingestion pipelines but not access other tenants’ data.
      • Internal ML engineers can deploy models but cannot see customer content.

    • Implementation:

      • IdP: Auth0/Keycloak with OIDC; each user has tenant_id and roles.
      • Backend (Python/Rust):
        • Extracts tenant_id from JWT.
        • Ensures all vector DB queries are scoped by tenant_id.
        • Uses Casbin/OPA policies for actions like rag:query, rag:ingest, model:deploy.
      • Cloud IAM:
        • Use AWS IAM roles for:
          • Training jobs accessing S3 buckets per tenant.
          • Lambda/ECS tasks with least-privilege access to required resources only.

    • Result:

      • Secure, multi-tenant GenAI platform with clear access boundaries.
      • Easier audits and compliance due to centralized IAM policies and logs.
Q160.WHAT IS SECRETS MANAGEMENT? [Input Token: 704 | Output Token: 3308] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition
    • Secrets management is the practice of securely storing, accessing, distributing, rotating, and auditing sensitive credentials such as:
      • API keys
      • Database passwords
      • Encryption keys
      • OAuth tokens
      • Certificates and private keys
  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews
    • ML/GenAI systems integrate with:
      • Vector DBs (Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus)
      • LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.)
      • Object storage (S3, GCS)
    • All require secrets; improper handling is a major security risk.
    • Interviewers check if you:
      • Avoid hard-coding secrets in code/notebooks
      • Use secure config patterns in training & inference pipelines
  • Importance in Python/Rust backend interviews
    • Backend services must:
      • Securely access DBs, message queues, external APIs
      • Implement 12-factor app config via environment or secrets stores
    • Shows you understand:
      • Secure deployment
      • Cloud-native best practices
      • Production-readiness

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • Core idea
    • Centralized, controlled system for managing secrets across environments:
      • Dev, staging, prod
      • Different services and microservices
  • Key functions
    • Storage: encrypted at rest (e.g., KMS, HSM-backed)
    • Access control: who/what can access which secret
    • Distribution: how secrets reach apps (env vars, sidecar, file mounts, API calls)
    • Rotation: automatic or manual key/password rotation
    • Auditing: logs of access, changes, and failures
  • Typical flow
    • Secret is created and stored in a secret manager service
    • Application authenticates using a short-lived identity (JWT, IAM role, service account)
    • Secret manager returns secrets over TLS with strict RBAC
    • Application uses secret in-memory; never logs or persists it
    • Rotation is handled centrally; apps reload secrets without redeploy

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Secret Store / Manager
    • Examples:
      • HashiCorp Vault
      • AWS Secrets Manager / SSM Parameter Store
      • GCP Secret Manager
      • Azure Key Vault
      • Kubernetes Secrets (often with KMS integration)
  • Identity & Access Management (IAM)
    • Service accounts / roles
    • OIDC / JWT tokens
    • Role-based access control (RBAC)
  • Client Integration
    • SDKs / APIs in Python and Rust
    • Sidecar containers (e.g., Vault Agent)
    • Init containers or CI/CD pipeline integration
  • Encryption
    • At rest:
      • KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault keys)
      • HSM-backed keys for high security
    • In transit:
      • TLS / HTTPS
  • Audit & Monitoring
    • Logs for:
      • Secret read/write
      • Rotation events
      • Access failures and anomalies

Technologies Used

  • Python
    • Secret access:
      • boto3 (AWS Secrets Manager / SSM)
      • google-cloud-secret-manager
      • azure-keyvault-secrets
      • hvac (Vault client)
    • Web frameworks:
      • FastAPI / Flask / Django using secrets for DB, Redis, etc.
  • Rust
    • HTTP clients:
      • reqwest, hyper
    • Cloud SDKs / crates:
      • aws-sdk-secretsmanager, aws-config
      • Custom REST clients for Vault/GCP/Azure
  • Infra tools
    • Kubernetes + Secrets + KMS
    • Helm charts with external secret references
    • GitOps with sealed secrets (e.g., Bitnami SealedSecrets)

Data Flow and Processing Stages

  • Creation
    • DevOps / security team creates secret in secret manager
    • Associate metadata: name, tags, rotation policy
  • Access
    • Service authenticates (IAM role, service account, token)
    • Secret manager verifies identity
    • Returns secret (JSON, string, binary)
  • Usage
    • App loads secret into memory
    • Uses it for:
      • DB connection
      • LLM API calls
      • Vector DB auth
  • Rotation
    • Secret manager rotates underlying credential
    • Notifies or automatically updates client (depending on integration)
  • Audit
    • Logs stored in central logging system (CloudWatch, Stackdriver, ELK, etc.)

API Endpoints and Contracts (Example)

Assume a secrets service API abstraction in front of a cloud provider:

  • GET /v1/secrets/{name}
    • Headers:
      • Authorization: Bearer <service_token>
    • Response:
      {
  "name": "db/password",
  "value": "s3cr3t",
  "version": "5",
  "updated_at": "2026-06-01T12:00:00Z"
}
  • POST /v1/secrets/{name}/rotate
    • Rotates secret and returns new version
  • GET /v1/secrets/{name}/metadata
    • Returns metadata, not the value

Model Lifecycle (ML/GenAI Context)

  • Training
    • Access:
      • Data warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift)
      • Object storage (S3/GCS)
    • Secrets:
      • Access keys, DB passwords, service account keys
  • Evaluation
    • May need temporary access to test datasets or evaluation services
  • Deployment (Inference / RAG)
    • Secrets for:
      • LLM providers (OpenAI API keys)
      • Vector DB (Pinecone, Qdrant)
      • Feature stores
  • Monitoring
    • Avoid leaking secrets in logs/metrics
    • Ensure secret access anomalies are monitored

Scalability Considerations

  • High QPS for secret reads:
    • Cache secrets in memory with TTL
    • Use local sidecar agents to reduce central load
  • Multi-region deployments:
    • Regional replication of secrets
    • Latency-aware secret retrieval
  • Multi-tenant systems:
    • Tenant-specific secrets
    • Strict isolation via IAM and namespaces

Performance Considerations

  • Latency
    • Fetch secrets at startup and cache
    • For frequently rotated secrets, use:
      • Background refresh
      • Sidecar agent that syncs secrets locally
  • Throughput
    • Avoid per-request secret fetch
    • Use connection pools (DB/API) built from secrets once

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    Dev[DevOps / Security] -->|Create / Update Secrets| SM[Secret Manager]

    subgraph Runtime
        App[Python/Rust Service]
        Cache[In-memory Secret Cache]
        IAM[Service Identity (Role / SA)]
    end

    App -->|Assume Role / Get Token| IAM
    IAM -->|AuthN / AuthZ| SM
    App -->|Fetch Secret (once)| SM
    App -->|Store Secret| Cache
    Cache -->|Provide Secret| App

    SM -->|Audit Logs| Logs[Logging / SIEM]

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Provisioning
    • DevOps creates secrets (e.g., db/password, openai/api_key) in secret manager.
    • Configure IAM policies for which services can access which secrets.
  2. Application Startup
    • Python/Rust service starts.
    • Uses its service identity (IAM role, service account) to authenticate to the secret manager.
    • Fetches required secrets and stores them in memory.
  3. Runtime & Rotation
    • Service uses secrets to connect to DBs, LLM APIs, vector DBs.
    • Secret manager rotates secrets per policy.
    • Service refreshes secrets periodically or on restart, without code change.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

High-Level Implementation in Python (FastAPI + AWS Secrets Manager)

from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends
import boto3
import json
import os
from functools import lru_cache

app = FastAPI()

@lru_cache()
def get_secrets_client():
    return boto3.client("secretsmanager", region_name=os.getenv("AWS_REGION", "us-east-1"))

@lru_cache()
def get_db_credentials():
    client = get_secrets_client()
    resp = client.get_secret_value(SecretId="myapp/prod/db")
    secret_str = resp["SecretString"]
    data = json.loads(secret_str)
    return data["username"], data["password"], data["host"]

@app.on_event("startup")
def init():
    # Warm up secret cache on startup
    get_db_credentials()

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}

@app.get("/items")
def list_items():
    user, pwd, host = get_db_credentials()
    # Use user/pwd/host to connect to DB (psycopg2, SQLAlchemy, etc.)
    return {"items": []}

Notes

  • Uses @lru_cache to cache secrets in memory.
  • Secrets are never logged or written to disk.
  • IAM role on the instance/pod grants access; no static AWS keys needed.

High-Level Implementation in Rust (Actix-Web + AWS Secrets Manager)

use actix_web::{get, App, HttpServer, Responder};
use aws_config::meta::region::RegionProviderChain;
use aws_sdk_secretsmanager as secretsmanager;
use once_cell::sync::OnceCell;
use serde::Deserialize;

static CLIENT: OnceCell<secretsmanager::Client> = OnceCell::new();
static DB_CREDS: OnceCell<DbCreds> = OnceCell::new();

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize, Clone)]
struct DbCreds {
    username: String,
    password: String,
    host: String,
}

async fn init_client() -> secretsmanager::Client {
    let region_provider = RegionProviderChain::default_provider().or_else("us-east-1");
    let config = aws_config::from_env().region(region_provider).load().await;
    secretsmanager::Client::new(&config)
}

async fn load_db_creds() -> DbCreds {
    let client = CLIENT.get_or_init(|| futures::executor::block_on(init_client())).clone();
    let resp = client
        .get_secret_value()
        .secret_id("myapp/prod/db")
        .send()
        .await
        .expect("failed to get secret");

    let secret_str = resp.secret_string().unwrap();
    serde_json::from_str(secret_str).expect("invalid secret json")
}

#[get("/health")]
async fn health() -> impl Responder {
    "ok"
}

#[get("/items")]
async fn items() -> impl Responder {
    let creds = DB_CREDS
        .get_or_init(|| futures::executor::block_on(load_db_creds()))
        .clone();

    // Use creds.username, creds.password, creds.host to connect to DB
    format!("Using DB at {}", creds.host)
}

#[actix_web::main]
async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    CLIENT.set(init_client().await).unwrap();
    DB_CREDS.set(load_db_creds().await).unwrap();

    HttpServer::new(|| App::new().service(health).service(items))
        .bind(("0.0.0.0", 8080))?
        .run()
        .await
}

Notes

  • Uses OnceCell to cache the client and secrets.
  • Uses IAM role for auth (no static credentials).

Advantages

  • Security
    • No secrets in code, Git, or container images.
    • Centralized encryption and access control.
  • Manageability
    • Easy rotation without code changes or redeploys.
    • Consistent management across services and environments.
  • Auditability
    • Full history of access and updates.
    • Supports compliance (PCI-DSS, SOC2, HIPAA, etc.).
  • Scalability
    • Works across microservices, multi-region, multi-cloud setups.

Limitations

  • Operational complexity
    • Requires setup and maintenance of secret manager and IAM policies.
  • Latency
    • Direct per-request calls to secret manager can be slow; requires caching patterns.
  • Misconfiguration risks
    • Overly broad IAM policies can expose secrets.
    • Incorrect rotation without app readiness can cause outages.
  • Local development friction
    • Needs dev-friendly flows (local env vars, dev secrets) that still follow best practices.

Interview Tips

  • Key points to mention
    • Never hard-code secrets in:
      • Code repositories
      • Docker images
      • Notebooks
    • Use:
      • Environment variables + secret manager
      • Kubernetes Secrets (preferably encrypted with KMS)
      • Cloud secret managers (AWS, GCP, Azure)
    • Emphasize:
      • Rotation and least privilege
      • Audit logging
      • Separation of duties (dev vs ops vs security)
  • Common interview questions
    • How do you manage API keys for LLM providers in a RAG system?
    • How do you handle secrets in a Kubernetes-based microservice architecture?
    • How do you rotate database passwords without downtime?
    • How do you prevent secrets from leaking into logs or client responses?
  • Tricky areas
    • Handling secrets in CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI):
      • Use CI secret stores, not plaintext in YAML.
    • Managing secrets across multi-tenant systems:
      • Tenant isolation, per-tenant keys.
    • Secrets in ML notebooks:
      • Use env vars or mounted secrets; avoid storing in notebooks.

Real-World Example

  • Use-case: Production RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) service

    • Components:
      • LLM provider (OpenAI / Anthropic)
      • Vector database (Pinecone / Qdrant)
      • Object storage (S3) for documents
      • Python FastAPI backend
      • Rust microservice for high-throughput embedding generation

  • Secrets needed

    • OPENAI_API_KEY
    • PINECONE_API_KEY
    • S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID / S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (or IAM role)
    • DB credentials for metadata store

  • Secrets management setup

    • All secrets stored in AWS Secrets Manager:
      • rag/prod/openai
      • rag/prod/pinecone
      • rag/prod/db
    • FastAPI and Rust services:
      • Run on EKS with IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA).
      • On startup, fetch secrets from Secrets Manager, cache in memory.
    • Rotation:
      • OpenAI and Pinecone keys rotated monthly.
      • DB password rotated via Lambda + Secrets Manager integration, apps reconnect using new secrets without redeploy.
    • Monitoring:
      • CloudWatch logs for secret access patterns.
      • Alerts on unusual access (e.g., unexpected region or service).

This pattern demonstrates to interviewers that you understand end-to-end production security for AI/ML and backend systems.

Q161.WHAT IS WORKFLOW AUTOMATION? [Input Token: 704 | Output Token: 3488] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition

    • Workflow automation is the design and execution of business or technical processes where tasks, data routing, and decision logic are automatically handled by software systems instead of manual human steps.
    • In AI/ML/GenAI context, it often means automating ML/LLM pipelines: data ingestion, preprocessing, training, evaluation, deployment, and inference workflows.

  • Why it is important in AI/ML/GenAI interviews

    • Modern ML/GenAI systems are pipelines, not single scripts.
    • Interviewers want to see if you can:
      • Orchestrate ETL → training → evaluation → deployment → monitoring.
      • Build RAG workflows, batch inference pipelines, and feedback loops.
      • Use tools like Airflow, Prefect, Kubeflow, Dagster, or LangGraph for LLM workflows.

  • Why it is important in Python/Rust Backend interviews

    • Backend engineers must:
      • Automate background jobs, cron tasks, data sync, notifications, ETL, CI/CD.
      • Design reliable, idempotent, observable workflows.
      • Integrate with message queues, task queues, and orchestrators (Celery, Redis, Kafka, Temporal, etc.).

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • Core idea

    • Break a process into discrete steps (tasks).
    • Define dependencies and order of execution.
    • Use an orchestrator or workflow engine to:
      • Schedule tasks
      • Handle retries
      • Pass data between steps
      • Log and monitor status

  • Key concepts

    • Task/Activity: A unit of work (e.g., "clean data", "call LLM", "store embedding").
    • Workflow/DAG: Ordered collection of tasks with dependencies.
    • Trigger: Event or schedule that starts the workflow.
    • Orchestrator: System that runs the workflow (Airflow, Temporal, Prefect, Dagster, Kubeflow, etc.).
    • Workers/Executors: Processes that execute tasks (Python/Rust services, containers).
    • State & Metadata: Status, logs, outputs, retries, timing.

  • In GenAI / LLM systems

    • Example workflow:
      • User uploads documents → embeddings generated → stored in vector DB → index updated → RAG inference pipeline uses new data.
    • Another workflow:
      • Daily fine-tuning job → evaluate new model → canary deploy → monitor metrics → auto rollback if degraded.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Workflow Engine / Orchestrator
    • Examples:
      • Airflow, Prefect, Dagster (Python-heavy)
      • Temporal, Cadence, AWS Step Functions
      • Kubeflow Pipelines for ML workflows
      • LangGraph, Haystack pipelines for LLM workflows
  • Task Runners / Workers
    • Python:
      • Celery workers, RQ workers, custom FastAPI workers
    • Rust:
      • Actix/Tokio workers, custom async executors, Temporal Rust SDK
  • Messaging / Queue
    • Redis, RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS, NATS
  • Storage
    • Relational: PostgreSQL, MySQL
    • Object: S3, GCS, MinIO
    • Vector DB (for GenAI workflows): Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, FAISS, pgvector
  • ML/LLM Components
    • Model training: PyTorch, TensorFlow, Hugging Face Transformers
    • Embeddings: OpenAI, Cohere, SentenceTransformers
    • RAG: LangChain, LlamaIndex, custom pipelines
    • Monitoring: Prometheus, Grafana, MLflow, Weights & Biases

Data Flow and Processing Stages (AI/ML Example)

  • Stage 1: Ingestion
    • Pull data from DB, logs, APIs, or files.
    • Validate and store raw data.
  • Stage 2: Preprocessing / Feature Engineering
    • Clean, normalize, tokenize, embed.
  • Stage 3: Training / Fine-tuning
    • Train models or fine-tune LLMs.
  • Stage 4: Evaluation
    • Compute metrics, compare with baseline.
  • Stage 5: Deployment
    • Push model to serving infra (FastAPI/TorchServe/TensorRT).
  • Stage 6: Monitoring & Feedback
    • Collect metrics, user feedback, drift; trigger retraining workflows.

Example API Endpoints & Contracts

  • Trigger workflow

    • POST /workflows/{workflow_name}/trigger
      • Body:
        {
  "params": {
    "dataset_id": "123",
    "model_name": "my-llm",
    "priority": "high"
  }
}
      • Response:
        {
  "run_id": "wf_20240601_abc123",
  "status": "queued"
}

  • Check workflow status

    • GET /workflows/runs/{run_id}
      • Response:
        {
  "run_id": "wf_20240601_abc123",
  "status": "running",
  "current_step": "generate_embeddings",
  "started_at": "2026-06-02T10:00:00Z"
}

  • List tasks in a workflow

    • GET /workflows/{workflow_name}/definition

Model Lifecycle (when workflow-automated)

  • Training: Scheduled or triggered by data drift.
  • Evaluation: Automated metrics + regression tests.
  • Approval: Auto or manual gate (human-in-the-loop).
  • Deployment: CI/CD pipeline to staging → production.
  • Monitoring: Latency, error rate, drift, LLM quality metrics.
  • Rollback: Automated rollback workflow on metric degradation.

Scalability Considerations

  • Horizontal scaling of:
    • Workers (more containers/pods)
    • Message queues
    • Orchestrator (if supported)
  • Use idempotent tasks to safely retry.
  • Partition workloads (e.g., by dataset, tenant, region).
  • For GenAI:
    • Scale embedding generation and LLM inference with batching and GPU pools.

Performance Considerations

  • Latency
    • Use async I/O for network-heavy tasks.
    • Co-locate tasks with data (same region/cluster).
    • Cache intermediate results (e.g., embeddings).
  • Throughput
    • Batch tasks (e.g., embed 128 documents at a time).
    • Use vectorized operations in ML tasks.
  • Reliability
    • Retries with backoff.
    • Dead-letter queues for failed jobs.
    • Timeouts and circuit breakers around external APIs (LLM providers).

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    A[Trigger<br/>Cron / API / Event] --> B[Workflow Orchestrator<br/>(Airflow/Temporal)]
    B --> C[Task 1:<br/>Data Ingestion]
    C --> D[Task 2:<br/>Preprocessing / Embeddings]
    D --> E[Task 3:<br/>Model Training / Fine-tuning]
    E --> F[Task 4:<br/>Evaluation & Metrics]
    F --> G{Metrics OK?}
    G -- Yes --> H[Task 5:<br/>Deploy Model / Update RAG Index]
    G -- No --> I[Notify / Open Ticket / Retrain]
    B --> J[(Metadata DB)]
    D --> K[(Vector DB)]
    H --> L[Online Inference API<br/>(FastAPI/Rust service)]

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Define Workflow
    • Break process into tasks.
    • Define dependencies (DAG) and parameters.
  2. Register Workflow
    • Declare it in the orchestrator (Python code / YAML / UI).
  3. Execute & Monitor
    • Trigger via schedule or API.
    • Orchestrator dispatches tasks to workers.
    • Workers execute tasks, store results, and update state.
    • Observability via logs, metrics, dashboards.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

High-Level Python Implementation (Airflow-style ML Workflow)

from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
from datetime import datetime

def ingest_data(**context):
    # Pull data from source and store in data lake
    ...

def generate_embeddings(**context):
    from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
    model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
    docs = ...  # load from storage
    embeddings = model.encode(docs, batch_size=64)
    # store embeddings in vector DB (e.g., Qdrant)
    ...

def train_model(**context):
    # Use PyTorch / scikit-learn to train model
    ...

def evaluate_model(**context):
    # Compute metrics, store in MLflow
    ...

with DAG(
    dag_id="ml_pipeline_workflow",
    start_date=datetime(2024, 1, 1),
    schedule_interval="@daily",
    catchup=False,
) as dag:
    t1 = PythonOperator(task_id="ingest_data", python_callable=ingest_data)
    t2 = PythonOperator(task_id="generate_embeddings", python_callable=generate_embeddings)
    t3 = PythonOperator(task_id="train_model", python_callable=train_model)
    t4 = PythonOperator(task_id="evaluate_model", python_callable=evaluate_model)

    t1 >> t2 >> t3 >> t4

High-Level Rust Implementation (Background Workflow Worker)

// Cargo.toml dependencies (example)
// tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
// reqwest = { version = "0.11", features = ["json"] }
// serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
// redis = "0.24"

use tokio::time::{sleep, Duration};
use redis::AsyncCommands;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Task {
    id: String,
    task_type: String,
    payload: String,
}

async fn fetch_task(conn: &mut redis::aio::Connection) -> Option<Task> {
    // Simple queue with BRPOP
    let res: Option<(String, String)> = conn.brpop("workflow_queue", 5).await.ok()?;
    let (_, payload) = res;
    // parse payload as JSON, map to Task
    // For brevity, simplified:
    Some(Task {
        id: "task_1".into(),
        task_type: "generate_embeddings".into(),
        payload,
    })
}

async fn handle_task(task: Task) {
    match task.task_type.as_str() {
        "generate_embeddings" => {
            // Call Python service or LLM API via HTTP
            // e.g., reqwest::Client::new().post("http://embedding-service").json(&...).send().await
        }
        "train_model" => {
            // Trigger ML pipeline or call training service
        }
        _ => {}
    }
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> redis::RedisResult<()> {
    let client = redis::Client::open("redis://127.0.0.1/")?;
    let mut conn = client.get_async_connection().await?;

    loop {
        if let Some(task) = fetch_task(&mut conn).await {
            handle_task(task).await;
        } else {
            sleep(Duration::from_secs(1)).await;
        }
    }
}

Python FastAPI Endpoint to Trigger Workflow

from fastapi import FastAPI
import uuid
import redis
import json

app = FastAPI()
r = redis.Redis(host="localhost", port=6379, db=0)

@app.post("/workflows/ingest-and-embed")
def trigger_ingest_and_embed(dataset_id: str):
    run_id = f"wf_{uuid.uuid4()}"
    task = {
        "run_id": run_id,
        "task_type": "ingest_and_embed",
        "dataset_id": dataset_id,
    }
    r.lpush("workflow_queue", json.dumps(task))
    return {"run_id": run_id, "status": "queued"}

Advantages

  • Consistency & Reliability
    • Reduces human error, standardizes processes.
  • Reproducibility
    • Same workflow can be re-run with same config/data.
  • Scalability
    • Easy to scale workers and parallelize tasks.
  • Observability
    • Centralized logs, metrics, and state tracking.
  • Faster Iteration
    • Quickly modify pipelines and redeploy.
  • For AI/ML/GenAI
    • Automates retraining, index updates, evaluation, and rollbacks.

Limitations

  • Complexity
    • Orchestrators add infra and operational overhead.
  • Learning Curve
    • Tools like Airflow/Temporal/Kubeflow require time to master.
  • Debugging Distributed Workflows
    • Failures can occur across multiple services and layers.
  • Vendor/Tool Lock-in
    • Workflow definitions may be tied to specific tools.
  • Latency Overhead
    • Good for batch and long-running tasks; not ideal for ultra-low latency critical paths.

Interview Tips

  • Common Questions

    • What is workflow automation? How is it different from simple scripting?
    • How would you design an automated ML pipeline end-to-end?
    • Compare Airflow, Prefect, Temporal, and simple Celery-based workflows.
    • How do you ensure idempotency and reliability in automated workflows?
    • How would you automate a RAG pipeline (document ingestion → embedding → indexing)?
    • How do you handle failures, retries, and compensation steps?

  • Key Points to Remember

    • Emphasize DAGs, idempotency, retries, observability.
    • Mention event-driven vs schedule-driven workflows.
    • Tie workflows to model lifecycle and RAG/LLM pipelines.
    • Talk about separation of orchestration vs execution:
      • Orchestrator (control plane) vs workers (data plane).

  • Tricky Areas

    • Handling partial failures and compensation (saga pattern).
    • Exactly-once vs at-least-once semantics.
    • Concurrency control and race conditions.
    • Security & access control across workflow steps.

Real-World Example

  • Use Case: Automated RAG Pipeline for a Knowledge Base

    • Goal: Keep a company’s internal chatbot always up to date with the latest documents.

    • Workflow Automation Steps:

      1. Trigger
        • Every hour or on file upload event (S3/GCS event).
      2. Ingest Documents
        • Fetch new/updated PDFs, Confluence pages, GitHub markdown.
      3. Chunk & Clean
        • Split documents into chunks, remove boilerplate, handle HTML/markdown.
      4. Generate Embeddings
        • Use SentenceTransformers or OpenAI embeddings.
        • Batch requests for throughput.
      5. Update Vector DB
        • Upsert embeddings into Pinecone/Qdrant/Weaviate.
      6. Run Sanity Checks
        • Sample queries, ensure no major degradation.
      7. Notify
        • Send Slack/Email that index updated.

    • Result:

      • Chatbot uses an always-updated vector index without manual intervention.
      • Engineers can focus on prompt design and evaluation rather than manual data updates.

This is workflow automation in practice: a structured, observable, and reliable pipeline that runs automatically, orchestrating multiple services (storage, embedding models, vector DB, notification systems) to keep an AI system up to date.

Q162.WHAT IS INFRASTRUCTURE AUTOMATION? [Input Token: 704 | Output Token: 3615] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition

    • Infrastructure automation is the practice of using code, tools, and scripts to provision, configure, manage, and tear down infrastructure (servers, networks, storage, Kubernetes clusters, databases, etc.) automatically instead of doing it manually.
    • Often summarized as Infrastructure as Code (IaC).

  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews

    • Modern ML/GenAI systems (LLM APIs, RAG pipelines, vector DBs, GPUs) need repeatable, scalable environments.
    • Interviewers expect you to understand:
      • How to spin up GPU clusters, vector databases, and model-serving infra reproducibly.
      • How to automate deployment of training and inference pipelines (CI/CD + MLOps).

  • Importance in Python/Rust Backend interviews

    • Backend engineers are expected to:
      • Deploy APIs and microservices in a consistent, version-controlled way.
      • Use tools like Terraform, Ansible, Docker, Kubernetes, Helm to automate infra.
      • Build reliable environments for FastAPI / Actix / Axum services, databases, and queues.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • Core idea

    • Treat infrastructure like software:
      • Define infra as code (e.g., Terraform, CloudFormation).
      • Version it in Git.
      • Review via PRs.
      • Deploy via CI/CD.
      • Rollback via previous versions.

  • Key concepts

    • Declarative vs Imperative
      • Declarative: “What I want” (e.g., Terraform: resource "aws_instance" {...}).
      • Imperative: “How to do it step-by-step” (e.g., Bash scripts).
    • Idempotency
      • Running the automation multiple times leads to the same state.
    • Immutable infrastructure
      • Instead of patching servers, you rebuild from images (e.g., Docker images, AMIs).
    • Configuration management
      • Tools like Ansible, Chef, Puppet to configure OS, packages, services.
    • Orchestration
      • Tools like Kubernetes, Nomad to orchestrate containers and services.

  • In AI/ML/GenAI context

    • Automate:
      • GPU cluster provisioning.
      • Model-serving infra (LLM servers, Triton, vLLM).
      • Vector DBs (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant).
      • RAG pipelines (indexing jobs, retrieval APIs).
      • Feature stores and data pipelines.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Infrastructure definition
    • Terraform, Pulumi, CloudFormation, CDK for IaC.
  • Configuration management
    • Ansible, Chef, Puppet, SaltStack.
  • Containerization & orchestration
    • Docker, Docker Compose, Kubernetes, Helm, kustomize.
  • CI/CD
    • GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, ArgoCD, Flux.
  • Cloud providers
    • AWS, GCP, Azure, on-prem (VMware, bare metal).
  • Monitoring & logging
    • Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, ELK, OpenTelemetry.

Data Flow & Processing Stages (for a GenAI system)

  • Infra layer
    • Provision:
      • VPC, subnets, security groups.
      • Kubernetes cluster or ECS/EKS/GKE.
      • GPU nodes.
      • Databases (Postgres), vector DBs (Qdrant, Pinecone).
  • Model layer
    • Deploy:
      • LLM serving (vLLM, TGI, Triton).
      • Embedding services.
      • RAG indexers & retrievers.
  • Application layer
    • Backend APIs:
      • Python (FastAPI).
      • Rust (Axum / Actix-web).
    • Frontend or API gateway.
  • Automation
    • CI/CD pipelines:
      • Run tests.
      • Build Docker images.
      • Apply Terraform.
      • Deploy Helm charts.

API Endpoints & Contracts (example for infra-managed GenAI backend)

  • User-facing APIs (served on auto-provisioned infra)

    • POST /v1/embeddings
      • Request: { "text": "string", "model": "text-embedding-3-large" }
      • Response: { "embedding": [float], "dim": int }
    • POST /v1/chat/completions
      • Request: { "messages": [...], "model": "local-llm" }
      • Response: { "choices": [...], "usage": {...} }
    • POST /v1/rag/query
      • Request: { "query": "string", "top_k": 5 }
      • Response: { "answer": "string", "sources": [...] }

  • Infra automation triggers

    • CI/CD pipeline file (e.g., .github/workflows/deploy.yml) acts as “API” to infra:
      • On merge to main → run:
        • terraform plan / apply.
        • helm upgrade --install.
        • kubectl rollout status.

Model Lifecycle (in automated infra)

  • Training
    • Use IaC to:
      • Provision GPU training cluster.
      • Attach object storage (S3/GCS).
    • Run training jobs via:
      • Kubeflow, Airflow, Argo Workflows, Ray.
  • Evaluation
    • Deploy evaluation services as Kubernetes Jobs/CronJobs.
  • Deployment
    • Build Docker images with trained model.
    • Deploy via Helm/ArgoCD.
  • Monitoring
    • Automated deployment of monitoring stack via Helm charts.
    • Track:
      • Latency, throughput.
      • GPU utilization.
      • Error rates.
  • Rollback
    • Roll back to previous:
      • Helm release.
      • Container image.
      • Terraform state.

Scalability Considerations

  • Horizontal scaling
    • Auto-scaling groups / node pools.
    • Kubernetes HPA (CPU, memory, custom metrics).
  • Vertical scaling
    • Larger instance types for GPU-heavy LLM inference.
  • Multi-region / multi-AZ
    • Terraform modules for multi-region infra.
    • Replication for DBs/vector DBs.
  • Stateless services
    • Backend APIs as stateless containers; state in managed DBs and object storage.

Performance Considerations

  • Latency
    • Co-locate:
      • LLM servers, vector DB, and backend in same region/VPC.
    • Use:
      • gRPC for internal calls.
      • Connection pooling.
  • Throughput
    • Auto-scale LLM pods based on QPS.
    • Use async frameworks:
      • Python: FastAPI + uvicorn.
      • Rust: Tokio-based frameworks (Actix/Axum).
  • Cost optimization
    • Spot instances for non-critical workloads.
    • Scale-to-zero for dev/test environments.
    • Schedule GPU clusters to shut down at night.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Define infrastructure

    • Developer writes:
      • Terraform for VPC, Kubernetes, DBs, GPU nodes.
      • Helm charts for LLM, embeddings, backend, vector DB.
    • Stores everything in Git (infra repo).

  2. Automated provisioning & deployment

    • On PR merge:
      • CI/CD runs:
        • terraform plan → terraform apply.
        • helm upgrade --install for services.
    • Kubernetes cluster gets:
      • LLM pods.
      • Embedding pods.
      • Backend API pods.
      • Vector DB pods.

  3. Operate & evolve

    • Monitoring & logs auto-deployed.
    • Changes to infra:
      • Done via PRs.
      • Reviewed, tested, and applied automatically.
    • Rollbacks:
      • Revert Git commit → pipeline restores previous infra state.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

High-level Python Implementation (FastAPI + Terraform + Helm)

# infra/deploy.py (simplified example)
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

INFRA_DIR = Path(__file__).parent / "terraform"
HELM_DIR = Path(__file__).parent / "helm"

def run(cmd, cwd=None):
    print(f"Running: {' '.join(cmd)}")
    subprocess.check_call(cmd, cwd=cwd)

def deploy_infra():
    # Terraform init & apply
    run(["terraform", "init"], cwd=INFRA_DIR)
    run(["terraform", "apply", "-auto-approve"], cwd=INFRA_DIR)

def deploy_k8s_services():
    # Example Helm deployments
    charts = ["llm-serving", "embeddings", "vector-db", "backend-api"]
    for chart in charts:
        run([
            "helm", "upgrade", "--install",
            chart, str(HELM_DIR / chart),
            "--namespace", "genai",
            "--create-namespace"
        ])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    deploy_infra()
    deploy_k8s_services()
