Advantages

  • Decoupling
    • Producers of events don’t need to know about consumers.
  • Scalability
    • Easy to scale workers that handle triggers.
  • Responsiveness
    • Immediate reaction to events (vs periodic batch jobs only).
  • Observability
    • Clear points to log, trace, and monitor system behavior.
  • MLOps / LLMOps
    • Automates retraining, evaluation, RAG updates, and monitoring.

Limitations

  • Complexity
    • Event-driven systems can be harder to reason about than simple request-response.
  • Debugging & Observability
    • Tracing a flow across many triggers/services requires good logging and distributed tracing.
  • Ordering & Idempotency
    • Handling duplicates, out-of-order events, and retries is non-trivial.
  • Operational overhead
    • Requires managing queues, schedulers, and workflow engines.

Interview Tips

  • Common questions

    • “What is a trigger in an automation system?”
    • “How would you design an event-driven pipeline for model inference or retraining?”
    • “How do you ensure idempotency in triggered workflows?”
    • “Compare cron-based triggers vs event-based triggers.”
    • “How would you handle spikes in trigger events (backpressure, scaling)?”

  • Key points to remember

    • Always mention event source → queue → worker pattern.
    • Emphasize idempotency, retries, dead-letter queues.
    • For AI/ML: link triggers to data ingestion, training, evaluation, deployment.
    • For GenAI: mention triggers for RAG index updates, prompt workflows, tool calls.

  • Tricky areas interviewers focus on

    • Handling failures and partial processing.
    • Ensuring exactly-once or at-least-once semantics.
    • Designing schema and versioning for events.
    • Coordinating multiple triggers (fan-in/fan-out patterns).

Real-World Example

  • Use-case: RAG-based Support Chatbot with Automated Index Refresh

    • Trigger sources

      • New knowledge base document uploaded to S3.
      • Admin triggers manual reindex via /admin/reindex.
      • Cron trigger at midnight to re-embed changed documents.

    • Automation

      • S3 upload event → webhook → queue → worker:
        • Extract text → generate embeddings (e.g., with sentence-transformers or OpenAI embeddings).
        • Upsert into vector DB (Pinecone, Milvus, Weaviate, Qdrant).
      • Cron trigger → re-run embedding for stale documents.
      • Chat endpoint /chat:
        • Trigger retrieval → LLM inference → logging.

    • Benefits

      • The support chatbot always uses fresh documents without manual re-deployment.
      • System reacts automatically to data changes using triggers instead of manual scripts.
Q176.WHAT ARE FAILURE HANDLING STRATEGIES? [Input Token: 705 | Output Token: 3664] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition

    • Failure handling strategies are patterns and mechanisms used to detect, isolate, mitigate, and recover from failures in distributed systems, microservices, and ML/GenAI pipelines.
    • They include techniques like retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fallbacks, idempotency, dead-letter queues, checkpointing, etc.

  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews

    • Production ML/GenAI systems run across multiple services: feature stores, model servers, vector DBs, LLM APIs, orchestrators.
    • Robust failure handling is critical for:
      • Reliable inference APIs (e.g., LLM-as-a-service)
      • RAG pipelines (vector DB, embedding service, LLM)
      • Training pipelines (ETL failures, job restarts, checkpointing)
    • Interviewers want to see if you can build resilient ML/GenAI systems, not just models.

  • Importance in Python/Rust backend interviews

    • Backend services must handle:
      • Network failures, timeouts, partial outages
      • Resource exhaustion (CPU, memory, file descriptors)
      • Downstream dependency failures (DB, cache, external APIs)
    • Rust + Python backends need well-defined error types, retry policies, and observability.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

Common failure handling strategies in system + ML/GenAI architectures:

  • 1. Timeouts

    • Prevent hanging calls by limiting maximum wait time.
    • If LLM/vector DB/model server is slow, abort and apply fallback.

  • 2. Retries with Backoff

    • Retry transient failures (e.g., 503, connection reset).
    • Use exponential backoff + jitter to avoid thundering herd.

  • 3. Circuit Breaker

    • Monitor failure rate to a dependency.
    • If failures exceed a threshold, open the circuit:
      • Immediately fail fast instead of calling the broken service.
      • Periodically probe to see if it recovered.

  • 4. Bulkheads / Isolation

    • Isolate resources so failure in one component doesn’t cascade:
      • Separate thread pools / connection pools per dependency.
      • Separate queues for different traffic types (e.g., LLM vs analytics).

  • 5. Fallbacks / Graceful Degradation

    • When main path fails:
      • Use cached response
      • Use simpler model (smaller LLM, heuristic)
      • Return partial results instead of total failure.

  • 6. Idempotency

    • Design APIs so retries don’t cause duplicate side effects.
    • Use idempotency keys for writes (payments, job submissions).

  • 7. Dead-letter Queues (DLQ) & Retry Queues

    • For async processing (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS):
      • Messages that repeatedly fail go to a DLQ.
      • Operators can inspect and reprocess.

  • 8. Checkpointing & Job Restart

    • For long-running training / batch jobs:
      • Save intermediate state (model checkpoints, offsets).
      • On failure, restart from last checkpoint.

  • 9. Health Checks & Auto-Healing

    • Liveness/readiness endpoints for containers.
    • Orchestrators (Kubernetes) restart unhealthy pods.

  • 10. Observability & Alerting

    • Metrics, logs, tracing to detect and diagnose failures.
    • SLOs and alerts on error rates and latency.

  • 11. Graceful Shutdown

    • Handle SIGTERM:
      • Stop accepting new requests
      • Finish in-flight requests
      • Flush logs/metrics

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Application Layer
    • Python FastAPI/Flask or Rust Actix-Web/Axum services.
    • LLM inference service / RAG orchestrator.
  • Dependencies
    • Vector DB (e.g., Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate)
    • Relational DB (PostgreSQL)
    • Cache (Redis)
    • Message queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS)
    • External LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.)
  • Resilience Layer
    • Retry policies
    • Circuit breaker middleware
    • Timeout configuration
    • Bulkhead (thread pools, connection pools)
    • Fallback handlers
  • Observability
    • Prometheus / OpenTelemetry metrics
    • Structured logging
    • Tracing (Jaeger, Tempo, X-Ray)

Data Flow & Processing Stages (Example: RAG API)

  • Request In
    • User → API Gateway → RAG service
  • Stage 1: Input validation
    • Validate prompt, user ID, rate limiting.
  • Stage 2: Retrieval
    • Call vector DB with timeout + retries.
    • If retrieval fails → fallback (e.g., no context or cached context).
  • Stage 3: LLM Generation
    • Call LLM with timeout + retries + circuit breaker.
    • If breaker open → fallback to smaller local model or canned answer.
  • Stage 4: Response Assembly
    • Combine LLM answer + metadata.
  • Stage 5: Logging & Metrics
    • Log errors, latencies, success/failure.
  • Stage 6: Return Response

API Endpoints & Contracts (Example)

  • POST /v1/rag/query
    • Request:
      {
  "query": "string",
  "top_k": 5,
  "user_id": "string",
  "request_id": "string"
}
    • Response (with failure handling info):
      {
  "answer": "string",
  "used_fallback": true,
  "retrieval_status": "partial_failure",
  "llm_status": "success",
  "trace_id": "string"
}

Model Lifecycle & Failure Handling

  • Training
    • Checkpointing to S3 / GCS.
    • Retry failed data loading steps.
    • Use idempotent job runs (job ID, run ID).
  • Evaluation
    • Handle metric computation failures (skip bad batches).
  • Deployment
    • Blue/green or canary deploys to avoid full outages.
    • Rollback on high error rates.
  • Monitoring
    • Error rates per model version.
    • Latency per dependency.
    • Alerts on:
      • High 5xx rate
      • High timeouts
      • Circuit breaker open rate

Scalability Considerations

  • Horizontal scaling
    • Multiple instances behind load balancer.
  • Rate limiting & backpressure
    • Protect downstream systems from overload.
  • Bulkhead patterns
    • Separate pools for:
      • LLM calls
      • DB calls
      • Vector DB calls
  • Queue-based async processing
    • Offload heavy tasks to workers with DLQ.

Performance Considerations

  • Latency
    • Use timeouts tuned to SLOs.
    • Avoid aggressive retries that increase tail latency.
  • Throughput
    • Use connection pooling, async I/O.
    • Limit concurrent calls per dependency (semaphore).
  • Optimization
    • Cache successful responses.
    • Pre-warm models and connections.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    U[User] --> G[API Gateway]

    G --> A[Python/Rust RAG Service]

    subgraph Resilience Layer
        R1[Timeouts & Retries]
        R2[Circuit Breaker]
        R3[Bulkheads]
        R4[Fallback Logic]
    end

    A --> R1
    R1 --> R2

    R2 -->|OK| V[Vector DB]
    R2 -->|Open/Fail| F1[Retrieval Fallback]

    R2 -->|OK| L[LLM Service]
    R2 -->|Open/Fail| F2[LLM Fallback]

    A --> M[Metrics & Logging]
    A --> O[Tracing]

    V --> A
    L --> A
    F1 --> A
    F2 --> A

    A --> G --> U

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Receive Request

    • API receives a request (e.g., /v1/rag/query).
    • Validate input, attach trace_id, request_id.

  2. Call Dependencies with Resilience

    • For vector DB:
      • Apply timeout + retry with backoff.
      • If repeated failures: circuit breaker opens → use fallback.
    • For LLM:
      • Apply timeout + retry.
      • If circuit breaker open: use fallback model / cached answer.

  3. Respond & Record

    • Assemble response with flags indicating fallbacks used.
    • Log structured event, emit metrics, traces.
    • Return HTTP 200/4xx/5xx depending on failure and fallback.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

Python Example (FastAPI + HTTPX + Tenacity)

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from httpx import AsyncClient, TimeoutException
from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential, retry_if_exception_type

app = FastAPI()
http_client = AsyncClient(timeout=5.0)

class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=5, reset_timeout=30):
        self.failure_threshold = failure_threshold
        self.reset_timeout = reset_timeout
        self.failures = 0
        self.open_until = 0

    def allow(self, now):
        if now < self.open_until:
            return False
        return True

    def record_failure(self, now):
        self.failures += 1
        if self.failures >= self.failure_threshold:
            self.open_until = now + self.reset_timeout

    def record_success(self):
        self.failures = 0
        self.open_until = 0

cb_llm = CircuitBreaker()

@retry(
    stop=stop_after_attempt(3),
    wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=0.2, max=2),
    retry=retry_if_exception_type((TimeoutException, ConnectionError)),
)
async def call_llm(prompt: str) -> str:
    resp = await http_client.post("https://llm.example.com/generate", json={"prompt": prompt})
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()["text"]

async def fallback_llm(prompt: str) -> str:
    # Simple heuristic fallback
    return "Service degraded. Unable to generate a full answer now."

@app.post("/v1/rag/query")
async def rag_query(payload: dict):
    import time
    now = time.time()

    if not cb_llm.allow(now):
        # circuit open -> fallback directly
        answer = await fallback_llm(payload["query"])
        return {"answer": answer, "used_fallback": True, "llm_status": "circuit_open"}

    try:
        answer = await call_llm(payload["query"])
        cb_llm.record_success()
        return {"answer": answer, "used_fallback": False, "llm_status": "success"}
    except Exception as e:
        cb_llm.record_failure(now)
        answer = await fallback_llm(payload["query"])
        # In production: log error, increment metrics
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=503,
            detail={"answer": answer, "used_fallback": True, "llm_status": "error", "error": str(e)},
        )

Rust Example (Axum + reqwest + tower)

use axum::{routing::post, Json, Router};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::{net::SocketAddr, time::Duration};
use tower::{limit::ConcurrencyLimitLayer, timeout::TimeoutLayer};
use reqwest::Client;

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct RagQuery {
    query: String,
}

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct RagResponse {
    answer: String,
    used_fallback: bool,
    llm_status: String,
}

async fn fallback_llm(prompt: &str) -> String {
    format!("Service degraded. Cannot fully answer: {}", prompt)
}

async fn rag_handler(Json(payload): Json<RagQuery>) -> Json<RagResponse> {
    let client = Client::new();

    let res = client
        .post("https://llm.example.com/generate")
        .json(&serde_json::json!({ "prompt": payload.query }))
        .send()
        .await;

    match res {
        Ok(resp) if resp.status().is_success() => {
            let json: serde_json::Value = resp.json().await.unwrap_or_default();
            let answer = json.get("text").and_then(|v| v.as_str()).unwrap_or("").to_string();
            Json(RagResponse {
                answer,
                used_fallback: false,
                llm_status: "success".into(),
            })
        }
        _ => {
            // In production: integrate tower-circuit-breaker, metrics, logging
            let answer = fallback_llm(&payload.query).await;
            Json(RagResponse {
                answer,
                used_fallback: true,
                llm_status: "fallback".into(),
            })
        }
    }
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/v1/rag/query", post(rag_handler))
        // Timeout all requests
        .layer(TimeoutLayer::new(Duration::from_secs(5)))
        // Limit concurrent requests (bulkhead-ish)
        .layer(ConcurrencyLimitLayer::new(100));

    let addr = SocketAddr::from(([0, 0, 0, 0], 8080));
    axum::Server::bind(&addr).serve(app.into_make_service()).await.unwrap();
}

Advantages

  • Higher reliability & availability
    • Failures are isolated and contained.
  • Better user experience
    • Graceful degradation instead of hard failures.
  • Operational visibility
    • Easier debugging via logs, metrics, traces.
  • Supports complex ML/GenAI pipelines
    • Robustness across multiple external dependencies (LLM APIs, vector DBs, feature stores).

Limitations

  • Increased complexity
    • More moving parts (circuit breakers, retries, DLQs).
  • Misconfigured retries
    • Can worsen outages (retry storms).
  • Hidden failures
    • Overuse of fallbacks can hide real issues.
  • Latency trade-offs
    • Retries and timeouts can increase tail latency.
  • State management
    • Idempotency and checkpointing require careful design.

Interview Tips

  • Common questions

    • “How do you design a resilient microservice calling an external API?”
    • “Explain circuit breaker vs retry vs timeout.”
    • “How would you handle failures in a RAG pipeline (LLM + vector DB)?”
    • “How do you ensure idempotency for retries?”
    • “How do you handle long-running ML training job failures?”

  • Key points to remember

    • Always mention timeouts + retries + backoff + jitter together.
    • Explain circuit breaker as protecting dependencies and failing fast.
    • Mention bulkheads and rate limiting for overload protection.
    • For ML/GenAI:
      • Checkpointing for training.
      • Fallback models for inference.
      • DLQ for async jobs.

  • Tricky areas

    • When not to retry (non-idempotent operations, 4xx errors).
    • Correct retry policies for idempotent vs non-idempotent endpoints.
    • Avoiding retry storms in large distributed systems.
    • Handling partial failures (some shards/vector nodes failing).

Real-World Example

  • Use-case: Production RAG Chatbot

    • Components:

      • Gateway: Receives chat requests.
      • RAG Service (Python/Rust):
        • Embedding model service
        • Vector DB (Qdrant)
        • LLM API (OpenAI)
      • Metrics / Logging stack.

    • Failure handling:

      • Embeddings service:
        • Timeout: 2s, retry 2 times with backoff.
        • If fails: fallback to cached embeddings or answer without new context.
      • Vector DB:
        • Circuit breaker: open after 5 failures in 10 seconds.
        • If open: fallback to previously cached top documents.
      • LLM API:
        • Retry on 429/5xx with exponential backoff.
        • If still failing: fallback to smaller on-prem LLM or canned message.
      • Training / Indexing jobs:
        • Use checkpointing and DLQ for failed documents.
      • Observability:
        • Dashboards showing:
          • Error rate per dependency.
          • Circuit breaker open events.
          • Percentage of requests using fallbacks.

    • Result:

      • Chatbot remains usable during partial outages.
      • Operators can see where failures occur and fix them quickly.
Q177.WHAT IS DISTRIBUTED JOB SCHEDULING? [Input Token: 705 | Output Token: 3793] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition

    • Distributed job scheduling is the coordination, assignment, and execution of jobs/tasks across multiple machines (nodes) in a distributed system.
    • A job can be a batch task, ML training run, data pipeline step, LLM inference batch, or background worker task.
    • The scheduler decides where, when, and how each job runs, ensuring reliability, scalability, and efficiency.

  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews

    • Large-scale ML training, feature pipelines, RAG indexing, and batch inference all rely on distributed job scheduling.
    • Evaluates your understanding of:
      • Resource management (GPU/CPU/RAM)
      • Fault tolerance and retries
      • Orchestration of complex ML workflows (DAGs, pipelines, Airflow, Kubeflow, Ray, etc.)
      • Running LLM workloads (batch inference, fine-tuning) at scale.

  • Importance in Python/Rust Backend interviews

    • Backend systems often require:
      • Background jobs (emails, notifications, ETL)
      • Scheduled tasks (cron-like behavior)
      • Asynchronous processing (queues, workers)
    • Tests your ability to design:
      • Scalable worker architectures
      • Reliable scheduling (idempotency, retries, deduplication)
      • Integration with infra (Kubernetes, Celery, Redis, Kafka, etc.)
      • High-performance schedulers in Rust for low-latency/throughput workloads.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • Core idea

    • Have a central or decentralized scheduler that:
      • Receives job definitions (what to run, when, resources needed)
      • Stores them persistently
      • Assigns jobs to available worker nodes
      • Monitors execution, handles failures, retries, and rescheduling.

  • Key components

    • Job Producer / Client
      • API or service that submits jobs (e.g., ML training request, data processing batch).
    • Scheduler / Orchestrator
      • Decides which node runs what, when.
      • Manages priorities, dependencies, and concurrency limits.
    • Queue / Broker
      • Message queue (Redis, RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS) holding pending jobs.
    • Workers / Executors
      • Processes or containers running on multiple nodes that pull jobs and execute them.
    • Metadata Store
      • Database for job status, logs, retries, scheduling metadata.
    • Monitoring & Control Plane
      • UI/CLI/API to monitor jobs, cancel, restart, or reschedule.

  • Common patterns

    • Centralized scheduler
      • Single logical scheduler node that assigns work (e.g., Airflow scheduler, Kubernetes scheduler).
    • Decentralized / Work-stealing
      • Workers pull tasks from queues and balance themselves (e.g., Celery workers, Ray).
    • Cron-like scheduling
      • Time-based triggers (every 5 minutes, nightly, etc.).
    • Dependency-based scheduling (DAGs)
      • Tasks depend on outputs of previous tasks (Airflow, Prefect, Dagster, Kubeflow).

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Scheduler service
    • Responsible for:
      • Job creation, validation, deduplication
      • Assigning jobs to workers based on:
        • Resource requirements (CPU/GPU/memory)
        • Priority
        • Node health and locality
      • Job lifecycle management (queued → running → success/failure).
  • Workers
    • Stateless processes/containers:
      • Pull jobs from queue or receive from scheduler.
      • Execute Python/Rust code, shell commands, ML pipelines.
      • Report status and metrics back.
  • Queue/Broker
    • Redis, RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS, NATS, etc.
  • Metadata store
    • PostgreSQL, MySQL, etc. for:
      • Job definitions, schedules, runs
      • Logs, error traces, retry counts.
  • Monitoring
    • Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry for:
      • Job latency, throughput, failure rates
      • Worker utilization.

Technologies (Python & Rust)

  • Python

    • Task queues: Celery, RQ, Huey, Dramatiq
    • Orchestration: Apache Airflow, Prefect, Dagster
    • Distributed compute: Ray, Dask, Spark (PySpark)
    • GenAI-specific: orchestrating RAG pipelines, batch LLM inference, embedding generation.

  • Rust

    • Job scheduling / orchestration:
      • Custom schedulers using Tokio (async runtime)
      • Lapin for RabbitMQ, rdkafka for Kafka
      • Actix-web, Axum for APIs
    • High-performance worker processes:
      • Embedding generation or LLM inference wrappers in Rust for performance-critical paths.
      • Coordination with Python-based ML components via gRPC/HTTP.

Data Flow & Processing Stages

  • Job submission
    • Client → Scheduler API:
      • Job payload + metadata (type, params, schedule, resources).
  • Scheduling
    • Scheduler:
      • Stores job in DB
      • Enqueues task in message queue or assigns directly.
  • Execution
    • Worker:
      • Fetches job
      • Runs code (e.g., Python script for ML training, Rust binary for inference)
      • Streams logs/metrics.
  • Completion
    • Worker:
      • Updates job status in DB
      • Emits metrics and events.
  • Retry / Failure
    • Scheduler:
      • Applies retry policies (exponential backoff, max attempts)
      • Dead-letter queue for permanently failed jobs.

API Endpoints & Contracts (Example)

  • REST/JSON example
    • POST /jobs
      • Request:
        {
  "type": "batch_inference",
  "schedule": "cron(0 * * * *)",
  "payload": {"model_id": "llm-1", "input_bucket": "s3://..."},
  "priority": "high",
  "resources": {"cpu": 4, "gpu": 1, "memory_gb": 16}
}
      • Response:
        {"job_id": "12345", "status": "queued"}
    • GET /jobs/{job_id}
      • Returns status, logs URL, metrics.
    • POST /jobs/{job_id}/cancel
    • GET /workers (health, capacity, utilization).

Model Lifecycle (ML/GenAI Context)

  • Training
    • Scheduler triggers:
      • Data preprocessing jobs
      • Model training jobs (distributed across GPUs)
      • Evaluation jobs.
  • Evaluation
    • Scheduled evaluation jobs on validation datasets.
  • Deployment
    • Jobs to:
      • Build Docker images
      • Apply Kubernetes manifests
      • Warm up models.
  • Monitoring
    • Periodic jobs:
      • Drift detection
      • Performance evaluation
      • Regeneration of embeddings for RAG index (e.g., weekly refresh).

Scalability Considerations

  • Horizontal scaling
    • Add more workers to handle more jobs.
    • Use Kubernetes HPA for auto-scaling based on queue length or CPU usage.
  • Sharding
    • Partition jobs by tenant, region, or job type.
  • High availability
    • Scheduler redundancy (leader election).
    • Highly available message brokers and DBs.
  • Distributed locking
    • Ensure only one scheduler instance acts as leader (e.g., using Redis, ZooKeeper, Consul, etcd).

Performance Considerations

  • Latency
    • Reduce scheduling overhead:
      • In-memory queues with Redis
      • Efficient worker polling strategies.
  • Throughput
    • Batch jobs where possible (e.g., batch LLM inference, batch embedding generation).
    • Use Rust workers for CPU-bound tasks for better throughput.
  • Optimization
    • Resource-aware scheduling:
      • GPU-aware placement for ML/LLM workloads.
    • Prioritization:
      • Separate high-priority queues.
    • Backpressure:
      • Limit job intake when system is overloaded.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart LR
    subgraph Clients
        A[API Client / Service]
    end

    subgraph ControlPlane[Control Plane]
        B[Scheduler Service]
        C[(Metadata DB)]
        D[(Message Queue)]
    end

    subgraph Workers[Worker Nodes]
        W1[Worker 1\n(Python)]
        W2[Worker 2\n(Rust)]
        W3[Worker N\n(Python/Rust)]
    end

    A -->|Submit Job| B
    B -->|Store job| C
    B -->|Enqueue task| D

    W1 -->|Poll tasks| D
    W2 -->|Poll tasks| D
    W3 -->|Poll tasks| D

    W1 -->|Update status| C
    W2 -->|Update status| C
    W3 -->|Update status| C

    B -->|Monitor & Control| W1
    B -->|Monitor & Control| W2
    B -->|Monitor & Control| W3

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Job Creation

    • A client (web app, ML pipeline, CLI) calls the scheduler API with job details.
    • Scheduler validates input, stores job metadata, and enqueues the task.

  2. Scheduling & Execution

    • Workers (Python/Rust) poll the queue or receive push notifications.
    • A worker claims a job, executes it, and streams logs/metrics.

  3. Completion & Monitoring

    • Worker marks job as success/failure with details.
    • Scheduler applies retry policies if needed.
    • Monitoring dashboards show job status, performance, and alerts.

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

High-level Python Implementation (FastAPI + Celery)

# scheduler_api.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
from celery import Celery

app = FastAPI()
celery_app = Celery(
    "distributed_jobs",
    broker="redis://redis:6379/0",
    backend="redis://redis:6379/1",
)

class JobRequest(BaseModel):
    type: str
    payload: dict
    priority: str | None = "normal"

@celery_app.task
def run_job(job_type: str, payload: dict):
    # Example: dispatch based on job type
    if job_type == "generate_embeddings":
        from my_ml.embedding import generate_embeddings
        return generate_embeddings(payload)
    elif job_type == "batch_llm_inference":
        from my_ml.llm import batch_infer
        return batch_infer(payload)
    else:
        # generic handler
        return {"status": "unknown_job_type"}

@app.post("/jobs")
def create_job(job: JobRequest):
    # In real system: store in DB, assign priority, etc.
    async_result = run_job.delay(job.type, job.payload)
    return {"job_id": async_result.id, "status": "queued"}

@app.get("/jobs/{job_id}")
def get_job_status(job_id: str):
    async_result = celery_app.AsyncResult(job_id)
    return {
        "job_id": job_id,
        "status": async_result.status,
        "result": async_result.result if async_result.ready() else None
    }
  • Notes
    • Celery workers run distributed across nodes.
    • Each worker can run ML tasks: embeddings, batch inference, RAG index updates.

High-level Rust Worker Implementation (Axum + Tokio + Redis)

// Cargo.toml (dependencies excerpt)
// tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
// redis = "0.25"
// serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
// axum = "0.7"
// anyhow = "1"

use axum::{routing::get, Router};
use redis::{AsyncCommands};
use serde::Deserialize;
use tokio::time::{sleep, Duration};
use anyhow::Result;

#[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
struct JobPayload {
    job_type: String,
    payload: serde_json::Value,
}

async fn worker_loop() -> Result<()> {
    let client = redis::Client::open("redis://redis:6379/0")?;
    let mut conn = client.get_async_connection().await?;

    loop {
        // BLPOP for blocking pop from a Redis list (queue)
        let res: Option<(String, String)> = conn.blpop("jobs_queue", 5).await?;
        if let Some((_queue, job_str)) = res {
            let job: JobPayload = serde_json::from_str(&job_str)?;
            // Execute job
            match job.job_type.as_str() {
                "rust_heavy_task" => {
                    // e.g., CPU-bound processing
                    // perform_heavy_computation(job.payload).await?;
                }
                _ => {
                    // fallback
                }
            }
        } else {
            // No job, sleep briefly
            sleep(Duration::from_secs(1)).await;
        }
    }
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<()> {
    // Start worker loop in background
    tokio::spawn(async {
        if let Err(e) = worker_loop().await {
            eprintln!("Worker loop error: {:?}", e);
        }
    });

    // Simple health endpoint
    let app = Router::new().route("/health", get(|| async { "OK" }));

    axum::Server::bind(&"0.0.0.0:8080".parse()?)
        .serve(app.into_make_service())
        .await?;

    Ok(())
}
  • Notes
    • Rust worker consumes jobs from Redis queue.
    • Suitable for high-throughput CPU-bound tasks (e.g., preprocessing, scoring, feature computation).

Advantages

  • Scalability
    • Horizontally scalable workers for large workloads (ML training, batch inference).
  • Fault tolerance
    • Retries, dead-letter queues, and failover.
  • Resource efficiency
    • Efficient use of CPU/GPU across cluster.
  • Decoupling
    • Separates request handling from heavy processing.
  • Scheduling flexibility
    • Time-based, event-based, and dependency-based scheduling.
  • GenAI-friendly
    • Ideal for:
      • Batch embedding generation
      • RAG index building
      • Offline evaluation of LLMs
      • Fine-tuning pipelines.

Limitations

  • Complexity
    • More moving parts (scheduler, queue, workers, DB).
  • Operational overhead
    • Requires monitoring, scaling, and troubleshooting distributed components.
  • Latency
    • Not ideal for ultra low-latency single-request operations (RPC might be better).
  • Consistency
    • Need careful handling of:
      • Idempotency
      • At-least-once vs exactly-once semantics.
  • Debugging
    • Harder to debug across multiple nodes and asynchronous flows.

Interview Tips

  • Common questions
    • Explain distributed job scheduling and why it’s needed.
    • How would you design a distributed job scheduler?
    • How do you handle:
      • Retries and idempotency?
      • Prioritization and fairness?
      • Worker failures and node crashes?
    • Compare cron vs distributed scheduler.
    • How would you schedule GPU-heavy ML/LLM jobs?
    • How to avoid duplicate job execution in distributed systems?
  • Key points to remember
    • Mention queue-based design (message broker).
    • Emphasize idempotent job handlers.
    • Talk about backpressure and rate limiting.
    • Mention monitoring & observability (logs, metrics, traces).
    • For ML/GenAI:
      • Explain how to schedule batch inference and embedding generation.
  • Tricky areas
    • Handling exactly-once semantics (usually simulated via idempotency).
    • Scheduler leader election and split-brain scenarios.
    • Job ordering and dependency management (DAG execution).
    • Multi-tenant isolation (sharding queues, resource quotas).

Real-World Example

  • Use-case: RAG System Indexing & Batch Inference

    • Scenario

      • You have a GenAI app that:
        • Ingests documents
        • Generates embeddings
        • Updates a vector database
        • Periodically re-embeds documents when the model changes.

    • How distributed job scheduling is used

      • Ingestion jobs
        • Parse and chunk documents.
      • Embedding jobs
        • Distributed workers generate embeddings in parallel using GPUs.
      • Index update jobs
        • Insert/update embeddings in vector DB (e.g., Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant).
      • Periodic maintenance
        • Scheduled jobs to:
          • Rebuild index
          • Run evaluation
          • Detect drift.

    • Example flow

      • User uploads large corpus → API creates embedding jobs per batch.
      • Scheduler enqueues jobs; GPU-enabled workers generate embeddings.
      • Rust workers handle heavy preprocessing and I/O-bound operations.
      • Python workers handle ML/LLM calls (e.g., using PyTorch, Transformers).
      • Once embeddings are ready, scheduler triggers index update jobs.
      • A nightly job evaluates retrieval quality and logs metrics.

This pattern is a textbook example of why distributed job scheduling is fundamental for production-grade AI/ML/GenAI systems.

Q178.WHAT IS RETRY LOGIC? [Input Token: 704 | Output Token: 3516] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:
    Retry logic is a programming pattern where a failed operation is automatically retried a configurable number of times, often with delays and backoff strategies, before finally giving up or escalating the error.

  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:

    • Critical for robust ML pipelines (data ingestion, model serving, vector DB calls).
    • Essential for LLM inference pipelines, especially when calling:
      • External APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.)
      • Vector databases / RAG backends
      • Microservices (feature store, metadata store)
    • Shows understanding of resilience, fault tolerance, and production readiness.

  • Importance in Python/Rust backend interviews:

    • Used in HTTP clients, database access, message queues, and distributed systems.
    • Demonstrates knowledge of idempotency, timeouts, backoff, and circuit breakers.
    • Key for high-availability microservices and API reliability.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

  • Core idea:

    • When an operation fails (e.g., network error, 5xx error), you:
      • Don’t fail immediately.
      • Retry the operation according to a policy.

  • Key concepts:

    • Retryable error vs non-retryable error:
      • Retryable: transient network errors, 5xx, rate-limit (429), timeouts.
      • Non-retryable: 4xx (e.g., 400, 401, 403, 404), validation errors, logic errors.
    • Retry policy:
      • Max attempts
      • Delay strategy (fixed, exponential, jitter)
      • Timeout per attempt and overall timeout
    • Backoff strategies:
      • Fixed delay (e.g., 1s between retries)
      • Exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s…)
      • Exponential backoff with jitter (adds randomness to avoid thundering herd)

  • In a GenAI / RAG system:

    • Retrying:
      • LLM API calls on rate-limit / transient failures.
      • Vector DB queries on connection issues.
      • Embedding API calls during batch processing.

  • In backend microservices:

    • Retrying:
      • HTTP calls to other services.
      • Database queries (when safe).
      • Message processing (e.g., Kafka, RabbitMQ).

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Client / Caller:
    • The code that wants to perform an operation (e.g., call LLM, query DB).
  • Retry wrapper / middleware:
    • Implements the retry policy.
    • Often a decorator, middleware, or library function.
  • Target operation:
    • HTTP request, DB query, RPC call, LLM inference, etc.
  • Error classifier:
    • Logic to decide if an error is retryable.
  • Backoff calculator:
    • Computes delay before next attempt.

Technologies (Python / Rust)

  • Python:

    • tenacity (popular retry library)
    • backoff
    • httpx / requests with custom retry logic
    • aiohttp for async retries
    • In GenAI: langchain and litellm often include retry wrappers

  • Rust:

    • reqwest + custom retry wrapper
    • tower middleware (for gRPC/HTTP retry)
    • retry, futures-retry crates
    • tokio for async sleep/backoff

Data Flow & Processing Stages

  • Input:
    • Operation parameters (e.g., HTTP request, query).
    • Retry configuration (max attempts, backoff, timeout).
  • Processing:
    • Execute operation.
    • If success → return result.
    • If failure → classify error:
      • Retryable? → compute delay → wait → try again.
      • Non-retryable? → fail immediately.
  • Output:
    • Successful result, or
    • Final error after all retries exhausted.

API Endpoints & Contracts (Example)

  • Suppose we have a /generate-answer endpoint in a GenAI service:
    • Request:
      {
  "query": "Explain retry logic",
  "top_k": 5,
  "max_tokens": 256
}
    • Internally:
      • Calls vector DB with retry.
      • Calls LLM API with retry.
    • Response:
      {
  "answer": "...",
  "metadata": {
    "llm_retries": 2,
    "vector_db_retries": 1
  }
}

Model Lifecycle (Where Retry Fits)

  • Training:

    • Retrying:
      • Data downloads from remote storage.
      • Feature store queries.
    • Helps long-running jobs survive transient failures.

  • Evaluation:

    • Retrying metric logging (e.g., to MLflow / Prometheus).
    • Retrying evaluation API calls (if external).

  • Deployment / Inference:

    • Retrying:
      • LLM providers
      • Embedding providers
      • Vector DBs
      • Feature stores
    • Often implemented as middleware in the inference service.

  • Monitoring:

    • Track:
      • Retry counts
      • Retry latency impact
      • Error types causing retries
    • Expose metrics: retries_total, retry_failures_total.

Scalability Considerations

  • Pros:

    • Absorbs transient failures at scale.
    • Reduces user-facing error rates.

  • Risks:

    • Thundering herd: many clients retry simultaneously.
    • Load amplification: retries increase traffic to a struggling service.
    • Resource usage: more CPU, memory, and connections.

  • Mitigations:

    • Exponential backoff with jitter.
    • Global rate limiting.
    • Circuit breakers (stop sending requests to failing services).
    • Cap total retry time.

Performance Considerations

  • Latency:

    • Retries increase worst-case latency.
    • Need per-request SLA vs reliability trade-off.

  • Throughput:

    • Retries can increase load; must ensure capacity.
    • Use metrics to tune retry counts and delays.

  • Optimization:

    • Use idempotent operations to safely retry.
    • Prefer short timeouts per attempt + multiple retries over long single attempts.
    • Apply retries only at edges (e.g., client → external service), not at every layer.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

flowchart TD
    A[Client Code\n(e.g., call LLM)] --> B[Retry Wrapper]
    B --> C[Attempt Operation]
    C -->|Success| D[Return Result]
    C -->|Failure| E{Retryable Error?}
    E -->|No| F[Return Error]
    E -->|Yes & Attempts Left| G[Compute Backoff Delay]
    G --> H[Sleep/Wait]
    H --> B
    E -->|No Attempts Left| F

Step-by-Step Flow

  1. Initial Attempt

    • Call the operation (e.g., POST /v1/chat/completions).
    • Set a timeout for the call.

  2. Error Handling & Decision

    • If success → return immediately.
    • If failure:
      • Inspect error type / status code.
      • Decide if retryable (e.g., 500, 502, 503, 504, 429, timeouts).

  3. Retry Execution

    • If retryable and attempts remain:
      • Compute delay (e.g., exponential backoff with jitter).
      • Sleep for delay.
      • Increment attempt count.
      • Try again.
    • If non-retryable or attempts exhausted:
      • Return error or trigger fallback (e.g., cached result, degraded mode).

Python-Rust / Implementation Approach

Python Example (Synchronous) with tenacity

from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential, retry_if_exception_type
import requests

class TransientError(Exception):
    pass

def is_retryable_status(status_code: int) -> bool:
    return status_code in {429, 500, 502, 503, 504}

@retry(
    stop=stop_after_attempt(5),
    wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=0.5, min=0.5, max=8),
    retry=retry_if_exception_type(TransientError),
    reraise=True,
)
def call_llm_api(payload: dict) -> dict:
    resp = requests.post("https://api.llm-provider.com/v1/chat/completions",
                         json=payload, timeout=5)
    if not is_retryable_status(resp.status_code) and not resp.ok:
        # Non-retryable error
        resp.raise_for_status()

    if is_retryable_status(resp.status_code):
        # Retryable error
        raise TransientError(f"Status {resp.status_code}")

    return resp.json()

# Usage in a RAG pipeline
def generate_answer(query: str) -> str:
    # ... vector DB call (also wrapped in retry) ...
    payload = {"model": "gpt-4", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": query}]}
    result = call_llm_api(payload)
    return result["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

Python Example (Async) with httpx

import asyncio
import httpx
import random

async def call_service_with_retry(url: str, max_attempts: int = 4):
    attempt = 0
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5.0) as client:
        while True:
            attempt += 1
            try:
                resp = await client.get(url)
                if resp.status_code in {500, 502, 503, 504}:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Retryable status {resp.status_code}")
                resp.raise_for_status()
                return resp.json()
            except Exception as e:
                if attempt >= max_attempts:
                    raise
                backoff = min(2 ** (attempt - 1), 8)
                jitter = random.uniform(0, 0.3 * backoff)
                await asyncio.sleep(backoff + jitter)

Rust Example with reqwest + custom retry

use reqwest::StatusCode;
use std::time::Duration;
use tokio::time::sleep;
use rand::Rng;

fn is_retryable_status(status: StatusCode) -> bool {
    matches!(
        status,
        StatusCode::TOO_MANY_REQUESTS
            | StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR
            | StatusCode::BAD_GATEWAY
            | StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
            | StatusCode::GATEWAY_TIMEOUT
    )
}

pub async fn call_service_with_retry(url: &str, max_attempts: u32) -> Result<String, reqwest::Error> {
    let client = reqwest::Client::new();
    let mut attempt = 0;

    loop {
        attempt += 1;
        let resp = client.get(url).send().await;

        match resp {
            Ok(r) => {
                let status = r.status();
                if !is_retryable_status(status) {
                    return r.text().await;
                }
                if attempt >= max_attempts {
                    return r.text().await;
                }
            }
            Err(e) => {
                // network/timeout error; consider retryable
                if attempt >= max_attempts {
                    return Err(e);
                }
            }
        }

        // exponential backoff with jitter
        let base = 2u64.pow(attempt - 1).min(8);
        let jitter_ms = rand::thread_rng().gen_range(0..(base * 300));
        let delay = Duration::from_millis(base * 1000 + jitter_ms);
        sleep(delay).await;
    }
}

Integration in a Python FastAPI GenAI Service

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

class QueryRequest(BaseModel):
    query: str
    top_k: int = 5

class QueryResponse(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    llm_retries: int
    vector_db_retries: int

# assume call_llm_api and query_vector_db are wrapped with retry decorators
@app.post("/generate-answer", response_model=QueryResponse)
async def generate_answer(req: QueryRequest):
    # vector DB call with internal retries
    docs, vec_retries = await query_vector_db(req.query, req.top_k)
    # LLM call with internal retries
    answer, llm_retries = await call_llm_with_context(req.query, docs)
    return QueryResponse(
        answer=answer,
        llm_retries=llm_retries,
        vector_db_retries=vec_retries,
    )

Advantages

  • Improves reliability:
    • Handles transient network and infrastructure issues.
  • Reduces user-visible errors:
    • Fewer 5xx/timeout errors returned to clients.
  • Critical for distributed systems & GenAI APIs:
    • Cloud LLM providers and vector DBs are network-dependent.
  • Configurable behavior:
    • Can tune for different endpoints/services.

Limitations

  • Increased latency:
    • Worst-case response time can grow significantly.
  • Load amplification:
    • Retries can overload already struggling services.
  • Complexity:
    • Need good error classification, backoff, and idempotency.
  • Not a fix for logic bugs:
    • Retries don’t solve deterministic failures (e.g., bad input, auth issues).

Interview Tips

  • Key points to mention:

    • Distinguish transient vs permanent failures.
    • Emphasize idempotency for safe retries (e.g., GET, PUT, POST with idempotency keys).
    • Talk about exponential backoff with jitter.
    • Mention timeouts and why they must be combined with retry logic.
    • Explain interaction with circuit breakers and rate limiting.

  • Common interview questions:

    • What is retry logic and when would you use it?
    • Which errors should be retried vs not retried?
    • Explain exponential backoff and why jitter is important.
    • How do you avoid thundering herd problems with retries?
    • How would you implement retry logic in Python/Rust?
    • How do you design retries for LLM API calls or vector DB queries?
    • Where should retries be implemented—client, server, or both?

  • Tricky areas:

    • Retrying non-idempotent operations (payments, writes).
    • Multi-layer retries (client + gateway + service) causing too many attempts.
    • Handling 429 (rate limiting): often needs backoff and respecting Retry-After header.

Real-World Example

  • Use Case: Production RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system

  • Scenario:

    • A user queries: “Summarize the latest company policies.”
    • System steps:
      • Step 1: Query vector DB for relevant documents.
        • If the vector DB returns 503 (maintenance), use retry with exponential backoff.
        • If still failing after N attempts, fall back to cached documents or a generic answer.
      • Step 2: Call LLM API with retrieved context.
        • If rate-limited (429), retry with delay respecting provider’s Retry-After.
        • If network timeout, retry a few times with shorter timeouts.
      • Step 3: Return answer to user.

  • Why retry logic is critical here:

    • Keeps the RAG system usable even with intermittent network issues or provider hiccups.
    • Reduces user-facing failures without requiring manual intervention.
    • Combined with metrics (retries per request), it helps monitor provider stability and tune retry policies.
Q179.WHAT ARE OBSERVABILITY PRACTICES? [Input Token: 705 | Output Token: 3750] +

Topic Overview

  • Definition:
    Observability practices are a set of methods, tools, and processes used to understand the internal state of a system (services, ML pipelines, LLM infra) based on its external outputs—primarily logs, metrics, traces, and events.

  • Importance in AI/ML/GenAI interviews:

    • Critical for debugging ML/LLM pipelines in production (data drift, model degradation, latency spikes).
    • Enables monitoring model quality, prompt/response health, and RAG pipeline performance.
    • Key for SLOs/SLAs in ML APIs and LLM inference services.

  • Importance in Python/Rust backend interviews:

    • Core to designing reliable microservices and low-latency APIs.
    • Shows understanding of production-readiness, not just code.
    • Often a must-have in system design and platform engineering discussions.

Architecture / Concept Explanation

Observability is typically broken into three pillars (plus ML/LLM-specific signals):

  • Logs

    • Textual, structured records of events.
    • Examples: request logs, error logs, feature extraction logs, LLM prompts/responses (with redaction).

  • Metrics

    • Numeric time-series data.
    • Examples: QPS, latency, error rate, token usage, GPU utilization, model accuracy over time.

  • Traces

    • End-to-end request flows across services.
    • Examples: trace of a RAG request from API → auth → vector DB → LLM → response.

  • ML/LLM-specific signals

    • Model performance metrics (AUC, BLEU, toxicity scores).
    • Data quality metrics (missing values, drift).
    • LLM-specific: hallucination rate, retrieval hit-rate, prompt token count, cost per request.

Technical Specifications

Components

  • Instrumentation

    • Python/Rust code that emits logs, metrics, and traces.
    • OpenTelemetry SDKs, custom middleware, decorators.

  • Collection / Agent

    • Sidecar/daemon that collects telemetry and ships to backend.
    • Examples: otel-collector, Datadog agent, Prometheus node exporter.

  • Storage / Backend

    • Logs: Elasticsearch, Loki, OpenSearch.
    • Metrics: Prometheus, M3, VictoriaMetrics.
    • Traces: Jaeger, Tempo, Zipkin, Honeycomb.
    • ML/LLM monitoring: Arize, WhyLabs, Evidently, Weights & Biases.

  • Visualization / Alerting

    • Grafana, Kibana, Datadog, New Relic, custom dashboards.
    • Alerting via PagerDuty, Slack, email, Opsgenie.

  • ML/LLM-specific monitoring layer

    • Model registry, experiment tracking (MLflow, W&B).
    • RAG metrics, prompt metrics, evaluation dashboards.

Technologies Used

  • Python

    • Web: FastAPI, Flask, Django.
    • Telemetry: opentelemetry-sdk, structlog, loguru, prometheus_client.
    • ML/LLM: PyTorch, TensorFlow, LangChain, LlamaIndex, MLflow, W&B.

  • Rust

    • Web: Axum, Actix-web, Warp.
    • Telemetry: tracing, tracing-subscriber, opentelemetry, metrics crates.
    • Performance-critical inference gateways, tokenizers, vector ops.

  • Infra

    • Kubernetes, Docker, Helm.
    • Ingress + service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) with telemetry.
    • CI/CD: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Argo CD.

Data Flow and Processing Stages

  • Logs

    • Service emits structured logs → agent/sidecar → log backend → indexed → searchable in dashboards.

  • Metrics

    • Service exposes /metrics endpoint (Prometheus format) → Prometheus scrapes → stores time-series → Grafana dashboards → alerts on rules.

  • Traces

    • Services propagate trace-id via HTTP headers → spans emitted per operation → collector → trace backend → visualization of end-to-end latency.

  • ML/LLM-specific

    • Inference service logs:
      • Input metadata (not raw PII), model version, features, prompt type.
      • Output metrics: score, latency, evaluation labels, safety flags.
    • Periodic batch jobs compute:
      • Drift, performance degradation, retrieval hit-rate, hallucination rate.

API Endpoints and Contracts (Example)

For a RAG-based LLM service:

  • POST /v1/chat
    • Request:
      {
  "user_id": "123",
  "session_id": "abc",
  "query": "How does observability work?",
  "top_k": 5
}
    • Response:
      {
  "answer": "...",
  "latency_ms": 220,
  "model_version": "llm-v2.1",
  "retrieval_hit_rate": 0.8,
  "trace_id": "9f2e..."
}
  • Telemetry contracts:
    • All requests must include:
      • X-Request-ID, X-Trace-ID headers.
    • Service logs must include:
      • request_id, trace_id, user_id (if allowed), model_version, status, latency_ms.

Model Lifecycle & Observability

  • Training

    • Log training metrics (loss, accuracy, token-per-second).
    • Track experiments (hyperparams, datasets, code version).
    • Store artifacts in model registry.

  • Evaluation

    • Offline eval metrics per model version.
    • LLM evals: automatic metrics + human feedback (RLHF-like labels).

  • Deployment

    • Canary or shadow deployments.
    • Monitor differences between old vs new model metrics.

  • Monitoring

    • Production metrics:
      • Latency, throughput, error rate.
      • Data drift, prediction drift.
      • LLM: prompt types, response length, safety violations.

  • Feedback Loop

    • Use telemetry to:
      • Trigger retraining.
      • Adjust prompts/templates.
      • Tune retrieval parameters (top_k, filters).

Scalability Considerations

  • High cardinality metrics:
    • Avoid labels like user_id in metrics; use them in logs instead.
  • Sampling:
    • Trace sampling (e.g., keep 1–10% of traces).
    • Log sampling for high-traffic endpoints.
  • Sharding / Retention
    • Short retention for high-volume logs, longer for aggregations.
  • Multi-tenant ML/LLM services
    • Tag telemetry with tenant_id, model_id, deployment_id.

Performance Considerations

  • Overhead

    • Asynchronous logging.
    • Non-blocking metrics emission.
    • Batching telemetry to the collector.

  • Latency

    • Avoid heavy synchronous logging in hot paths.
    • Use background tasks for heavy telemetry (e.g., full prompt/response logging with redaction).

  • Cost

    • Control log volume via log levels and sampling.
    • Downsample metrics where possible.

Diagram (MANDATORY)

    subgraph Client
        U[User / App]
    end

    subgraph API["Python/Rust API (FastAPI/Axum)"]
        H[HTTP Handler]
        I[Instrumentation\n(OpenTelemetry / tracing)]
    end

    subgraph ML["ML / LLM Layer"]
        P[Preprocessing\nFeature/Payload]
        M[Model / LLM Inference]
        RAG[RAG Retrieval\n(Vector DB)]
    end

    subgraph Telemetry["Observability Stack"]
        L[Logs Backend\n(ELK / Loki)]
        Me[Metrics Backend\n(Prometheus)]
        T[Traces Backend\n(Jaeger / Tempo)]
        D[Dashboards & Alerts\n(Grafana / Datadog)]
    end

    U -->|Request| H

    H --> P --> RAG --> M --> H
    H -->|Response| U

    I -->|Logs| L
